column1: #IMPORTANT: COUNTRY NAMES MAY NOT BE TOO LONG

column2: The Jalayirids were a Mongol tribe that supported the Il-Khan Hülegü's rise to power and eventually provided the successors to the Il-Khan dynasty as rulers of Iraq and Azerbaijan. A Jalayirid dynasty made its capital at Baghdad (1336-1432). Hasan Buzurg, founder of the dynasty, had served as governor of Anatolia (Rum) under the Il-Khan Abu Sa'id (reigned 1317-35). Following the death of Abu Sa'id, Hasan Buzurg competed for real control of the empire with his rival, the Chupanid amir Hasan Kücük ("the Small," so designated to distinguish him from Hasan Buzurg, "the Great"), they set up rival khanates. Soon afterward the empire broke down into local dynasties in Anatolia, Iran, Azerbaijan, Georgia, and Armenia. Hasan Buzurg had, meanwhile, established his line in Baghdad, from which he conducted his agitation against the Chupanids. His son The most prominent of the Jalayirids, Sheikh Uways (1356-74) finally wrested control of Azerbaijan from the Süldüz Chupanids in 1360, creating a polity based on Arabian Iraq and Azerbaijan. He enlarged Jalayirid domains by seizing Azerbaijan (1360) and placing the Mozaffarid principality of Fars under his suzerainty (1361-64). In addition to this and other military exploits, he fostered trade and commerce and won renown as patron of poetry, painting, and calligraphy. He also undertook a number of architectural projects in Baghdad. The dynasty, however, was beset by the westward migrations and invasions of various Turkic and Mongol tribes. The khans of the Golden Horde, successors of Batu, unsuccessfully attempted the conquest of Azerbaijan in 1356-59. The later Jalayirids, however, dissipated their energies in fruitless foreign adventures and fratricidal struggles. During the reign of Sultan Ahmad Jalayir (1382-1410), Timur (Timur Barlas, or Tamerlane), a new conqueror from Central Asia, took Baghdad and Tikrit in 1393. Forcing Sultan Ahmad to leave Baghdad and seek the protection of the Mamluks of Egypt until Timur's death in 1405. Although Sultan Ahmad was able to reoccupy his capital briefly, Timur again besieged and sacked Baghdad in 1401, dealing it a blow from which it did not recover until modern times. Timurid administration in Arabian Iraq, first under Timur and later under his grandson Abu Bakr, was sporadic and short-lived: they controlled the area during the years 1393-94, 1401-02, and 1403-05. After Timur's death, Sultan Ahmad Jalayir regained Baghdad for a time, but in 1410 he was killed in a dispute with his former ally, Kara Yusuf (1389-1420), chief of the Kara Koyunlu (Black Sheep) Turkmen tribal confederation from eastern Anatolia, who had just driven the Timurids out of Azerbaijan. The remnants of the Jalayirid dynasty were pushed south to Al-Hillah, Wasit, and Basra. They were finally extinguished by the Kara Koyunlu in 1432.

Of the medieval centralized state systems of Somali history, Adal was prominent. During the sixteenth century, its borders extended from Zeila, its capital, through the fertile valleys of the Jijiga and the Harer plateau to the Ethiopian highlands. Adal was founded by the former people of Ifat, a sultanate destroyed by the Ethiopians in the 14th century. Holding true to this legacy, Adal is famous for its conflicts with the expansionist Ethiopians. Eventually, this would prove to be its undoing.

Aden's strategic location and its importance as a commercial center long made it a coveted conquest for its rapacious neighbors. Muslim Arabs held the region from the 7th to the 16th centuries. The Portuguese, desiring more bases for further exploration and trade in the Indian Ocean, failed in an attempt to capture it in 1513, but in 1538 it fell to the Ottoman Empire. At the end of the 18th century Aden's importance as a strategic post grew as a result of British policy to contain French expansion in the region.

Bâbur (Arab for Tiger), a descendant of Tamerlane and Genghis Khan, used Kabul as the base for his conquest of India and the establishment of the Mughal Empire in the early 16th century. In the 18th century the Persian ruler, Nadir Shah, extended his rule to the North of the Hindu Kush. The first Afghan state in the modern sense arose after Nadir's death in 1747 under his lieutenant Ahmad Shah - an Afghan tribal leader who forged a united state covering most of present-day Afghanistan. His dynasty gave the Afghans a name (Durrani) that they themselves frequently use.

Ahmadnagar was one of several sultanates that was formed during the collapse of the Bahmani Sultanate. Constantly at war with its neighbors, Ahmadnagar would remain independent until conqued by Mughal Shah Jahan in 1636.

Ajuuraan was a powerful Somali empire that existed between the 14th and 17th centuries.  The Ajuuraans managed to unify many of the querulous Somali tribes, creating a strong centralized administration. Having weathered the Oromo invasions and the dethronement of its most important vassals in Mogadishu, the empire would eventually collapse because of the whims of its later Imams would. Wracked by numerous rebellions, Ajuuraan was only a shell of a state by the turn of the 18th century.

The Aq Qoyunlu ('White Sheep') were a Turkmen tribal federation that ruled northern Iraq, Azerbaijan and eastern Anatolia. In constant tension with the Ottomans and lesser Turkish principalities in Anatolia, as well as their cousins to the south - the Qara Qoyunlu ('Black Sheep') - the Aq Qoyunlu first sided with Timur and then attacked his successors. Though for a time their lands grew to include modern-day Iraq and most of Persia, they finally succumbed to the Shi'a heretics under the great Ismail Safavid, their last territories conquered by the Ottomans in the early 16th century.

Throughout its history, the autochthonous populations of Albania, have been forced to retreat into the mountains by various invaders. In the XIVth century they were occupied by the Serbs and, after a short time of autonomy, by the Ottomans in the XVth century. In the first half of the XVth century, the sons of a local chief were brought to the Sultan as hostages to ensure their father's good behavior. One of the sons converted to Islam, performed well in the Ottoman war school and on the battlefield and was awarded by the name of Iskander Bey ('Lord Alexander'). This name, known as Skanderberg in Albania, was to be the flag of a renewed resistance when he returned to his country home and reconverted to Christianity. Supported by three Italian states, his efforts gained Albania's independence. Following his death, a twelve year struggle ensued where by Albania eventually succumbed to the might of the Muslims. Albania became an Ottoman province, providing fierce soldiers and many capable administrators.

After the 'Reconquista', many of the Moors expelled from Granada in 1492 settled in the city of Al-jaza'ir (Algiers). Trying to stem their incessant piracy, the Spanish occupied the island of Peñon in the Bay of Algiers, but they were driven out when Turkish corsair Barbarossa captured Algiers for the Ottoman Empire in 1529. Algiers became an important base for the Muslim fleet that preyed upon Christian commerce in the Mediterranean. Under the Ottomans the city's population reached 100,000. The ruling Turkish officials in Algeria, the Deys of Algiers, finally made themselves virtually independent of Istanbul in the 18th and 19th century.

The Almohad dynasty, founded in the 12th century by Ibn Tumart, was a Berber Muslim empire that rose to power in North Africa and Al-Andalus (Moorish Iberia). Known for their strict adherence to a puritanical form of Islam, the Almohads overthrew the Almoravid dynasty in 1147 and established their capital in Marrakesh. Under the leadership of Abd al-Mu'min, they expanded their territory significantly, reaching their zenith in the late 12th and early 13th centuries. The dynasty is noted for its cultural and intellectual contributions, including the works of philosophers like Ibn Rushd (Averroes). However, their power began to decline after the decisive defeat at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212, leading to the eventual fall of their empire by 1269.

The Altmark ('Old March') is an historic region in northern Saxony. It is considered the cradle of the March of Brandenburg and, by extension, the Prussian state, earning it the nickname 'the Cradle of Prussia.' This region is characterized by its picturesque medieval towns and villages, some of which date back over a thousand years. The Altmark played a significant role in the early development of Brandenburg and later Prussia, contributing greatly to her rise as a great power.

Armagnac, an historic region in southwestern France, is renowned for its production of the world's oldest brandy, dating back to the 13th century. Located in Gascony, Armagnac was originally part of the duchy of Gascony and became an autonomous political unit in the 10th century. The region gained strategic importance during the Hundred Years' War, serving as a buffer zone between French and English-controlled territories in Aquitaine, and being the powerbase of Bernard VII of Armagnac - the original leader of the pro-royalist, anti-Burgundian party (the Armagnacs). Its cultural contributions are significant, including the production of its famous brandy, which was initially used for medicinal purposes and later became a prized commodity.

Armenia Minor or Little Armenia was born from a double invasion. In 1021, the Byzantine Empire annexed the Vaspurakan Kingdom, in Greater Armenia, and supported the migration of Armenians across the empire, to serve as traders and administrators. Half a century later, the area was invaded by Seljuk Turks, prompting many of the remaining Armenians to flee. A group of Armenians, led by the Prince Reupen, settled in 1080 in Cilicia where some Armenian communities already existed. They created the kingdom of Armenia Minor (Little Armenia). They lasted in the area, allied to the Byzantine Empire and to the new Crusader States in the Holy Land, until they were conquered by the Mameluks in 1375.

Anhalt, an historic region in central Germany, was once a duchy located between the Harz Mountains and the River Elbe. It was ruled by the House of Ascania and became a principality in 1218. Over the centuries, Anhalt experienced numerous divisions and reunifications, resulting in various principalities such as Anhalt-Dessau, Anhalt-Bernburg, and Anhalt-Zerbst. The region played a significant role in the power-politics of the Holy Roman Empire, and later became part of the German Empire in 1871.

Anjou, in the lower Loire Valley of northwestern France, was originally organized as the Civitas Andegavensis during the Gallo-Roman period. It later became the county of Anjou and, in 1360, was elevated to a duchy. Anjou was ruled by the powerful Angevin dynasty, scions of which went on to rule Jerusalem, Naples, Hungary and England - whose latter branch became known as the Plantagenets. From its influential capital Angers, it played a crucial role in medieval European politics, particularly during the expansion of the Angevin Empire (1154-1214) under Henry II and his sons. Anjou later became an external territory of Provence, finally being annexed to the French crown in 1480.

'Annam' is a Chinese name meaning 'Pacified South'. It was given by the Chinese after their conquest in 111 B.C. and the land kept it until the inhabitants drove out the Chinese in 939. The land was then renamed Dai Co Viet and later Dai Viet. It remained independent but always under the threat of its powerful northern neighbour. It even knew a short period of Chinese occupation from 1407-1428. Perpetually unstable, by 1558, Dai Viet was divided between two great families, the Trinh, in the north in Tonkin (present-day Hanoi) and the Nguyens in the center and south with their capital in Hue. The civil war was interspersed with conflicts involving the neighboring kingdoms of Champa and Cambodia. In 1802, the Nguyen family eventually united both Tonkin-Dai Viet and Annam-Dai Vie and the country was renamed as Vietnam.

The Navaho are a composite tribal group consisting of over 50 separate clans. In the 17th century they occupied the region between the San Juan and Little Colorado rivers in Northeast Arizona, but they ranged far outside that territory. The were a predatory tribe who, often in alliance with the Apache, constantly raided the Pueblo and later the Spanish and Mexican settlements of New Mexico.

Apulia, also known as Puglia, was originally inhabited by the Iapygians, and became a significant part of Magna Graecia when Greek settlers established colonies along its coast in the 8th century BC. The region was later conquered by the Romans in the 4th century BC, who left behind numerous archaeological sites. Throughout the Middle Ages, Apulia was ruled by various powers, including the Goths, Lombards, Byzantines, and Normans, each leaving their mark on its culture and architecture.

Aquileia, founded by the Romans in 181 BC, was a prominent city located at the head of the Adriatic Sea in what is now northern Italy. It served as a strategic military outpost and a major commercial hub, facilitating trade between the Roman Empire and northern Europe. By the 2nd century AD, Aquileia had grown into one of the largest cities of the Roman Empire, with a population of around 100,000. The city was also a significant center for early Christianity and played a crucial role in the spread of the religion throughout the Roman Empire, with the powerful Patriarchate of Aquileia existing from the 4th century until its dissolution in 1751. Despite being sacked by Attila the Hun in 452 AD, Aquileia's well-preserved basilica, walls and monuments continue to offer valuable insights into Roman urban life and early Christian history.

The name Guyenne first became widespread with the Treaty of Paris (1259) between Louis IX of France and Henry III of England. By this treaty Louis IX accepted Henry III as his vassal for Guyenne and also for Gascony, which the English King had previously held in fief. (England had received both Aquitaine and Gascony in the 12th century through Henry II's marriage to Eleanor of Aquitaine.) Guyenne was retaken by the French at the beginning of the Hundred Years' War but the Treaty of Brétigny in 1360 restored it with the whole of the old Aquitaine to the English. In the final stages of the Hundred Years' War France took back all these areas. The last attempt by the English to retake the territory was repulsed at the Battle of Castillon in 1453. Louis XI gave the duchy to his brother Charles in 1469, but after the latter's death in 1472 it once more became a Crown holding.

The Hedjaz is the eastern area of the Arabian Peninsula, along the Red Sea.  It is famous for the two holy cities of Medina and Mecca. In 1258, after the fall of the Caliphate in Bagdad, the land fell under the control of the Egyptian Mameluks. In 1517, this sovereignty went to the Turkish Ottomans. However, the local power was actually still in the hands of the Sharifs of Mecca whose continuous dynasty began in the XIIth century. These sharifs would defend the Holy Cities against Wahhabist fundamentalists in the early XIXth century, and one century later, would lead the revolt against the Ottomans.

The Crown of Aragon was created in 1137 when the Count of Barcelona, Ramon Berenguer, married Peronella of Aragon when she was only 2 years old. The two nations became united and began their drive to the south to expel the Moors from Spain, conquering Valencia and the Balearic Islands. In 1412 Martí l'Humà, the last Catalan King of the Barcelona dynasty died heirless and the nobles gathered to elect Ferran I d'Antequera, putting a Castillian King on the Aragonese throne for the first time in history in spite of strong Catalan opposition. John II of Aragon (1458–79), countered residual Catalan resistance by arranging for his heir, Ferdinand, to marry the heiress of Henry IV of Castile - Isabella. In 1479, upon John II's death, the kingdoms of Aragon and Castile were finally united to form the kingdom of Spain.

Arakan, or Rakhine, extends along the Bay of Bengal and lies at the foot of the Arakan Yoma mountain range. The Arakanese were of Burmese heritage with Indian and Muslim influences. The region was geographically isolated and in the 15th century was the seat of a powerful kingdom. Their capital was a strongly fortified city called Mrohaung. The Arakanese sold rice and slaves to the Dutch and the Portuguese, allying with the latter when the Mughal Empire threatened their freedom and the rich trade. The Arakanese ceased to be a power in 1666 when the Mughals defeated them in a decisive battle. In 1783 they were finally absorbed into Burma. Part of their cultural legacy was the construction of a colossal image of Buddha.

Dating back to the 6th century B.C, Armenia is one of the oldest nations in the world and also reckoned as the oldest Christian state. Armenia was conquered and ruled in turn by Alexander the Great, Syria, Rome and Persia until it could enjoy a period of autonomy under native rulers 886-1046. Then it was reconquered by the Byzantines, who promptly lost it to the Seljuk Turks following the Byzantine defeat at the battle of Manzikert in 1071. In the late 14th century the Mongol conqueror Timur (Tamerlane) seized Greater Armenia and massacred a large part of the population. After Timur's death in 1405 the Ottoman Turks whom Timur had crushed in 1402 invaded Armenia, and by the beginning of the 16th century held all of it. Under Ottoman rule the Armenians, although often persecuted and always discriminated against because of their religion, nevertheless acquired a vital economic role. Constantinople and all other large cities of the Ottoman Empire had quarters with Armenian merchants and financiers.

The Kingdom of Arles, also known as the Second Kingdom of Burgundy, was established in 933 through the merger of the kingdoms of Burgundy and Provence under the Welf King Rudolf II. It became a significant realm within the Holy Roman Empire, stretching from the Mediterranean Sea to the Rhine, encompassing parts of modern-day France, Italy, and Switzerland. The kingdom was known for its strategic importance and cultural influence during the High Middle Ages. However, by the mid-13th century, it had lost much of its political relevance and was eventually absorbed into the Holy Roman Empire. Thereafter, Arles existed purely as a vague ceremonial entity, and - like Italy and Lotharingia - was a crown held by the Emperor personally.

Artois, an historic region in northern France, has a rich history dating back to Roman times when it was inhabited by the Atrebates. It became a feudal county in the Middle Ages and was annexed by the County of Flanders before coming under direct French royal control in 1180 as part of a dowry. The region experienced periods of Burgundian and Habsburg rule before being permanently integrated into France in 1659 following the Treaty of the Pyrenees. Artois played a significant role in European history, particularly during the Hundred Years' War and the later Franco-Spanish conflicts. Its capital, Arras, is noted for its beautiful Flemish Baroque architecture.

Sometime prior to the 13th century, Akani tribes migrated into the forests of present-day Ghana, establishing small states in the hilly country near modern Kumasi. By the late 17th century the states had been welded together by the Oyoko clan into the Ashanti confederation, with its capital at Kumasi and the Oyoko chieftain as king. After subduing various neighboring states the confederation eventually came into conflict with British settlers on the coast, although treaties of friendship were negotiated in 1817 and 1820.

Assam is a nation with a long and rich history, situated high above the Ganges delta in the plateaus surrounding the mighty Bramhaputra river and the surrounding hilly jungles. The Kings of Kamarupa ruled this isolated area until 1228 when the Ahom Kings usurped power in this Hindu Kingdom. Playing as Assam, your traditional enemies are the Burmese, who reside in the southeast and have not yet grown strong enough to threaten you while your larger neighbors the Bengalis seem to have their attention fixed on the oncoming Islamic threat. Will you break your isolation and ally with the Muslims against your old foes, or will you follow history and remain a Hindu stronghold until falling to the Burmese in 1819?

The Astrakhan Khanate was a splinter of the Golden Horde that existed as an independent state from 1459 to 1556, when it was conquered by Ivan the Terrible and incorporated into Russia. In 1608 it was conquered by the Kalmyks, migrating west from their homeland in Dzungaria. The Kalmyk Khanate lasted until 1771, when it was finally reclaimed by Russia.

Asturias, located in the northwestern part of Spain, has been inhabited since the Paleolithic era, with evidence of early human settlements in its numerous caves. The region became a significant part of the Roman Empire and later emerged as the Kingdom of Asturias in 718 AD, founded by the Visigothic nobleman Pelagius. This kingdom played a crucial role in the Christian Reconquista against the Moors. Asturias is known for its rugged landscapes, including the Cantabrian Mountains, and its cultural heritage, which includes traditional music, dance, and cuisine.

The Duchy of Athens was created after the Fourth Crusade and the creation of the Latin Empire of Constantinople in 1204. Othon de la Roche , a French lord and templar from Besançon in Franche-Comté, became the first megaskyr (great lord) of Athens and Thebes. The land enjoyed great prosperity under his rule and that of his successors. Many French nobles settled in Greece, bringing some of their institutions, which led them to clash with their Greek neighbors. In 1311, the Duke of Athens rented a mercenary troop from Catalonia in order to fight the ruler of Epirus. He foolishly refused to pay them and they revolted, capturing the duchy and offering it to the House of Aragon. Catalan and Aragonese nobles settled in the area and the Duchy expanded to the north. In 1388, the Duchy was conquered by a Florentine noble, Nerio I Acciajuoli. Numerous Florentine merchants established themselves in Athens. Christian rule was to end in 1458 when the Ottomans seized the Acropolis beginning four centuries of Turkish occupation and the city's slow decline. Venice, which had held Athens from 1394 to 1402, took it again shortly in 1466 and besieged it in 1687. It is during this siege that the Parthenon was blown out when a powder reserve exploded.

The Samudera Pasai Sultanate, also known as Samudera or Pasai or Samudera Darussalam or Pacem, was a Muslim kingdom on the north coast of Sumatra from the 13th to the 16th centuries. Little evidence has been left to allow for historical study of the kingdom. The kingdom was believed to have been founded by Merah Silu, who later converted to Islam and adopted the name Malik ul Salih, in the year 1267 CE. After the 1521 Portuguese invasion, the garrison evacuated Pasai in 1524 and the first Sultan of Aceh, Ali Mughayat Syah, annexed the territory.

Auvergne was a part of the Roman province of Aquitaine. When Aquitaine passed to the English in 1154 through the marriage of Eleanor of Aquitaine with Henry II Plantagenet, the count of Auvergne became a vassal of the English king. In the 14th century the old county was divided into a dauphiné and a duchy, the latter given to duke Jean, son of king John II of France. The duchy eventually descended to Charles, the famous constable of France, who was able to unite duchy and dauphiné when he became Duke de Bourbon in 1503. But these Bourbon domains were confiscated by King Francis I after the constable's treason, and was to remain a crown holding.

The city of Ayutthaya was founded by Phya U-Thong in 1350. After consolidating his power he proclaimed himself king Ramathibodi I. Over the next 80 years the Ayutthayans expanded their territory, and in 1431 they captured Angkor - capital of the Khmer empire. The Ayutthayan kings adopted Khmer cultural influences and assumed the title devaraja, or god-king. The city of Ayutthaya became one of the wealthiest cities in the known world. By the 18th century the Ayutthayans had established trade with the Portuguese and diplomatic relations with several other western countries. In 1767 the Burmese captured Ayutthaya, although she regained her independence shortly thereafter.

The Ayyubid dynasty, founded by the legendary Saladin in 1171, was a Sunni Muslim dynasty of Kurdish origin that ruled over Egypt, Syria, Yemen, and parts of Iraq and the Levant during the 12th and 13th centuries. Saladin, originally serving under the Zengid rulers, rose to prominence by uniting Muslim forces against the Crusaders and displacing the Fatimid Caliphate in Egypt. The Ayyubids are renowned for their military prowess, architectural achievements, and the establishment of madrasahs (religious schools) in Egypt and Jerusalem. Despite internal family disputes and eventual decline, the Ayyubid legacy persisted in some regions until the mid-14th century.

The Aztecs settled in the Mexico valley toward the end of the XIIth century. Originally they came from the north and were a poor nomadic tribe. They founded their capital Tenochtitlán around 1325, on an island of the Lake Texcoco.  When they first settled at their capital, the Aztecs paid tributes to the surrounding tribes and used their city in the middle of swamps as a refuge to prevent destruction. Eventually through alliances, by conquests and many intrigues they managed to rise into a powerful regional power in the XVth and early XVIth centuries. They subjugated most of the peoples around Mexico and rewrote their own history to create a myth about their destiny to rule over all the surrounding people and the necessity of make sacrifices to the Sun, a divinity that had made them so powerful. Neighboring peoples, such as the Tlaxcalans were happy to use the opportunity of the Spaniards arrival to shake free of Aztec domination. In time, the Spaniards would conquer those minor states, as well.

Baden, a geographical area in Germany, along the Rhine, was historically fragmented into many petty margraviates and ecclesiastical states. The margraviate of Bade, created in the Holy Roman Empire in the XIIth century was often divided in different branches until its short unification under Christopher I of Baden-Baden in the early XVIth century. Religious strife would split it again, this time into a Catholic state and a Lutheran state, the remaining lands went to the Habsburgs and the Rhenish Palatinate. In 1771, Baden was reunited again under a branch of the house of Zähringen. Charles Frederick of Baden became an Elector of the Holy Roman Empire in 1803 and joined the Confederation of the Rhine in 1806, gaining the title of grand duke. With Napoleon's help, he became the master of the entire state of Baden in 1810 which would remain in the hands of his descendants even after the Vienna Congress.

The Balearic Islands, an archipelago in the western Mediterranean Sea, were initially inhabited by the prehistoric Talayotic people. The islands later came under the influence of Carthage in the 6th century BC, and subsequently Rome from around 120 BC. Following the fall of the Roman Empire, the islands experienced a series of conquests by the Vandals, Byzantines, and Moors. In the 13th century, they were incorporated into the Kingdom of Aragon and later became part of Spain.

The Baluchistan is a desert area covered by many hills and mountains. The nomadic Baluchi arrived in the XIth century, fleeing from Mongol migrations. They lived in tribes, in loose confederations. The area became famous when Persian intellectuals, architects, scientists, poets, theologists arrived in the XIIIth century fleeing the Arab invasion in Persia. Many settled before the creation of the Mughal Empire. The Baluchi tribes managed to unite to create the Kalat Kingdom in the XVIIth century which would remain independent until the XIXth century.

Prior to the European conquest of Africa the Bantu tribes were either pastoral and warlike or agricultural and pacifist. There were some highly developed Bantu states including Buganda in present-day Uganda. Possibly as a reaction to the European encroachments, several additional Bantu states developed in the 19th century, notably the Zulu and the Sotho. Other well-known Bantu tribes include the Ndebele (Matabele) and the Shona.

The Duchy of Bavaria was given to the Wittelsbach family, by the Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa in 1180. The duchy expanded during the following centuries, especially during the reign of the Emperor Louis IV of Bavaria who gained Brandenburg, Holland, Zeeland, Tyrol, amongst other territories. At his death, the lands are divided among his sons and it is only in 1502 that Albert II managed to reunite Bavaria in the single biggest possession next to the Habsburg's lands in the Empire. With the Reformation, Bavaria remained staunchly Catholic and played a major role in the Thirty Years War. The Duke of Bavaria was rewarded with the title of Elector that had been taken from the rebellious Palatinate. Bavaria was to remain at the center of most of European wars either on the Austrian side or the French one. During the Wars of the French Revolution, Bavaria was an ally of France and was stylized the Kingdom of Bavaria by Napoleon, a title the country would keep until 1871.

Béarn, an historic province in southwestern France, nestled in the Pyrenees, boasts a rich and varied history. Originally inhabited by the Venarni tribe, it became part of the Roman province of Aquitania. Over the centuries, Béarn maintained a degree of autonomy, even as it was absorbed into the Kingdom of France in 1620. Its capital shifted from Beneharnum to Morlaàs, Orthez, and finally Pau. Known for its pastoral traditions and resilient spirit, Béarn has preserved its unique cultural identity, symbolized by its iconic flag featuring two red cows on a golden field.

Although the Majapahit Empire, in Java, noted in 1365 the Brunei was one among their hundred vassals, the area was actually a little more than a trading post. With the fall of the Majapahit Empire, Brunei began to rise, extending on the north coast of Borneo and became a native Sultanate in 1520. It has been said that at one time the sultan controlled nearly all of Borneo, but during the XVIIIth century the sultanate was already declining, faced with the competition of the European powers. By the XIXth, century Brunei had become a pirates' nest.

The Kingdom of Benin was founded in the XIIIth century and had its 'Golden Age' between the XIVth and the XVIIth centuries. Power originally belonged to a council of chiefs but overtime was subsumed by the monarchy, to a single king, the Oba. The Oba ruled with the help of a sophisticated bureaucracy when the kingdom became an empire. In the late XVth century, Benin began to trade ivory, pelts, slaves and clothes, to Portugal, for weapons, clothes and spyglasses. In the XVIth century, the Oba sent a priest in Portugal and requested missionaries. The rulers of both nations exchanged gifts. Overtime, the empire entered into decline under the pressure of the Yorubas on the west, the Nupes on the north and the British on the coast. The kingdom's exports had been reduced only to palm oil when in the late XIXth century, a British expedition destroyed the capital.

Bengal was a Muslim kingdom from late XIIth century, remaining independent from the neighboring kingdoms of Delhi and Bihar. The kingdom extended its rule over parts of Bihar and Assam in the XVIth century, the same period that it first encountered Portuguese traders. It was conquered by the Mughal Empire in 1576 and it is only in the XVIIIth century that a new dynasty emerged as Mughal power declined. During the XVIIIth century, the British were given privileges by the Mughal Emperors and the British East India Company put a heavy pressure on Bengal. The British seized Bengal in between 1757 and 1764

Bijapur was one of several sultanates founded upon the demise of the Bahmani sultanate.  Founded by Yusuf Adil Shah in 1490, the sultanate's existence was always in peril. Bounded by rival sultanates (Ahmadnagar, Bidar, and Golconda) as well as the Vijayanagar Empire, the Shiite state formed no lasting alliances. Despite its disadvantages, the sultanate would go on to conquer most of the Deccan plateau, as well as much of what had constituted the northern provinces of the Vijayanagar Empire.  Eventually, Adil Shah dynasty met its end by the swords of Mughal armies under Aurangzeb.

Banjar was originally part of the powerful Majapahit Empire, but gained self-rule after the empire fell apart in the late 15th century. The Kingdom converted to Islam in the 17th century, and became a power in Borneo, controlling most of the southern region of the island. Its acceptance of the Dutch, however, would prove to be its downfall, as the Dutch formally integrated Banjar into the Dutch East Indies in the late 19th century.

Bolivia, a landlocked country in west-central South America, has a rich and tumultuous history. It was once the center of the ancient Tiwanaku Empire and later became part of the Inca Empire in the 15th century. Following the Spanish conquest in the early 16th century, Bolivia was incorporated into the Viceroyalty of Peru, providing immense wealth to Spain through its vast silver minining operation at Potosí. The country gained independence in 1825, named after the revolutionary liberator Simón Bolívar.

The legendary founders of Bohemia, or Cechy, were Premysl and the princess Libuse of the Czechs, who was told to marry a man she would see building a threshold (Praha) in the middle of the forest. Bohemia became a part of the Holy Roman Empire in 950 but kept internal freedom and still enjoyed the status of kingdom inside the Empire. The Golden Age of Bohemia came with the reign of the Emperor Charles IV (1346-78) who made Praha his residence. Bohemia saw the first serious attempt of religious reformation with the Hussite wars in 1434. The Habsburgs acquired the throne of Bohemia in 1526, beginning the process of assimilation that would end with the Thirty Years War and the full annexation of Bohemia to the lands of Austria.

Bone was a pagan kingdom based at Watampone in the south-west of the island of Sulawesi. It remained fairly isolated and resisted conversion for centuries, but traded and fought with neighbouring peoples like the Luwu and Wajo. In 1611, Bone was invaded by armies of the powerful Gowa (Makassar) sultanate to the south, whose sultan forced the king of Bone to convert to Islam. This led to an era of prosperity for Bone but also saw the loss of her independence, and subsequently the island kingdom would be a vassal of Gowa, (briefly) the British, and then the Dutch.

Bornu, an historical kingdom and emirate in northeastern Nigeria, originally served as the southernmost province of the Kanem Empire, which reached its zenith in the 12th and 13th centuries. As Kanem's power waned in the late 14th century, Bornu emerged as a dominant force, eventually recapturing and incorporating Kanem into the reconstituted Kanem-Bornu Empire in the early 16th century. The empire flourished under rulers like Mai Idris Alawma, who reigned from around 1571 to 1603. Despite facing challenges, including the Fulani jihad in 1808 and subsequent conflicts, Bornu maintained its significance until the late 19th century.

In the early 11th century the Eastern Roman Empire lost its grip on Bosnia, which became a vassal state of Hungary. During the 12th century the rulers of Bosnia started acting independently, which caused subsequent Hungarian raids of the country. The next century saw Bosnia gaining independence from Hungary and enter a period of great territorial expansion. However, In 1419 Bosnia had once more entered a period of decline. Hungarians to the north and the west of the country wanted to regain territories that they had lost during the reign of Bosnian king Tvrtko I, while the Ottoman Empire was rapidly expanding to the east and south of the country. Between 1448 and 1463 Bosnia was swallowed up piecemeal by the Muslim behemoth.
The counts (later dukes) of Bourbon held Bourbonnais as an apanage until 1527, when Francis I of France confiscated it upon the death of the traitor constable Charles of Bourbon.

Brandenburg was originally a northern march for the Holy Roman Empire, bordering pagan lands. The March of Brandenburg was settled by Germans and soon extended greatly under the rule of the houses of Bavaria and of Luxemburg from 1325 to 1415. It was raised to the title of Elector in 1247. In 1415, the Margraviate of Brandenburg was sold to the burgrave of Nuremberg, Frederick, scion of a lower branch of the house of Hohenzollern. Frederick would begin a dynasty whose members would acquire the Ducal Prussia and later become Kings of Prussia, Emperors of Germany.

Bremen has been founded in the late VIIIth or the early IXth century and may be the  oldest German port city. As an archbishopric, it acted as a departure point for missionaries on their way to Christianize Scandinavia. In the XIIth century the bishop's authority was curtailed by Henry the Lion, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, who became the overlord of the city and surrounding areas. The city then became a trading hub
column3: its ships would dominate the southern part of the North Sea until the rise of the Hanseatic League. Bremen initially commissioned privateers against the ships of the League, but in 1358, to prevent an open war, negotiated its entry to the League. Ever a reluctant member of the league, Bremen was finally expelled from it in 1427. Soon the surrounding lords claimed its lands and the city lost most of its power. Bremen accepted the Reformation in 1522 and became a free imperial city in 1646. It maintained its autonomy despite ceding the archbishopric to Sweden in the Peace of Westphalia.

column2: Brittany was an important and semi-autonomous duchy that had been a bone of contention between the English and French crowns ever since it was conquered by Henry I in 1113 and made a part of the 'Angevin Empire'. During the Hundred Years War, the dukes of Montfort tried to secure Brittany's neutrality between France and England. The unsuccessful rebellion of Duke Francis II against the French crown finally led to the absorption of Brittany into France after the accession of his daughter Anne of Brittany in 1488. King Francis I formally incorporated the duchy in 1532.

Pinya and Sagaing were two petty kingdoms that had ruled central Burma since the collapse of the Pagan Empire in the late 13th century. The two petty kingdoms would collapse due to Shan raids and be replaced by the new dominant Kingdom of Ava (which this tag also represents). Ava was a Burmese Shan Kingdom that succeeded an earlier Kingdom based on the city of Pagan. The city of Ava was founded in 1364. The location allowed the Shans to control the rice supply from the Kyaukse irrigated area to the south, which became vital after the traditional rice-growing area in southern Myanmar had been lost to a Mon Kingdom. The Kingdom of Ava flourished until it was destroyed by a rival group of Shans in 1527. In 1634 the city became the capital of the Taungu dynasty which had united the Ava and Taungu Kingdoms in 1531.

It was Pedro Alvarez Cabral who officially claimed Brazil for the Portugal in 1500. It is probable that others Portuguese sailors had already discovered these lands and at least one Spanish sailor, Vicente Yáñez Pinzón, did so. Brazil was part of the Portuguese share of the Treaty of Tordesillas, although it was sparsely settled until the XVIIth century. Despite French and Dutch attempts to take control of Brazil, Portugal managed to maintain its authority. The nation gained its independence in 1822, already rich in population and raw materials.

The Khanate of Bukhara, an Uzbek state in Central Asia, existed from 1501 to 1785. Founded by the Abu'l-Khayrid dynasty, a branch of the Shaybanids, it initially had its capital in Samarkand before moving to Bukhara. The khanate reached its zenith under Abdullah Khan II in the late 16th century, encompassing much of Central Asia. In the 17th and 18th centuries, it was ruled by the Janid dynasty until it was conquered by Nader Shah of Persia in 1740. Following Nader Shah's death, the Manghit dynasty took control, eventually transforming the khanate into the Emirate of Bukhara in 1785.

The history of the Bulgarians begins in the 7th Century, when a group of tribes of Turk-Altaic origin established a Kingdom in the old Roman province of Thracia. At its height the Bulgarian Kingdom rivaled the Byzantine Empire, but it fell into decline in the 10th Century and was eventually conquered by the Byzantines in 1018. Although the Bulgars successfully revolted in 1185 and established a new kingdom, they never quite managed to regain their former power. Weakened by Tartar incursions and internal strife, the last independent Bulgarian Kingdom fell to the Ottomans in 1396. Although there were numerous uprisings over the next centuries Bulgaria did not regain her independence until 1878.

John II of France gave the duchy of Burgundy to his son Philip the Bold in 1361. The line of Valois-Bourgogne thrived and greatly expanded Burgundy, gaining Franche-Comté and Flanders under Philip and his son John the Fearless, who was assassinated in 1419. Burgundy played a major role in the Hundred Years War, siding with England until the Peace of Arras in 1435. By the time of Charles the Bold's death in 1477 Burgundy had expanded by marriage and conquest to include most of the Netherlands and north-eastern France. Killed on the field of battle at Nancy, most of Charles' lands came under the control of Maximillian I of Habsburg, save Picardie and the Duchy of Burgundy itself, which were French fiefs and thus reverted to the French crown.

Banten was a Muslim sultanate among Hindu kingdoms in the island of Java. Its port was directly in front of the Sunda Straits, which allowed it to control trade in the area. The sultanate was already a Muslim state when Marco Polo visited in the XIIIth century. In 1526, the sultanate allied itself with the Sultanate of Demak to expand in Java. The initial enterprise failed, as neighboring Hindu states allied themselves with the Portuguese, who controlled Malacca, however, in the long term, the Muslims eventually prevailed. In the XVIth century, the sultanate flourished thanks to the lucrative pepper trade. But by 1596, the Dutch had arrived in Banten and in 1603 the British settle with a permanent trading post. The Dutch eventually prevailed and they annexed the Sultanate in 1813.

The island Kingdom of Butung was founded by migrants from Johore who established a Hindu state in the late 14th century. While often dominated by greater powers, it survived and even thrived well into the 20th century.

The Eastern Roman Empire was founded around 330 when Emperor Constantine transferred his capital from Nicomedia in Anatolia to the ancient Greek city of Byzantium, which he renamed Constantinople. From its capital, the Empire oversaw a thousand years of various glories.  No longer the seat of a powerful empire, Constantinople had been taken several times, notably in 1204 when the fourth Crusade created the Latin Empire and in 1261 when the Greek Michael VIII took it back. The empire came to an end in 1453 when the Ottoman Turks capture Constantinople. Impoverished and looted, the city recovered fast, becoming the seat of the new Muslim empire.

The Caliph was the heir of Muhammad and the political and religious head of Islam. The title was instituted after Muhammad's death and the dispute for power that caused the Islamic schism between Sunnites and Shiites. Under the Omeya Caliphs and later the Abassides, the Caliphate was taken to the height of its power, spanning from Spain to Persia. In 1258 the Mongols took Baghdad and slaughtered its population, marking the definitive end to the already decadent Caliphate. However, the dream of a reunited Islamic Empire was far from dead and several Muslim nations attempted to revive it - the Ottoman Empire being the only power that almost achieved it.

In 1419 Cambodia was a part of the mighty but waning Khmer Empire that lasted until 1431 when the capital city of Angkor was sacked by an invading Thai army. Much of her history up until that point had seen the country wedged between the empires of Ayutthaya and Dai Viet, forcing her to side with one country against the other for survival. From 1432 to 1859 Cambodia entered a dark age from which few historical records have survived. Prior to that, under the Khmer rulers, Cambodia enjoyed an unparalleled period of prosperity that saw the construction of the great temples of Angkor Wat and Bayon and fantastic sculptures like the Aspara.

Candar was established in the closing years of the 13th century by Yaman Candar - a chieftain of the Turkic tribes who had settled the northwestern Black Sea coasts of Asia Minor. Vassalized but never annexed by the Ottomans before the arrival of Timur in Anatolia, Candar regained much of its lost territory when pretenders to the Ottoman throne engaged in a civil war that lasted for eleven years. However, despite the best military and diplomatic efforts of Isfendiyar Beg, Ottoman forces finally conquered the Candar state in 1462.

The Castilian kingdom started its existence as a rebellious duchy of the older Christian kingdom of León in the 9th century. However, the dynastic marriages and the need for a united front against the Moors soon united the two kingdoms again and in the 13th century that union was made permanent. The Reconquista against the Moors culminated with the battle of the Navas de Tolosa (1212) that crushed the Almohade Empire soon after the biggest cities of Al-Andalus (Cordoba, Seville) were conquered, leaving the little vassal kingdom of Granada as the last vestige of Muslim presence in Iberia. The practical end of the fight against the Moors meant that there was a big and rebellious aristocracy with too much time on their hands, and Castile was plagued by chronic instability during the 14th and 15th centuries. Castile's internal strife continued unabated until a civil war erupted between the partisans of princess Juana (supported by the Portuguese) and those of her sister Isabella (married to Fernando de Aragón and backed by the Aragonese), at the death of King Enrique IV. The victory of the latter faction resulted in the union of the Castilian and Aragonese kingdoms as the new kingdom of Spain.

The 'Marca Hispanica' had been part of the Carolingian Empire as a protection against the Moors of Spain since 800. The grateful Carolingian Emperor relieved the Count of Barcelona from his vassalage in 988, and thus Catalunya was born. Catalunya merged with the Kingdom of Aragon in 1137, creating the political entity that would become a superpower in the Mediterranean during the 14th century. In 1412 the last Catalan King died heirless and the electors of the non-Catalan lands voted to elect a Castillian king against the Catalan candidate. Catalunya lost its primacy inside the Crown of Aragon as the new Castillian dynasty drifted the kingdom more and more towards a merging with Castile.

Champa was the kingdom of the Chams, a people living in what is now the central Vietnam, who were strongly influenced by Indian cultures. In the IInd century, following the fall of the Chinese Han Empire, the first Kingdom of Champa emerged, surviving mainly on the sea trade and piracy. The Kingdom quickly came into conflict with the Khmers in the south and west, and starting in the XIth century, began feuiding with the kingdom of Dai Viet which encroached on its northern border. Champa fared poorly at the hands of its neighbors and the kingdom was finally dismembered in the late XVth century. The remnants of the kingdom survived until the XVIIth century when a final Vietnamese offensive forced the Chams to scatter in Cambodia.

The Cherokee Indians settled along the Tennessee River millennia before Europeans arrived in North America. Connecting a network of villages by roads and streams through mountain gaps, the Cherokee nation traded prosperously with other tribes of the Mississippi River system. In 1540 the Spaniard Hernando De Soto encountered the Cherokee while searching for gold. For the next two centuries most of the Cherokees' contact with Europeans was friendly, until 1715 when the combined tribes of the area launched a war against the South Carolina colony. Alternately allying with the French and English the Cherokee were eventually decimated by disease and war.

Chagatai Khanate was the part of the Mongol Empire originally designated for the younger son of Gengis Khan after his death in 1227, when his older brother Ogodei became Great Khan. Chagatai's part was situated in Central Asia and was mainly populated by Turkish people. While the Mongols maintained a nomadic culture, they soon intermarried and by the end of the XIVth century the local Turkish language was named Chagatai. In the XIIIth and XIVth centuries, the Chagatai Khanate was one four Mongol Khanates (China, Persia, Russia and Central Asia). The Chagatai Khanate split in the 1330s and 1340s into a western, later ruled by Timur, and an eastern khanate that held close to Mongol traditions. The latter would survive until the XVIIth century when it was annexed by Dzungar tribes.

Even before the blood had dried on the rebellion of Zhu Yuanzhang, the Han Chinese of the Ming Dynasty began to make the might of the Middle Kingdom known to the rest of East Asia. In 1398 Korea become a puppet to the Chinese government and soon afterwards Dai Viet fell to Ming troops. Zheng He made his glorious voyages, discovering faraway lands in Africa and Arabia. Emperor Cheng Zu, a usurper, came to the throne early in the 15th century. A cruel but able administrator, Cheng Zu established an absolute rule over the Empire, and by 1419 the Ming had reached a new age of might and glory.

Chile, a long, narrow country stretching along the western edge of South America, has a rich and diverse history. Originally inhabited by indigenous peoples such as the Mapuche, it was later incorporated into the Inca Empire in the 15th century. Spanish conquistadors, led by Pedro de Valdivia, began colonizing the region in the mid-16th century. Chile declared its independence from Spain in 1818, and over the 19th and 20th centuries, it developed into a relatively stable republic.

A people heavily influenced by the Tiahuanaco culture, the Chimu rose to power in modern-day Peru around 1200. They were urban dwellers that built magnificent cities, had a powerful military and a complex social system. They remained a great power in the region until they were finally absorbed by the Inca Empire in 1460.

Circassia, located along the northeastern shore of the Black Sea, has a history marked by its strategic, cultural and religious importance. From ancient times, it was home to the Circassian people, who developed a distinct language and culture. The region was known for its fierce independence and resistance to external domination, and for centuries forged a careful network of alliances with neighboring Byzantine, Georgian and Tatar realms. However, during the Russo-Circassian War (1763-1864), Circassia was conquered by the Russian Empire. Despite these hardships, the unique Circassian identity and heritage endured.

The State of Calicut, ruled by an ambitious dynasty known as the Samoothiris (Samorins to Europeans) came to control the bulk of India's Malabar coastline during a series of expansionist wars in the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. Europe would gain its first holdings in India by expoliting Calicut's envious vassal states, but the efforts of the Samoothiri to thwart European aims would be a major stumbling block for the earliest colonizers of India.

Champagne, located in northeastern France, dates back to the 5th century when the Romans first planted vineyards there. Its main cities are Reims and Troyes, and for much of the medieval era it was the hereditary powerbase of the influential Blesevin dynasty. Initially known for its still wines, Champagne evolved over centuries into the world-renowned sparkling wine celebrated today. This transformation is often credited to the 17th-century innovations of Dom Pérignon, a Benedictine monk who perfected the méthode champenoise. The region's wines gained international acclaim, particularly after being featured at the coronation banquets of the French kings in Reims.

Champassak, a province in southwestern Laos, dates back to ancient times. It was part of the Funan and Chenla Kingdoms from the 1st to 9th centuries AD and later became a significant region within the Khmer Empire. In 1354, it was incorporated into the Lan Xang Empire under King Fa Ngum. Following the decline of Lan Xang, Champassak emerged (along with Vientiane and Luang Prabang) as one of three successor kingdoms in 1707. The Kingdom of Champassak maintained its autonomy until it became a vassal state of Siam in 1778 and was eventually annexed by the French in 1904.

Cornwall, located in the southwestern tip of England, was initially inhabited by the Celtic tribe of the Dumnonii, and later became part of the Roman Empire before reverting to independent Romano-British rule. Throughout the Middle Ages, Cornwall maintained a distinct cultural identity, often clashing with neighboring Wessex. The creation of the Duchy of Cornwall in 1337 solidified its unique status within England. Known for its tin mining industry, which peaked during the Industrial Revolution, Cornwall also experienced significant emigration, leading to a global Cornish diaspora.

A Small Principality dominated by neighboring Calicut, Cochin gained historical importance by using Portuguese aid in breaking free of Calicut's dominance, thereby providing Europe's first toehold in India.

Before the arrival of the Spanish, the land was inhabited by the Chibcha and Carribean people who were nomadic hunters or raisers . After the Spanish conquest, the native peoples were used as slaves to mine gold and gems that they then were forced to trade for grains and tools. Many natives lost their lives when killed while resisting, in the mines, and from various European diseases. Black slaves were brought in to handle their mining duties which eventually produced a mixed population. The Napoleonic invasion of Spain provided an opportunity for the independence of Colombia. On September 1810, the inhabitants of Bogota created a representative board defying the Spanish authority and shortly thereafter, in 1813, independence was proclaimed. Only following the victory of Simón Bolívar at Boyacá in 1819, was the independence of Greater Colombia secured, a sizable territory including what is now Colombia, Venezuela, Panama and Ecuador.

Connaught was the westernmost Irish kingdom. Traditional quarrels between the Irish kingdoms were interrupted in the late XIIth century by the settlements of Anglo-Normans lords, who encouraged by Henry II of England, dethroned the king of Leinster. The Irish lords were gradually replaced by English nobility. Henry III granted the lands of Connaught to the Norman baron Richard de Burgh (or de Burgo) whose family would held the lordship of Connaught from then on.

After centuries of conquest and rule by various invaders including Ostrogoths, Vandals, Byzantines, Lombards and Saracens, Corsica was entrusted to the city of Pisa by Pope Gregorious VII in 1077. In 1284 the island was taken by Genoa, the arch rival of Pisa, and held for five hundred years. The island suffered invasions from the Aragonese and the French during the Genoese occupation and underwent countless insurrections from the disgruntled population. In the 1600s they were a constant target of pirate raids from the Barbary Coast. In 1768 the Genoese sold the island to France, which soon lost it to the British (1794).

The Caliphate of Córdoba, established in 929 by Abd al-Rahman III, marked a golden age for Muslim Spain, known as Al-Andalus. This period saw Córdoba become one of the most advanced cities in Europe, renowned for its cultural, economic, and intellectual achievements. The Caliphate fostered a flourishing of arts, science, and architecture, exemplified by the Great Mosque of Córdoba. However, internal strife and political fragmentation led to its decline, culminating in its disintegration into smaller taifa kingdoms by 1031.

The Cree, a confederacy of many Muskogean-speaking tribes and villages, were named so by the English for the countless waterways crossing their territory in what is now Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina. Primarily hunter-gatherers, the Cree people thrived on commerce and thus welcomed the first Europeans, trading deer pelts for firearms. By the early 1700s however, the Cree were being displaced by English settlers. Battles with whites and other Indians continued sporadically until the American General Andrew Jackson, known to the Cree as 'Sharp Knife', destroyed the Cree chieftain Red Eagle and his main force of warriors at the Tallapoosa River in 1814.

Chernigov, also known as Chernihiv, is one of the oldest cities in Ukraine, with archaeological evidence suggesting its origins date back to the 7th century. First mentioned in the Rus'-Byzantine Treaty of 907, it became a prominent center in the Kievan Rus' and the capital of the Principality of Chernigov. The city flourished during the 10th and 11th centuries, known for its impressive cathedrals, such as the Transfiguration Cathedral, built in 1036. Despite suffering from the Tatar invasion in the 13th century, Chernigov remained an important regional trade hub.

From the XIIIth century, Crimea was the gate to the Orient trade. Although the Byzantine Empire had been expelled by the nomadic tribes, Venice and later Genoa settled trading posts in the Crimea peninsula. The Genoans were expelled in 1430 by the establishment of a khanate of Crimea. Many succession struggles threatened the stability of the newly formed khanate and in the late XVth century, the Tatars asked for the protection of the Turkish Ottomans. The Ottomans were the first to call the peninsula 'Crimea'. The khanate remained powerful enough to block the Russian access to the Black Sea for quite some time until it was finally annexed in 1783, marking the start of a period of slaughter and deportation of the Tatar population.

Upon the death of the last heir of the crown of Croatia, in 1090, and facing internecine strife, the lords of Croatia elected King Ladislaus I of Hungary to be King of Croatia. This established a personal union of Croatia and Hungary under the Hungarian monarch. For the next four centuries, the king of Hungary attempted to limit the power of the local Croatian feudal lords while allowing some autonomy to Croatia. The land had its own diet and was governed by a Ban, or Viceroy. With the Ottoman invasion of Europe, Croatia became a border land until the battle of Mohacs in 1526 which resulted in the annexation of most of Croatia by the Ottomans. With the fall of Hungary, the Croatian feudal lords accepted the Habsburgs as their overlords. In exchange for providing soldiers for the Habsburg armies, Croatia gained some autonomy and privileges.

Cuba, the largest island in the Caribbean, has a rich and tumultuous history. Originally inhabited by the Taíno people, it was claimed by Christopher Columbus for Spain in 1492. The island became a crucial part of the Spanish Empire, particularly for its sugar production. Following a series of independence wars, Cuba gained formal independence from Spain in 1898, only to fall under American influence.

The Island Kingdom of Cyprus, once a Roman province, was placed under the control of crusading knights by Richard the Lionheart in 1192, during the third crusade. The crusaders couldn't keep peace on the island so they sold it to the king of Jerusalem. Cyprus and Jerusalem shared royal house until 1359, when Islam finally forced the last Christian king out of the Holy Land. Cyprus was a land of serfs, so the king incited French nobles to come and help improve the domestic infrastructure. In 1489 Queen Caterina Cornero married into the Venetian nobility and Cyprus became another Venetian holding.

Cyrenaica was an ancient Roman desert province bordering the Eastern Mediterranean Sea. It was conquered by the Arab armies in 642 and lightly settled by them between the IXth and XIth centuries. The XIVth century saw the climate improve, allowing another wave of settlement, this time, from Mameluk Egypt. The area fell under Ottoman control in 1517.

In the early 17th century, a quarrel between three brothers with a right to the throne of Great Ardra led to one retaining that small nation and the other two forging their own. One of these was Dahomey, centered around the town of Abomey, while the other was Ajatche (called Porto Novo by the Portuguese). By the end of the century Dahomey was in control of the slave trade on the Bight of Benin. Using their remarkable female soldiers (called Amazons by outsiders) the kingdom grew rapidly in all directions.

The people of what is now Vietnam, but was then scornfully labeled 'Annam' by the Chinese overlords, finally drove out the occupiers in 939 and renamed their country Dai Co Viet and later Dai Viet. It remained independent except for another brief period of Chinese occupation from 1407-1428. In 1558 Dai Viet found itself divided between two great families: the Trinh and the Nguyens. The Trinh ruled from Tonkin (present-day Hanoi) as far south as Porte d'Annam. The Europeans called this area Tonkin when they arrived in the 1600s. The Nguyens ruled from the city of Hue over territory that extended south from Porte d'Annam to Quy Nhon. In 1802 the two halves, Tonkin-Dai Viet and Annam-Dai Viet, were united by Nguyen-Anh and renamed Vietnam.

The Dakota Sioux lived west of the northern Mississippi River. During the summer they roamed vast areas of the Great Plains, often traveling as far as the hot springs of Arkansas to gather with other Indians and share the healing waters. After the arrival of Europeans the horse became the most valuable commodity of the Dakota. Skilled artisans and weavers, the Sioux also thrived off trade with other tribes and Europeans. The image of the blanket-wrapped painted Indian upon his horse was born in this era. In 1701 the Dakota attended the gathering of tribes initiated by the governors of New France. After a century of varying alliances and wars the Sioux sided with Tecumseh of the Shawnee and fought with the British in the War of 1812, winning huge victories at first, only to be squandered by the British. The decades that followed saw the demise of the Sioux, highlighted by the massacre at Wounded Knee in 1889.

One of the oldest kingdoms in Europe, Denmark has its roots in the little known age prior to the Viking era. Its destiny was always intertwined with those of its brother nations of Norway and Sweden, and the three kingdoms sometimes allied and sometimes bitterly fought each other. In 1419, Denmark was the dominant kingdom and a Danish king ruled over all three in the 'Union of Kalmar'. In 1448 Christian I became king and established on the Danish throne the house of Oldenburg. In 1460, he incorporated Schleswig and Holstein into the Danish crown. Denmark was now at the apex of its power, rivaling the days of King Canute (Knut), but the malcontents in Sweden were already causing much grief. When Sweden finally broke away from the union in 1523, Denmark was still the most powerful realm in the North, getting rich off the Sound due, but the balance of power was to shift during the coming century. The two nations fought innumerable wars with varying outcomes, until Denmark finally got demolished by Charles X of Sweden in 1658, who, with his veterans from the 30 years war forced Denmark to cede almost half its territory to Sweden. Charles shortly renewed the war, and Denmark came within a hairsbreadth of being absorbed into the Swedish Great Power, but escaped that fate by heroically defending Copenhagen (and thanks to the help of England and the Netherlands). An serious attempt was made to gain the lost territory back in 1676, but the plans were thwarted at the battle of Lund on Dec 4th. The battle lasted for 20 hours and was the bloodiest in Scandinavian history - even worse than the battle of Poltava. Of the 18,000 participants, about half fell and many more were wounded. Denmark now entered a period of decline, but so did Sweden a few decades later.

The Delaware were an Algonquin-speaking people who originally inhabited the Delaware River Valley. The name was given to them by the English when they named the bay after Sir Thomas West, Third Lord de la Warr. The name stuck. The Delaware called themselves Lenape which meant 'original people', and many Algonquins viewed them as the original tribe of all Algonquin-speaking people. Their society was a loosely based collection of agricultural villages ruled by a tribal council composed of three sachems or leaders. Their first contact with Europeans was in 1524, and distrust was quickly sown. Much of their subsequent history was one of warfare against the Susquehannock and later the Iroquois. In 1633 they contracted small-pox, which in addition to the wars halved their population.

In the late XIIth century, the armies of the Muslim Afghan leader Muhammad Ghûri  crushed the Hindu kingdoms in northern India. Delhi was conquered in 1192 and became the seat of a Muslim sultanate. The sultanate was to successfully fend off invasions by the Mongols and the Rajputs before falling to the armies of Timur in 1399. The conquest initiated a period of decline and the last of the Sultans felt before Bâbur, who founded the Mughal Empire in 1526, on the remains of the Sultanate of Delhi.

The Dali Kingdom, established in 937 by Duan Siping, was a Bai-dominated state in present-day Yunnan Province, China. It succeeded the Nanzhao Kingdom and became a significant regional power, known for its strategic location on trade routes connecting China with Southeast Asia and India. The kingdom was notable for its long duration, lasting until 1253 when it was conquered by the Mongol Empire. Despite the conquest, members of the former ruling house continued to administer the area as tusi chiefs under the Yuan dynasty until the Ming conquest of Yunnan in 1382. The Dali Kingdom is remembered for its cultural and religious influence, particularly in spreading Buddhism throughout the region.

A large independent Turkish principality in south-eastern Asia Minor, the Beylik of Dulkadir fought against both the Timurids and the Mamelukes and was largely unsuccessful against both. A buffer state between stronger nations, the Dulkadirs passed from the world stage in 1522 when they were finally absorbed by the Ottomans.

Ecuador, located in northwestern South America, was originally inhabited by various indigenous groups, including the Valdivia culture, one of the oldest in the Americas. In the 15th century, it became part of the Inca Empire before being conquered by the Spanish in the 16th century. Ecuador gained independence from Spain in 1822 and initially joined Gran Colombia before becoming a sovereign republic in 1830. The country has since experienced periods of political instability and economic challenges but remains known for its incredible biodiversity and cultural heritage, in particular due to its control over the Galápagos Islands.

The County of Edessa, established in 1098 during the First Crusade, was the first Crusader state in the Levant and Upper Mesopotamia. Its capital was the city of Edessa (modern-day Sanliurfa, Turkey), and it played a crucial role as a buffer state against Muslim forces. Founded by Baldwin of Boulogne, who later became the King of Jerusalem, the county was unique among Crusader states for being landlocked and geographically isolated. Despite its strategic importance, Edessa fell to the Muslim leader Zengi in 1144, marking the first major Crusader defeat and prompting the Second Crusade.

Eire, the Emerald Island, had a long and mysterious history in the legendary times preceding the Christian era. When the Vikings began their bloody raids all over northern Europe, they came to fancy Ireland so much that many of them stayed there, settling down chiefly in the Dublin region (which was ruled by a Norse king). The Irish problems did not end with the Vikings however, as the island was invaded by the Normans from England in the 12th century. Ireland remained an English vassal, if usually a rebellious one, until well into the 20th century, even if the attempts by the English kings in the 16h and 17th centuries to enforce Protestantism sparked several serious rebellions that could have resulted in freedom for the Green Island.

The Norman Invasion of England in 1066 is one of the most important events in English History. The Norman lords built castles, instituted laws and organized a feudal system, which, while oppressive, was more in line with continental Europe. Their ties with Normandy and France also brought England into the highlight from having been little more than a Danish playground. In 1419, England was ruled by the Lancaster king Henry V, a very able man who, had he lived longer, might very well have become the ruler of a united France and England. However, he died in 1422, and England soon started to lose its grip on France, having lost everything but Calais by 1453. The War of the Roses followed, fought between House Lancaster and York, ending only with the death of Richard III at Bosworth field in 1485. The Tudors ruled England from 1485 to 1603 - a period that saw the Reformation under Henry VIII and a golden age under Queen Elizabeth I. Then came the Stuart kings and the Civil War between Parliamentarians and Royalists that started in 1642 and ended only when Charles I was beheaded on Jan. 30,1649, at the order of the Lord Protector, Oliver Cromwell. Cromwell's death in 1658 initiated the collapse of his strange new rule and Charles II was restored to power in 1660. The Stuarts were followed by the House of Hanover in 1714, uniting England with the German electorate. From this time onward, England's power grew explosively, seeing great expansion of the navy, trade and colonial involvement.

Legend states that the Ethiopian royal line comes from the son of King Solomon and Queen of Sheba in the Bible. Isolated for many centuries after the decline of the Roman Empire, Ethiopia remained Christian, and the Europeans thought they had found the mythical kingdom of Prester John in Ethiopia in the 16th century, which would help the Catholics destroy the Muslims forever and gain the Holy Land back. However, the ancient Ethiopian Empire was always on the defensive by 1419 and continued to fight for its life when in 1535 Portuguese explorers helped out with new technology to beat the Muslims back. The Catholic Europeans, however, were ultimately rejected by the Coptic Ethiopian rulers. Ethiopia amazingly survived well past 1820 - perhaps a miracle surpassing its own mythical origins.

The Fatimid Caliphate, established in 909 AD by Abdullah al-Mahdi Billah, was an Isma'ili Shi'a dynasty that ruled over a vast region stretching from North Africa to the Middle East. Originating in Ifriqiya (modern-day Tunisia), the Fatimids expanded their influence, eventually conquering Egypt in 969 AD and founding the city of Cairo, which became the Caliphate's capital. The Fatimid period is noted for its cultural and intellectual achievements, as well as its relative religious tolerance towards non-Shi'a Muslims, Christians, and Jews. Despite internal instability and foreign invasion, the Caliphate lasted until 1171, when it was overthrown by Saladin, leading to the establishment of the Ayyubid dynasty.

Fez was founded in the late VIIIth century in northern Morocco. It became a capital for several dynasties, due to its location at the crossroads of several trade roads and the abundance raw materials available. The city flourished during the Merinids dynasty in the XIVth and XVth centuries and in 1475 became the capital of the kingdom of Fez. The kingdom had to deal with the Portuguese ambitions in North Africa, the Spanish war against Granada, the subsequent migrations of Muslims and Jews, and later with the growing power of Marrakech.

From the mid 11th century Christian missionaries from Sweden were active in Finland, and in 1249 the Swedish king Birger Jarl mounted a 'crusade' against the wild men of the forests, which was more of an expedition of conquest. Finland soon became an integrated part of Sweden, and the frontier was constantly pushed further east, until the Swedes came into conflict with Great Novgorod. For almost six centuries, Sweden fought off the constant encroachments of Novgorod and later Muscovy and Russia, but the defeat in the Great Northern War initiated a period of decline that was to cost Sweden its eastern half in 1809. Finland now became a Russian Grand Duchy with a certain measure of independence in order to avoid offending the bitter Swedes too much.

The County of Flanders was a French fief grown from the area around Brugge which first stepped into the foreground under count Baldwin Iron Arm. This rich county fought for centuries to break free from France with changing fortunes but eventually was able to get out from under French wings. They enjoyed their Golden Age when cities which were all-powerful in Flanders, like Brugge and Gent, were at the height of their power in the late Middle Ages before the merchants, due to various reasons, turned to Antwerpen as their new center in the late 15th and early 16th century.  In 1419 Flanders had been under Burgundian rule for over 3 decades and was enjoying a prosperous age in the arts and, while in decline, was still a major commercial center. It was still easily the richest, most densely populated and most important county in the Low Countries. Together with the rest of the Burgundian inheritance they passed eventually to Spain, against whom they revolted as part of the Dutch Revolt. But Flanders succumbed to Farnese's Reconquista, which effectively ended its glory days.

Huguenot is a word that the Catholics gave to members of the French Reformation. The ideas of the Reformation were already spreading in France when the Jean Calvin published his Institutes of the Christian Religion in 1536. He was forced into exile in Geneva but the Reformation still spread. Reprisals against Protestants became more severe under Henri II but as nobility became involved, political factions emerged. Great noble families exploited the conflict to take more power from the royal authority. The Protestant faction was led by the houses of Montmorency and Bourbon. The last head of the Huguenots, Henri de Navarre would become King of France under the name of Henri IV.

France was first used as the name of the kingdom in the XIIth century, previously known as the Kingdom of the Franks. Although the king's demesne was only a small part of the whole kingdom, his position was secured in holy character of his person, through his consecration in the Cathedral of Rheims. All great nobles had to swear fealty to the king for their French territories, even if they were kings in their own right, like the Kings of England or Navarre. In the XIVth century, the beginning of the Little Ice Age, the Black Death, and the Hundred Years War triggered a period of social and economic upheaval. The HYW war saw the King of France pitted against the King of England over who had the right to the French throne. Many great French nobles, also took part, notably the house of Burgundy, which saw a great opportunity for increased autonomy. In 1419, the king of England, Henry V, forcefully pressed his claim to the French throne on the French fields. Never before had the Kingdom of France been so close to losing its independence. Against all odds, France managed to rally and defeat English invaders, which allowed for the creation of strong, centralized nation that could constrain the ambitions of its great feudal families. Throughout its history, France would never cease to expand until the end of Napoleon's rule.

Franconia is an historic region in southern Germany with a history dating back to ancient times. Initially inhabited by Celtic tribes, it later became a significant part of the Frankish Empire under Charlemagne in the 8th century. The region was one of the five stem duchies of medieval Germany and played a crucial role in the formation of the Holy Roman Empire in 962 AD. Franconia's political landscape was characterized by fragmentation into numerous smaller states and territories, a feature that persisted until the Napoleonic era.

Friesland is a vast territory extending from the Scheldt River in the south to the Weser in the east. The land's topography changed greatly with floods during the XIth and XIIth century that eventually created the Zuiderzee. Western Friesland came to be associated with the county of Holland. Eastern Friesland tried to individualize itself through the Opstalboom League of Free Frisians but the diverging interests of its constituents led quickly to the League's demise. A short lived county of East Frisia emerged in the XVth century that was soon reduced by Hamburg and Denmark. In 1498, Emperor Maximilian I bestowed what remained of Friesland to its last invader, Duke Albert of Saxony. Friesland resisted his authority and forced Albert's son to give it back to the Emperor.  Emperor Charles V sent an army that reduced the province by force in 1523 and appointed stewards to rule it. Friesland eventually joined the Union of Utrecht against Spain in 1579, but maintained its own stadtholders until 1748.
The French Ultra Catholics represent the faction led by the Dukes of Guise, who hated the huguenots and were at times prepared to seize power in order to end the protestant threat.

The Duchy of Gelre was the part of the Netherlands that held out the longest against the unification process started by the Dukes of Burgundy. When Karl V added it to his possessions in 1543 the territorial unification process was completed. The Provinces of the Netherlands were united at last. It was conquered before in 1473 by Charles the Bold of Burgundy but after his death in 1477 it regained its independence. It passed to the House of Habsburg in 1543 and joined (1579) the Union of Utrecht of the Netherlands against Spain. It was part of the Dutch Republic which gained its independence from Spain. Part of Gelre including Geldern, the ducal capital, was ceded in 1715 by the Netherlands to Prussia.

With a poor and thin hinterland, it was inevitable that Genoa became a naval power. It benefited greatly from the crusades, making wealth both by transporting the pilgrims and crusaders and by trading silks, ivory and spices for weapons and wool clothes. The Genoan navy then established its preeminence in the western Mediterranean Sea with the victory of Meloria in 1284 over Pisa. In the eastern Mediterranean Sea, Genoa helped Michael Palaiologos to secure the Byzantine Empire from the Latin lords who had settled there since the Fourth Crusade.
