Genoa was rewarded with possessions and trading privileges from Spain to the Black Sea. Its only true rival was Venice and that fight dragged on until the Peace of Turin in 1381, the beginning of Genoa's decline. Genoa had lost not only its fleet but its monopoly of trade in the Mediterranean Sea, as well. While it managed to gain some land around the city, it lost its outlying possessions. The rise of the Ottomans in the XVth century blocked trade with the Black Sea, pushing Genoa to become only a shadow of its former glory for the next several centuries.

The Kingdom of Georgia was located on the Caucasus mountains , at the border of the Christian world during the Middle Ages. It found itself a Christian island in the middle of a Muslim sea of emirates when, in 1461, the fall of Trabzon, made it the only Christian kingdom in the Middle East. In 1490, King Alexander I under external and internal pressure was forced to divide Georgia into three kingdoms among his sons and himself (Imertia in the west, Kakhetia in the east and Karthlia in the middle).  To remain free, the three kingdoms had to play a game of alliances and were often subjugated to the surrounding Muslim powers. In the midst of conflicts between the Ottomans and Safavids, the various lords pulled out all the stops, converting back and forth between Islam and Christianity, when the situation warranted. In the XVIIIth century, Heraclius II of Kakhetia managed to unify Georgia again with the Russian help. This assistance changed in protection and 1801, threatened by a Persian invasion, George XIII, last king of Georgia, abdicated in favor of the Czar.

The Kingdom of Germany emerged from the eastern part of the Carolingian Empire following the Treaty of Verdun in 843 AD. It was a key component of the Holy Roman Empire, with its kings often being elected by the rulers of the stem duchies. The kingdom played a crucial role in medieval European politics, particularly during the Investiture Controversy and the reign of Emperor Otto I, who was crowned in 962. Over time, the title 'King of the Romans' was used to emphasize the imperial and transnational nature of the ruler's office. The Kingdom of Germany's influence waned as the Holy Roman Empire fragmented, but its legacy persisted in the region's complex political and cultural landscape.

Gondwana is a region in India named after the Gond people.  Three powerful Gond kindoms existed in the period between the 14th and 18th centuries. Nominally subjects of the Mughals, the Gond kingdoms were largely left to manage their own affairs. The Gonds would actually prosper under Mughal rule, allowed their independence and yet protected from foreign powers.  The rise of the Marathas would end the independent nature of the Gond kingdoms.

Since the 10th century, Gotland had been a part of Sweden, paying an annual tax for protection but otherwise remaining an independent peasant community. Early on Gotland became a commercial center and by the 12th century Gotland dominated the routes between Russia and Western Europe. Until the mid-14th century most of the Novgorod trade passed through the island. They became Christianised in the 12th century, brought by a Norwegian King, on the run from his own people. In 1361 the Danish King Valdemar IV Atterdag conquered Gotland after which the trade routes shifted and Gotland declined. For the next three centuries Denmark, Hanseatic League, pirates, and Teutonic Knights variously controlled it, until in 1645 it came again under Swedish rule.

Heir to the splendid Caliphate of Cordoba, the province of Granada became in 1238 the seat of the kingdom of Granada - last refuge of the Moors whom the Christian reconquest had driven south. The concentration of Moorish civilization in Granada gave the city great splendor and made it a center of commerce, industry, art and science. However, the kingdom was weakened by continuous feuds among noble families which prevented any attempt at restoring the Moorish power in the peninsula. It was conquered by Ferdinand V and Isabella I during the reign of Boabdil. With the surrender in January 1492 of the city of Granada the Moors lost their last hold in Spain and the kingdom was united with Castile.

Before the arrival of the Spanish, the land was inhabited by the Chibcha and Caribbean people who were nomadic hunters or raisers. After the Spanish conquest, the native peoples were used as slaves to mine gold and gems that they then were forced to trade for grains and tools. Many natives lost their lives when killed while resisting, in the mines, and from various European diseases. Black slaves were brought in to handle their mining duties which eventually produced a mixed population. The Napoleonic invasion of Spain provided an opportunity for the independence of Colombia. On September 1810, the inhabitants of Bogota created a representative board defying the Spanish authority and shortly thereafter, in 1813, independence was proclaimed. Only following the victory of Simón Bolívar at Boyacá in 1819, was the independence of Greater Colombia secured, a sizable territory including what is now Colombia, Venezuela, Panama and Ecuador.

The fourth Crusade saw Latin overlords installed over most of Greece. The restoration of the Byzantine Empire by the Palaeologos family only recovered part of it, as much of Greece under the rule of French, Italien or Aragonese princes.  Ottoman conquest of the region was completed in 1456, although a few islands remained as Christian outposts. The Knights Hospitaller had to flee Rhodes in 1522, Genoa retained Khios until 1566, Venice held Naxos until 1576, Crete until 1669 and the Ionian Islands until 1797. The possessions of Venice and its eastern trade led it into numerous wars with the Ottomans, but it never managed to shake the Turkish grip on Greece.  Greece became an Ottoman province, poor in the hinterland, prosperous in its trade ports. The oppressive power and the weight of the taxes led to many revolts and a rise in nationalistic feeling, which gave way to  independence in the early part of the XIXth century.

Greenland, the world's largest island, has a history marked by resilience and adaptation to extreme Arctic conditions. The first humans arrived around 2500 BC, with successive waves of Paleo-Inuit cultures following. Norse settlers from Iceland established colonies on the southwestern coast in the 10th century, but these had disappeared by the 15th century. The Inuit, ancestors of today's Greenlandic people, migrated from northwestern Greenland around 1200 AD. Danish colonization began in the 18th century, and Greenland became part of the Kingdom of Denmark in 1953.

Guatemala, located in Central America, was a major center of the ancient Maya civilization, which flourished from around 250 to 900 AD. Following the Spanish conquest in the 16th century, Guatemala became part of the Captaincy General of Guatemala, a significant colonial territory. The country gained independence from Spain in 1821 and experienced a series of political changes, including periods of authoritarian rule and civil conflict.

Gujarat became an independent Sultanate in 1390. Its immense wealth invited attack and in 1509 the ever-enterprising Portuguese wrested the colony of Diu from the Sultan. In 1572 the Sultanate was annexed by the Mughal Empire. The Marathas were powerful in the area in the first half of the 18th century, but the British East India Company took over control of the region in 1818. Under the British overlords much of the region retained its various local princely rulers.

In 1419 Austria was not so much a nation as a political entity. Since the Privilegium Majus charter of the Habsburg Duke Rudolf IV in 1359, it was ruled by an Archduke, but essentially Austria simply represented the hereditary lands of the House of Habsburg. The 15th century saw the Habsburgs gaining ever more power. Albert V was elected Hungarian King in 1438 (but the title was lost again) and Maximilian I married the Burgundian heiress in 1477, thus acquiring the rich Low Countries. Though the last years of the century were hard for the Habsburgs, the next would see them more powerful than ever. The son of Maximilian, Philip, was married to the daughter of Ferdinand and Isabella of Spain in 1496, and their son Charles became King of Spain in 1516, thus adding that nation to the Habsburg realm. In 1526, the Habsburg Archduke Ferdinand I was elected King of Bohemia and King of Hungary. House Habsburg was now the incomparably most powerful dynasty in Europe. However, the event of the reformation and the uncompromising catholicism of the Habsburgs brought Austria no end of trouble, eventually resulting in the catastrophic 30 Years War.

The island of Hispaniola was discovered by Columbus in 1492. The Arawak inhabitants gave its name to the island, Haiti meaning the land of mountains in their language. The native population was ravaged when the Spanish forced them to work in gold mines and they contracted European diseases. The eastern part of the island, holding the mines, was exploited by the Spanish who brought black slaves to care for the cane sugar plantations. The western part of the island was mainly deserted and was the base for French and English buccaneers, especially in Tortuga Island. Gradually, French settlers claimed the northern part of Haiti, that they named Saint Domingue. By the Ryswick Treaty in 1697, Spain no longer claimed the French part of the island and by 1790, St. Domingue the most flourishing island in the Antilles thanks to 400,000 slaves. The French Revolution inspired a slave revolt in 1791, led by Toussaint Louverture . Slavery was abolished in 1793 in St. Domingue, becoming official by the French government in all French islands in 1794. In 1795, Spain ceded its part of the island to France but it is only in 1801 that Toussaint could conquer it. He abolished slavery in the whole island and began to inspire rumors that he sought independence for Haiti.  Though, he claimed loyalty to France, Bonaparte, lobbied by the creole pro-slavery faction, sent his brother-in-law Charles Leclerc with a huge punitive force to restore order. Initially successful, the expedition was forced to retreat, allowing Haiti to become the second independent nation in America.

The Hammadid dynasty was a medieval Islamic kingdom located in the central Maghreb, encompassing present-day Algeria. Established in 1014 by Hammad ibn Buluggin, it emerged from the split of the Zirid domains. The dynasty reached its peak under Emir Al Nasir, becoming the most important state in Northwest Africa during the 11th century. The Hammadids built impressive cities like Qal'at Bani Hammad and later Bejaia, which became major cultural and economic centers. Despite their achievements, the dynasty faced challenges from the Almoravids, Zirids, and Normans, ultimately falling to the Almohads in 1152.

The city of Hanover was first mentioned in documents from the 12th century. It was chartered in 1241 and joined the Hanseatic League in 1386. In 1386 it joined the Hanseatic League, and in 1692 it became the capital of the Electorate of Hanover, which was soon joined to England in dynastic union.

The first seven Hausa cities were Biram, Daura, Kano, Zaria, Gobir, Rano, and Katsina. Eventually, the states of Zamfara, Kebbi, Nupe, Gwari, Yauri, Kororofa, and Illorin were added once Hausa influence spread. Despite the richness of their folklore and the existence of chronicles of the Kings of Kano and Katsina dating to 1100, little is known of this early period. During the fifteenth century Kano was the most important of the Hausa states, although its rulers paid tribute to the Kingdom of Bornu. In the sixteenth century, Hausaland became a battleground among Bornu, Songhai, and the Junkun empire. Partially due to this, Kano lost its economic supremacy to the rival city of Katsina. Eventually in the early nineteenth century, Usuman dan Fodio created the first united empire in Hausaland.

The county of Brabant was created by the Emperor Henry IV in 1086 and raised to the title of duchy in 1184. Becoming locally powerful, it gained its independence from the Holy Roman Empire in the XIVth century. Its cities, Antwerp, Brussels, Louvain, and outlying lands were extraordinarily prosperous and famous for their wool, textiles and banking institutions.  In 1430, lacking an heir, the duchy passed to Philip the Good of Burgundy and in 1477 to the Habsburgs.

The Holy Roman Empire, established in 800 AD when Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne as Emperor, was a complex political entity in Central and Western Europe. It evolved from the Carolingian Empire and lasted until its dissolution by Francis II in 1806 during the Napoleonic Wars. The empire was characterized by its decentralized structure, with numerous semi-autonomous territories governed by princes, dukes, and bishops under the nominal authority of the Holy Roman Emperor. Despite its fragmented nature, the empire played a crucial role in European politics, religion, and culture for nearly a millennium.

What is now Switzerland once belonged to the Empire of Charlemagne, and, when it was split among his sons, it went to the Kingdom of Burgundy before being Switzerland itself was split, with parts of it going to the duchy of Burgundy and the rest to the duchy of Swabia. From the XIIIth century, the Habsburgs tried to seize little Swiss fiefdoms, especially those controlling the trade through the Alps. To resist the Habsburg's might, three forest cantons, Uri, Schwyz, and Unterwalden, created a league of mutual defense in 1291. The defensive league expanded in the XIVth century to other cantons and in the XVth century to include all the surrounding lands. Switzerland became a recognized nation in 1474 when they allied to Louis XI of France against the Duke of Burgundy. Switzerland left the Holy Roman Empire in 1499 and gained a reputation for its fierce and disciplined soldiers.

Henri of Brabant  became the first landgrave of Hessen in 1263 and was titled Prince of the Empire in 1292. Philip the Magnanimous was a leading figure in the German Reformation and Renaissance. He converted to the Protestantism and became a leader in the league of Smalkald. Pursuant to his death in 1567, the landgraviate was divided among his four sons with Kassel, Marburg, Rheinfels, and Darmstadt becoming their respective capitals. Two lines were to die out soon, Rheinfels in 1583 and Marburg 1605 lines, and the whole territory was held by the remaining lines of Hesse-Kassel and Hesse-Darmstadt. The two lines fought on opposite sides during part of the Thirty Years War. Hesse-Kassel became an electorate in 1803 but was annexed by Napoleon in the Kingdom of Westphalia, in 1806. Restored in 1813, the Electorate of Hesse became a Great-Duchy until it was annexed by Prussia in 1866.

Holland was a wealthy and influential province of the Holy Roman Empire, emerging in the early 12th century as a fief ruled by the Counts of Holland. During the medieval era it fought most of its neighbours in order to remain independent, a struggle it eventually lost in 1433 with its acquisition by Philip the Good. Subsequently, Holland became a significant economic and maritime power, especially during the Dutch Golden Age, and played a crucial role in the formation of the Dutch Republic in 1579. Over the centuries, it transitioned from being part of the Burgundian (and later Habsburg) Netherlands to becoming the leading province of the Dutch Republic until the Batavian Revolution in 1795.

The lands of Western Friesland (between the Scheldt river and the Weser) began to be thoroughly settled in the Xth and XIth century. In the next two centuries, major floods created what is now the Zuiderzee. The counts of Holland were among the most powerful lords of the area, along with the dukes of Brabant and the counts of Flanders. In the XIVth and XVth centuries, Flanders, Holland, Zeeland, Gelderland and Brabant passed to the dukes of Burgundy and through inheritance went to the Habsburgs in 1477. The seventeen provinces of the Spanish Low Countries rebelled and the seven most northern provinces became the United Provinces, forming the Republic of Netherland in 1588. The republic dominated the world trade in the XVIIth century, establishing settlements in most parts of the world and creating a huge stock market in Rotterdam and later in Amsterdam. Officially recognized in the Treaty of Westphalia in 1648, the republic became the Batavian Republic at the hands of French revolutionaries in 1795, then the Kingdom of Holland in 1806 and finally the United Kingdom of Netherland in 1815.

Honduras, located in Central America, was inhabited by various indigenous peoples, including the Maya. The region became part of the Spanish Empire in the early 16th century following the arrival of Spanish explorers. Honduras gained independence from Spain in 1821 and briefly joined the First Mexican Empire before becoming part of the Federal Republic of Central America. By 1838, Honduras emerged as an independent nation. Throughout its history, Honduras has experienced periods of political instability and social strife, but it remains a country with a diverse cultural heritage and significant archaeological sites, such as the ancient Mayan city of Copán.

At the end of the 13th century, a powerful alliance of cities - the Hanseatic League - had developed from a merchant's union with Lübeck taking on the leadership position of the Hanseatic Council. Despite the commercial power that she wielded, the Hanseatic League was never war-like, and not even a country in the true sense. The Latin phrase on the Holstein Gate in Lübeck reads 'Concordia Domi Foris Pax' - Harmony within Peace without, which was the prerequisite for the functional community and the undisrupted free trade which the Hanseatic League thrived on.

In the Middle Ages, Hungary expanded with the vassal states of Croatia and Slavonia and the Serb and Romanian banates (marches) and voivodships (duchies).  The land was mostly rural and sparsely inhabited, the cities were small. In peripheral areas, immigration came mainly from Germany and Poland. After the end of the House of Anjou, several foreign monarchs ruled in Hungary, notably, Sigismund and Albert II of Austria and Ladislaus III of Poland. In the late XIVth century, the Ottoman Turks began their advance in the Balkans, defeating the Hungarians and their allies at Kosovo in 1389, and later at Nikopol in 1396 and Varna in 1444. There was a short respite during the rule of the Regent Hunyadi and his son Matthias Corvinus, elected king in 1458, but the Ottomans quickly returned to the offensive and at the battle of Mohács in 1526, Sulayman the Magnificent's victory, led Ottoman domination over Hungary. The House of Habsburg claimed the Hungarian crown and tried to stop the impending invasion of Europe.

The Huron, named so by the French, meaning 'Bristly Head', called themselves the Wyandot meaning 'Island People' in Iroquoian. Living in dense longhouse villages along the shores of the Great Lakes they raised vast crops of corn and tobacco that were traded to other tribes for meat, copper and furs. In the 1600s the Huron allied with the French, acting as middlemen for the fur trade and receiving French support against the Mohawk tribe. Around 1640 the Iroquois League launched the Beaver Wars against Christianized Huron towns and other tribes, forcing them from their traditional lands. In 1701 the governor of New France brought together the leaders of the Iroquois and other Great Lakes Indians to promote friendship among the tribes but it accomplished little in the end. Then, at Fort Pitt in 1763, the British traded blankets purposely infected with smallpox to the Indians. The disease almost annihilated many Indian tribes and the last full-blooded Huron died in the early nineteenth century.

The Hussites were a proto-Protestant Christian reform movement that emerged in Bohemia in the early 15th century, inspired by the teachings of Jan Hus. Hus, a Czech priest and philosopher, criticized the Catholic Church's practices and called for reforms, which led to his excommunication and execution in 1415. His followers, known as Hussites, continued his mission, leading to a series of religious conflicts known as the Hussite Wars (1419-1434) which embroiled most of Central Europe. The movement was marked by its emphasis on vernacular worship, communion in both kinds (bread and wine for all believers), and a strong sense of national identity. Despite facing significant opposition, the Hussites left a lasting impact on the religious landscape of Europe and paved the way for later Protestant movements under Luther and Calvin.

In modern times the central Deccan has always been home to a succession of some of the most powerful nations in southern India. In the 15th century this nation was the Bahmanid Sultanate, in the 16th and 17th centuries Golconda dominated the area, while Hyderabad was the great nation in the area during the 18th century. In For The Glory, Hyderabad represents this succession of nations, from the Sultans of Bahmanid Dynasty in 1419 to the Nizams of Hyderabad in 1820.

Iceland was settled by Norse explorers and their Celtic slaves in the late 9th century, with the first recorded settlement conventionally dated to 874 AD. The settlers established the Althing in 930 AD, one of the world's oldest parliaments. Iceland remained independent during the Old Commonwealth period (930-1262) until internal strife led to its subjugation by Norway in the 13th century. Later, it fell under Danish rule, which lasted until the 20th century. Despite its small population, Iceland has a rich cultural heritage, including the famous sagas that chronicle its early history.

In the Cuzco area, the Inca people were only a member of a group of small power and were far from being the most powerful. They took preeminence in this confederation during the XIVth century, by reinforcing their position in the Cuzco area and expanding in the XVth century. The kingdom of the Chimu was defeated around 1470 and in the early XVIth, under the rule of Huayna Capac, the Inca Empire extended from the modern Ecuador to southern Chile. At his death, in 1527, the empire was divided between his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa. A civil war erupted, which provided an opportunity for the newly arrived Spanish under Francisco Pizarro.

Iraq had been the seat of powerful Caliphate but the destruction of Baghdad by the Mongols in 1258 had begun a decline that was reinforced by the slaughter of the population of the city by Timur in 1401. Iraq was dominated by the surrounding powers: the Timurids, the Jalayrids, the Qara Koyunlu, the Ak Koyunlu, the Persians and later the Ottoman Empire. The Ottoman Sultan had already taken the title of Caliph from the last Abbassid in Egypt in 1517 and Iraq became an Ottoman Province when Suleyman the Magnificent took Baghdad in 1534.

Istria, the largest peninsula in the Adriatic Sea, was initially inhabited by the Illyrian tribe of the Histri. The region was conquered by the Romans in 177 BC, and under Roman rule Istria became a crucial province of the empire, with notable developments such as the establishment of the city of Pula. Following the fall of the Western Roman Empire, Istria experienced periods of Byzantine, Lombard, and Frankish control. In the medieval period, it came under the influence of the Venetian Republic, which left a lasting cultural and architectural legacy. After the fall of Venice, Istria was incorporated into the Habsburg Monarchy and later became part of the unified Kingdom of Italy.

Italy boasts a rich and diverse history that spans over three millennia. It was the heart of the ancient Roman Empire, which profoundly influenced Western civilization through its contributions to law, politics, architecture, and culture. After the fall of Rome in 476 AD, Italy fragmented into numerous city-states and kingdoms, including the influential maritime republics of Venice and Genoa. The Renaissance, which began in Italy in the 14th century, marked a period of extraordinary cultural and artistic achievement which made Italy the focal point of Europe for three centuries. Italy was unified in the 19th century under the leadership of figures like Giuseppe Garibaldi and Count Cavour, culminating in the establishment of the unified Kingdom of Italy in 1861.

Jodhpur was the most important and powerful principality in the Rajputana region in north-western India. Despite at times being forced to pay tribute to the Muslim rulers of Delhi, and later the Mughal Empire, Jodhpur always retained its autonomy and its Hindu religion - an amazing feat considering that the principality was completely surrounded by Muslim powers.

The first crusade was successful in recovering the holy city of Jerusalem, from the Muslims, in 1099. In the XIIth century, the Latin knights created fiefdoms in the Holy Land and Jerusalem was the capital of a new Kingdom. The divisions of the crusaders and their poor knowledge of their Muslims neighbors allowed Saladin to take back the city. The struggle between Christians and Muslims over the eastern Mediterranean coast lasted for nearly two centuries and ended with the loss of the last Frankish fortress in 1291 at St Jean d'Acre. Jerusalem would be ruled by Mameluks and later Ottomans, but the Christian nations would never lost the hope to take back Jerusalem.

Jutland, a peninsula in Northern Europe, forms the continental part of Denmark and extends into northern Germany (Schleswig-Holstein). Historically known as the Cimbric Peninsula, it has been inhabited since prehistoric times by various tribes, including the Jutes, after whom it is named. The region was significant during the Viking Age and later became a crucial part of the Danish kingdom. Jutland's strategic location has made it a focal point in various conflicts, including the notable Battle of Jutland during the First World War, which was the largest naval battle in history.

As an ancient city, Kabul has seen its share of local sovereigns and empires.  During the 14th century, Kabul rose to fame as a powerful trading outpost in the Timurid Empire.  Located in between Transoxiana, Indian and Persia, Kabul was an important nexus for trade routes as well as great starting point for would be emperors.  In 1504, conquered by Babur, Kabul became the capital of the nascent Mughal Empire.  It would maintain this distinction until the fall of Delhi in 1526.

The Kalmyks were an Oirat (western Mongol) tribe who migrated from Mongolia across the Eurasian steppe into the lands of the Kazakhs (whom they fought) and eventually into the Caucasus, where they settled in the 17th century after displacing the western remnant of the Nogai horde. Though a small and largely pastoral realm, the Kalmyk Khanate was an important regional vassal for the Russian Tsar and provided skilled horsemen for Russian expeditions against the Tatars and Turks, before finally being annexed into Russia in 1771.

The Kalmar Union was a political union that brought together the kingdoms of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden under a single monarch from 1397 to 1523. Initiated by Queen Margaret I of Denmark, the union aimed to consolidate power and create stability in the region. The union was formalized in the Swedish city of Kalmar, where the three kingdoms agreed to be ruled by Margaret's grandnephew, Eric of Pomerania. Despite its initial success in unifying the Scandinavian countries, the union faced internal conflicts and power struggles, particularly from the cantankerous Swedish nobility. The Kalmar Union ultimately dissolved in 1523 when Sweden declared independence under King Gustav Vasa.

The Kingdom of Kanem, located in modern-day Chad, flourished from the 9th to the 14th century AD. It was established by a confederation of nomadic peoples and ruled by the Saifawa dynasty. Positioned on the eastern shores of Lake Chad, Kanem became a significant hub for trade, connecting central African peoples with the Nile Valley and North African states. The kingdom adopted Islam in the 11th century through contact with Muslim traders and clerics. The late 14th century saw the kingdom's decline, and its rulers relocated to establish the Bornu Empire on the western side of Lake Chad.

The greatest Turkish principality to emerge from the ruins of the Seljuk Empire, the Beylik of Karaman was often in conflict with the upstart Ottomans whose initial subjugation of them was ended with the Ottoman defeat at Ankara in 1402 by the forces of Tamerlane. While the Ottoman defeat and subsequent civil wars allowed the Karamans to regain most of their previously lost territories in Anatolia, the Beylik never regained the upper hand and by 1470 was reduced to a province of the resurgent Ottoman Empire.

The Khanate of Kazan was a splinter faction of the Golden Horde that broke off in 1437 and became a power to be reckoned with in its own right. It lasted until Yadigar Muhammad's army was crushed by the forces of Ivan the Terrible in 1552.

Nomadic Uzbeks had been raiding Sogdiana for some time in the late XVth century when they used quarrels for succession to Timurid throne to invade the Timurid empire. The Uzbeks took Samarkand and Boukhara in 1500. Bâbur, one of the last Timurids, had fled in Kabul in 1504. The Persians stopped the Uzbeks advance in 1510, allowing the rise of the new Safavid dynasty in Persia. The Uzbeks conquered Khwarazm in 1511 and from there created what would be the Khanate of Khiva. Far from being a united nation, it was at first a confederation of four tribes, whose heads, the sultans, elected a Khan, generally the oldest member. The Khanate expected to benefit of the caravans passing through the land, but the trade and generally all the activities in the Khanate stagnated for more than a century, with religious imams taking precedence over the rulers. A change of dynasty, the arrival of Turkmens and a change toward a more centralized rule allowed more stability and economic progress. The land was still poor and the Khanate relied heavily on the raids performed on the surrounding states.

The Khmer Empire was a powerful state in Southeast Asia that flourished from 802 to 1431 AD. Centered in present-day Cambodia, it was founded by Jayavarman II, who declared himself a universal ruler, or chakravartin. The empire is renowned for its impressive architectural achievements, particularly the construction of Angkor Wat, one of the largest religious monuments in the world. At its height, the Khmer Empire controlled vast territories - including parts of modern-day Thailand, Laos, and Vietnam - and was the main bastion of the Hindu religion and Sanskrit language in Southeast Asia. The empire's decline began in the 13th century due to internal strife, external invasions, and ecological challenges, culminating in the fall of Angkor to the Siamese in 1431.

Khorasan was occupied by Arabs in the mid-7th century and Abu Muslim used Khorasan as his poer base to attack the Umayyad Caliphate. It contributed to the power of the early Abbasid Caliphate but was severely devestated by Turkish invasions in the mid 12th century, the Mongols from 1220-1222 and Timur in 1383. With the fall of the Timurid Empire Khorasan has again asserted its power as a possible succesor kingdom to Timur's failing empire.

Kievan Rus' was established in the late 9th century by the Viking leader Oleg the Wise, and was the first East Slavic state and a significant medieval political federation. Centered around the city of Kiev, it united various Slavic and Finnic tribes under the rule of the Rurik dynasty. The state reached its zenith in the 10th and 11th centuries, particularly under the reigns of Vladimir the Great and Yaroslav the Wise, who expanded its territory and promoted Orthodox Christianity. Kievan Rus' played a crucial role in the cultural and political development of Eastern Europe before gradually declining due to dynastic infighting, culminating in the Mongol invasion of the 13th century.

The people known as the Zanj (a name given to them by the early Arab traders) have dominated the eastern African coastline for centuries, long before the arrival of Islam. The early tribal peoples and clans that make up this region are better known as the Swahili, which derives its name from the Arabic word 'sawahil' meaning 'the coast people'. From around 1200 to 1500, powerful Swahili city-states, most of them from the native Bantu tribes, began to emerge as thriving centers of commerce in the east African trade. Kilwa became the most important coastal trading center by 1000 A.D. In the 13th century, it captured Sofala whose gold resources made it the most prosperous Zanj state. By 1490, the decline in gold trade and its rivalry with Mombasa would remove Kilwa's glory permanently During the 1500s, the Portuguese began occupying areas of the Zanj coastline, starting with Kilwa.

The Kipchaks were a Turkic nomadic people who played a significant role in the Eurasian Steppe during the Middle Ages. Originating near the Altai region, they expanded westward by the 9th century, forming a powerful confederation with the Cumans. By the 11th century, the Kipchaks controlled vast territories from the Aral Sea to the Black Sea. They were known for their skills as pastoralists and warriors, often engaging in conflicts with neighboring states such as the Kievan Rus', Byzantines and Hungarians. The Kipchak confederation eventually fell to the Mongol invasions in the 13th century, with many Kipchaks being absorbed into the Golden Horde or fleeing to other regions. Their legacy includes significant cultural and linguistic contributions, such as the Codex Cumanicus, a trilingual dictionary of Kipchak, Latin, and Persian.

The county of Cleve existed from the XIth century, with the town, itself, chartered in 1242. The county was united to the neighboring county of Mark and was made a duchy in 1417. In 1521 it expanded again, gaining the Duchies of Berg and Jülich. At the end of the House of Jülich-Berg-Cleve, in 1609, a short war of succession saw the Palatinate taking to the field against Brandenburg. With the treaty of Xanten in 1614, the Palatinate took Jülich and Berg and Brandenburg took Cleve and Mark. The lands were held by the French during the Revolution and Napoleonic Wars and it were given back to Prussia in 1815.

The Order of the Hospital of Saint John of Jerusalem was originally a monastic brotherhood founded on the basis of an existing hospital in the Holy Land dedicated to care for the pilgrims. With the first Crusade and the conquest of Jerusalem, it evolved in a religious and military order. When Acre fell in 1291, the order moved to Cyprus first then to Rhodes. From there they preyed on the Muslim traders and Barbary pirates. They benefited of the dissolution of the Templar order, gaining many possessions in all Europe. They withstood many invasions from the Mameluks and the Ottomans, but in 1522 they had to flee Rhodes when confronted to the 400 ships and 200,000 men of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent. At first, withdrawing in Sicily, the King Charles I of Spain gave them the island of Malta where the order continued its fight against Muslims. They finally fell to Bonaparte on his way to Egypt in 1798. They ceased to be a military order, but still continue to exist as a humanitarian organization and as a sovereign nation in Rome.

Kokand, a city in the Fergana Valley of eastern Uzbekistan, has a history dating back to at least the 10th century when it was known as Khavakand. It was a significant hub on the Silk Road, facilitating trade between South Asia and East Asia. The city was destroyed by the Mongols in the 13th century but later revived. In 1709, Kokand became the capital of the Khanate of Kokand, a powerful Central Asian state that lasted until 1876. The khanate was known for its cultural and economic prosperity, as well as its strategic importance in the region.

The Archbishop of Cologne was one of the seven Electors of the Holy Roman empire since 1356. But the city of Cologne was self-governing since 1288 and was a trade city, member of the Hanseatic League. Its trade flourished because of its location on the River Rhine, in the heart of Germany. Cologne became a free imperial city in 1475. The city and the trade declined with the forced emigration of the Jews in the XVth century and the restrictions on Protestants in the following centuries when most of the neighbor states were Protestants. Cologne was seized by the French Revolutionaries in 1794 and held until 1815, when the land was ceded to Prussia.

In the XVth century, the kingdom of Congo ruled over from what is now the south of Gabon to Angola and from the Atlantic Ocean to the Kwango River. Other small and more or less autonomous kingdoms paid it tribute. Kongo was ruled by the manikongo or king and was divided into provinces around the central capital area. Each province was administered by a governor appointed by the manikongo. The country was administratively developed with a large trade network and a finance administration. The Portuguese were the first European nation to establish relations with the King of Kongo, in the 1480s. Christian missionaries were sent and the king of Kongo converted to Christianity and took a Portuguese name. But the relations became less friendly in the XVIth century when the slaves trade grew, lowering the power of the kingdom. The kingdom fell apart in the XVIIth century.

Squeezed in between China, Japan, and the warlike Manchu tribes, Korea was always in peril of becoming swallowed up by one of its great neighbors. Despite this precarious situation, Korea managed to survive and thrive under the Choson dynasty that was established in 1392 and lasted till 1910, although they did pay tribute to the Chinese Emperor. The peace was shattered in 1592, when Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the Japanese Shogun who had just reunified Japan, sent a large force to Korea in an alleged attempt to invade China. The Korean land forces suffered a series of defeats, but Korean naval forces, led by Admiral Yi Sun-shin, secured full control of the sea. With the help of China, the Japanese were finally driven out in 1598. The next serious threat appeared when the nomadic Manchu violated the borders of both Ming China and Korea in the early 17th century. Ming Chinese and Korean punitive attacks on Manchu strongholds in 1619 were beaten back, and in 1627 the Manchu overran northern Korea, forcing them to pay tribute to them instead of the Ming dynasty.

Kurdistan, the ethnic homeland of the Iranian Kurdish people since ancient times, spans parts of eastern Turkey, northern Iraq, western Iran, and northern Syria. Throughout history, various Kurdish dynasties, such as the Hasanwayhids, Marwanids, and Ayyubids, have ruled parts of the region - often fighting either with or against neighboring Arab, Persian and Turkish rulers. The Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 marked a significant turning point, aligning the Kurds with the Ottoman Empire. Despite never achieving political unity, Kurdistan has long been a significant cultural and political entity in the Middle East, and its proud people have never accepted foreign occupation.

Crete, the largest of the Greek islands, has a history that stretches back to ancient times and is renowned as the cradle of the Minoan civilization, Europe's first advanced society, which flourished from around 2700 to 1420 BC. The island's strategic location made it a significant cultural and trade hub in the Mediterranean. Following the decline of the Minoans, Crete was successively ruled by the Mycenaeans, Romans, Byzantines, Venetians, and Ottomans. Each of these periods left a distinct mark on the island's cultural and architectural heritage, and under the four centuries of Venetian rule (1205-1667) the island kingdom was known as Candia.

Carniola, an historical region in present-day Slovenia, was initially inhabited by the Celtic tribe of the Carni, and was later incorporated into the Roman province of Pannonia. In the 6th century, Slovenes settled in the area, and it became part of the Holy Roman Empire in the 11th century as the March of Carniola. The region was ruled by the Habsburgs from the late 13th century and was elevated to a duchy in 1364. Carniola remained under Habsburg control, becoming part of the Austrian Empire in 1804 and later Austria-Hungary in 1867.

The Kashmir Sultanate was a medieval Islamic kingdom located in the Kashmir Valley, with its capital at Srinagar. It was founded in the early 14th century by Rinchan Shah, a Ladakhi Buddhist noble who converted to Islam. The sultanate saw significant cultural and political development under the Shah Mir dynasty (1339-1561) but experienced rapid decline under the later Chak dynasty (1561-1589), including the Mughal conquest and the fall of Srinagar. The sultanate's greatest legacy was its religious and cultural syncretism - a concept known as 'Kashmiriyat' - and the gradual transition of Kashmir from Hinduism to Islam, as well as the emergence of a distinct Punjabi identity and religion (Sikhism) to the southwest.

The early Baltic tribes who inhabited the region, the Letts and Kurs, were subjugated in the 13th century by the Livonian Brothers of the Sword. In 1561 the Order disbanded and its grand master became the first duke of Courland under Polish suzerainty. In the Northern War (1700-21) it was taken (1701) by Charles XII of Sweden. Empress Anna who was by marriage duchess of Courland before her accession in Russia forced (1737) the nobles of Courland to elect her favorite Ernst Johann von Biron their duke. Russian influence became paramount and with the third partition of Poland (1795) the duchy finally passed to Russia.

Küstrin, now known as Kostrzyn, is a town on the eastern bank of the Oder River in present-day Poland. Originally settled by Slavic tribes in the 10th century, it became a significant site when the Knights Templar established a market and received a city charter in the 13th century. The town developed into a fortified stronghold with the construction of a castle and additional fortifications in the mid-1500s. Küstrin played a strategic role in various conflicts, including the Thirteen Years' War - following which the Teutonic Knights sold it to Brandenburg - the Seven Years' War, and the Napoleonic Wars.

Kutei (Kutai Karta Negara) is one of the most ancient Hindu states in South-East Asia. The oldest available yupa (sacrificial pole) dates from about 400 AD, and mentions both Maharaja Mula Varman and his son Acwa Varman. Thereafter, the state virtually disappears from the view of the outside world. Little is heard about the state or its ruling dynasty until 1365, when brief mention is made in the epic Javanese historical poem Negarakartagama. The ruler converted to Islam in 1565. Contact with the outside world gradually expanded thereafter. The Dutch first visited the area in 1635 under Gerrit Thomassen Pool, but achieved little and retired. Bugis mariners arrived in 1721, defeated the ruler, established a permanent settlement at Samaranda and took control of the principality of Pasir. In time, they intermarried with the local Malays and Dayaks. They became a permanent feature of the state and served as the ruler's soldiers and policemen. Under Bugis influence, Islam took a more prominent role in state affairs. The ruler assumed the Islamic title of Sultan ca. 1732 and implemented a number of religious decrees. Nevertheless, traditional Hindu practices continued to enjoy a pre-eminent place in cultural affairs. The arrival of the British during the Raffles administration increased European interest in Kutei. Explorers and military officers visited and wrote about its unique culture. However, it wasn't until 1825 that permanent relations were established with the Sultan. In the meantime, commercial relations had progressed quite rapidly with British traders in Singapore. Rattan, gutta-percha and bees-wax were amongst the major exports. This did not please the Dutch and they appointed a local civil administrator in 1846.

The Kazakhs were (and are) a people of Turkish and Mongol ancestry with a Khan descended from the Mongol conqueror Chenghis Khan. Originally part of the White Horde which inhabited the steppes of what is today northern Kazakhstan, they split with the group later known as the Uzbeks because of a dispute over the leadership of the White Horde, causing the disintegration of that Mongol Horde. The Kazakhs later settled in all parts of modern Kazakhstan and eventually became divided into three hordes - the Small, the Middle, and the Great, with the leaders of the Great and Middle Hordes fighting each other for overall supremacy.

When Carlos III rose to the throne in Spain a great reform of the Spanish American possessions was started. One of those reforms was the division of the 'Virreynato del Perú' for political reasons, creating a new Virreynato called 'de la Plata' with its capital in Buenos Aires. The new Virreynato included the territories of Charcas Tucumán Cuyo Paraguay and Buenos Aires. Later, in 1810 when Napoleon Bonaparte invaded Spain and replaced Carlos V with his brother José Bonaparte, several 'juntas' were created in Spain and Spanish America to govern in the name of the true king. One of those was the 'Primera Junta' of Buenos Aires. First they swore loyalty to Fernando VII, the heir of Carlos V, but later they broke their links with Spain and declared independence in July 1816.

The Teutonic Order was a military and religious order founded in the late XIIth century during the siege of Acre in the Third Crusade. Preferingly chosen by German knights, its role was to help the pilgrims and the crusaders in the Holy Land. After the fall of Acre in 1291, the Order withdrew in their land possessions of Prussia and Livonia where they went on the crusade, against the pagan people living in Eastern Europe. It founded a new nation where more Germans came either to fight or to settle. Their capital was set in Marienburg in 1309. The decline of the order began with the rise of Poland as a major power. The battle of Tannenberg, won by the Poles, the Lithuanians and Bohemian or Tatar mercenaries, stopped the expansion of the order. In 1525, the Grand-Master of the Teutonic Order, Albert of Brandenburg, who had embraced the Reformation, created a secular duchy of Prussia, vassal to Poland.

The Lan Xang Hom Khao or 'the land of a million elephants and of the white parasol' was created in the XIVth century by the Prince Fa Gnum. This Lao prince, educated in the Khmer Empire, at Angkor Vat, went through the valley of Mekong and unified the states of what is now Laos. Supported at first by the Khmer Empire, the land would know sixty years of prosperity and then one century of decline and instability before falling prey to its neighbours.

Leinster was the southeastern Irish kingdom. Traditional quarrels between the Irish kingdoms were interrupted in the late XIIth century by the settlements of Anglo-Normans lords, who encouraged by Henry II of England, dethroned the king of Leinster. The Irish lords were replaced by English nobility such as the Fitzgeralds and the Butlers except in the more mountainous areas. In the XVIIth century, the Cromwellian campaigns ensured English rule and land ownership.

León, in northwestern Spain, was originally founded as a Roman military encampment in the 1st century BC. It became the capital of the Kingdom of León in 910 AD, playing a crucial role in the Christian Reconquista against the Moors. The city flourished during the Middle Ages, becoming a center of political and cultural activity in Iberia, and co-capital of the unified Kingdom of Castile-León after 1230. Notable landmarks from this period include the León Cathedral, a masterpiece of Gothic architecture, and the Basilica of San Isidoro, which houses the Royal Pantheon.

The name is known in Western Europe since the early Xth century when the Liths settled in the area as early as 1500 B.C. The pagan tribes were rarely united until they were attacked in the XIIIth century by the Livonian Brothers of the Sword and the Teutonic Knights. The Christian orders conquered an area which now comprises Estonia, Latvia, and parts of Lithuania. The Liths united under a single grand-duke and converted to the Orthodox religion. Their lands extended in actual Belarus, Ukraine and part of Russia. In 1386, Grand Duke Jagiello became king of Poland marrying with the daughter of Louis I of Poland. He converted to Christianity and also made it the state religion in the Lithuanian part of the new Commonwealth. This Commonwealth would become a single nation, the largest in Europe, in 1569.

First German attempts to penetrate into Baltic region can be traced back to the second half of the XII century, when German merchants began to establish numerous trading posts on the Baltic coast. German missionaries came right after them and tried to thrust a new religion - Christianity on the local tribes of Livs, Estes and Kurs. In 1201 Germans founded the first city in the conquered lands - Riga, which later became the main citadel of German colonization in the area. Pope Innocentius III declared a special crusade against the pagans, Livs, Kurs and other neighboring tribes. A special order, called Livonian Order or Swordbrothers' Order (in accordance with a depiction of a sword on the capotes of the brethern). The statute of newly established Order was copied after those in Palestine. In 20-30s of XIII century Livs, Kurs and other neighboring tribes were already conquered and force-converted. The Order imposed a heavy duty on the peasants in favor of the Church. Political power was shared by the Archbishops of Riga and Grandmasters of the Order. As time passed by, the Order was losing its possessions and fully disintegrated towards the beginning of the Livonian War 1558-1583. The last Grandmaster of the Order, Gotthard Kettler, seculirized the Order after the Ergem battle of 1560, and formed an independent Duchy of Courland.

The north Thailand area was inhabited by the Mons. In the XIIIth century, Meng Rai, a Thai King born in a small independent principality in Chiang Saen, destroyed the last Mon kingdom. He unified the Thai tribes and created a new kingdom, 'Lan-Na-Thai', meaning 'land of a million rice fields'. He extended his kingdom to Lampang in the south and to Lamphun and received tribute from several surrounding kingdoms. He created the cities of Chiang Rai and Chiang Mai, the latter one becoming the capital in 1345. The country resisted the expansion of the southern Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya, but also from the invasions from Burma or Laos. The XVth century was the golden age of both Thai kingdoms of Lan Na and Ayutthaya in spite of their rivalry. Many temples were built and in 1455 the king of Lan Na managed to hold the Eight World Buddhist Council in Chiang Mai. The country entered in a decline phase in the XVIth century with quarrels over the succession of the throne, a devastating earthquake in Chiang Mai and the fall of the capital to the Burmese kingdom of Pegu. Lan Na would remain partially controlled and subjugated by Burmese kings for two centuries.

The first Singhalese population probably came from Orissa or Bengal. The legend claim that the first Singhalese prince was the son of a Bengalese princess and a lion (sinha) whence de name of Sinhala for Lanka. The Tamul people originated from the southern tip of India and came in the XIIIth century. Their kingsdoms pushed the Singhalese kingdoms to the south of the island. The island was a major trade center, with traders coming from Persia, Arabia, Burma or Malaysia. The island flourished and was a major Buddhist center with many temples, monasteries or schools. The first Portuguese mission arrived in Lanka in 1505 and the Dutch came in the XVIIth century. Both settled in the island and only the hilly area in the middle of the island remained independent. The British  East India Company would take the island in 1796 and the last independent kingdom disappeared in 1815.

Lorraine, or Lothringen, was created as a German duchy in the Xth century. The House of Alsace was given the duchy and became House of Lothringen, ruling the land until 1738. In the XVth century, the duchy is the objective of Burgundy to get a continuous territorial access between Burgundy and its possessions in the Low Countries. The Duke of Lorraine, René II, took an alliance with the King of France and defeated Charles the Bold at Nancy in 1477. The XVIth century was a flourishing era at the beginning but plagues and then religion wars stroke the duchy in the second half of the century. In France, a cadet branch of the House of Lorraine, the Guise family, led the Ultra-Catholic faction but was unable to seize the throne of France. The XVIIth century was a difficult one with plague again, the Thirty Years war and the French occupation. Lorraine would be occupied during nearly all wars involving France in spite of the repeated guaranties of Lorraine's independence in the treaties of Westphalia, Pyrenees or Ryswick. The duchy was occupied once again in the XVIIIth century, maintained for a time as a puppet state and finally annexed in 1766.

Louisiana, established in 1682 by French explorer René-Robert Cavelier de La Salle, was a vast territory named in honor of King Louis XIV. It stretched from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico and from the Appalachian Mountains to the Rocky Mountains. The region served as an administrative district of New France and included notable settlements such as Mobile, Biloxi, and its capital of Nouvelle-Orléans (later New Orleans), founded in 1718. Louisiana was a hub for trade, particularly in furs, and developed a unique cultural blend influenced by French, African, and Native American traditions. The territory changed hands several times, being ceded to Spain in 1762, briefly returned to France in 1800, and finally sold to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.

The Kingdom of Lotharingia was established in 855 AD as a medieval successor state of the Carolingian Empire, and named after King Lothair II who inherited the territory following the Treaty of Prüm. It encompassed regions of present-day Lorraine (France), Luxemburg, the Netherlands, Belgium, and parts of western Germany. Lotharingia was formed from the division of Middle Francia, itself a result of the Treaty of Verdun in 843. The kingdom experienced frequent conflicts between East and West Francia due to its strategic and prestigious location. In 959, Lotharingia was divided into Upper and Lower Lorraine, eventually becoming buffer states of the Holy Roman Empire and losing its identity as an independent realm.

The city of Luang Prabang was named after a sacred gold Buddha called 'Pra Bang' which was a gift from the Khmer court to Fa Ngum. Fa Ngum was a Lao prince raised in the court of Angkor Wat who carved out the kingdom of Lan Xang in 1353. It encompassed all of present-day Laos and most of northeast Thailand. Luang Prabang became the centre of Lao culture trade and religion for the next 200 years. When King Souligna Vongsa died in 1694 without an heir the leadership of Lan Xang was contested. In 1713 the nation split into three kingdoms: Luang Prabang, Vientiane and Champassak. This division attracted outside aggressors, and by the 1800s most of Lan Xang had become a satellite state of Siam, with the exception of Luang Prabang, which held on to a the remnants.

The city of Luxemburg was founded in the 10th century on the ruins of a Roman settlement. In the 14th century the Dukes of Luxemburg rose to become the most powerful noble family in Germany by acquiring Bohemia, Brandenburg, and Hungary. From 1347 on the family also held the office of Holy Roman Emperor. In 1437 Luxemburg's glory came to an abrupt end with the death of Sigismund, the last ruler of the House of Luxemburg. The city itself was soon conquered by Philip of Burgundy. In 1477 Burgundy and with it Luxemburg were inherited by Maximilian of Habsburg and the city remained under Habsburg control for the next three centuries. In 1795 Luxembourg was conquered by the armies of revolutionary France but in 1815 the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg was reestablished ruled by the Kings of the Netherlands.

The classical era of the Maya civilization rose to its highest in the IXth century. Climatic changes and human induced ecologic disasters probably caused the drastic depopulation of the area. The Toltec civilization rose after the Mayas, mixing a Mexican influence to the Maya culture. Metallurgy and ceramics appeared. But these lands in Central America were still poor and their manpower was quite not high enough to resist the Spanish troops arriving in Yucatan and Guatemala after the destruction of the Aztecs in 1521. The lands were even more desert by the diseases brought by the Spanish in the early XVIth century. Without major needs for slaves with few mines and an unfavorable climate and vegetation, the Maya population was neither exterminated nor fully incorporated in a Métis society.  They still form the mass of the rural population.

Madurai is an ancient city which once visited by traders from Rome and Greece in the 3rd century BC. During the 15th century, Madurai was one of several nayaka states under the rule of Vijayanagar. Upon the fall of that empire, the Nayaks of Madurai rose to power in southern India, frequently threatening the neighboring states of Tanjore and Travancore. In the 18th century, its own existence was threatened by the Nawab of Arcot and the Maratha Empire. In 1752, the kingdom passed into the hands of the British.

The city of Magdeburg was founded in 805 by Charlemagne. It became an archbishopric in 968. In the next century, the city received a chart that would be a pattern for many others city charts in Germany. The city flourished through its trade to The Low Countries and the North Sea, becoming a member of the Hanseatic League in the XIIIth century. The city was brought to the Reformation by Martin Luther. It joined the Schmalkaldic League in 1531 and resisted to the Emperor, leading to the siege and the fall of the city in 1551 by Maurice of Saxony.  In 1630, during the Thirty Years War, the imperial troops led by the count of Tilly sacked and burnt the city, slaughtering the inhabitants. After the Peace of Westphalia in 1648, Magdeburg was given to the elector of Brandeburg.

By the middle of the 16th century the Maharashtra region of India was fragmented among several independent Muslim rulers, who fought each other endlessly but paid tribute to either the Mughals, Bijapur or Golconda. It was in the midst of this chaos that a great leader, Sivaji Bhonsle, was born in 1627. Sivaji was outraged at the oppression that the mainly Hindu people had to suffer at the hands their Muslim overlords. In a long series of campaigns, he showed astonishing prowess, and eventually founded a large Maratha Empire that would shake the Mughal Empire to its foundations. During the 18th century almost all of western and central India, as well as large segments of the north and east, had been brought under Maratha suzerainty.

Founded on the back of Srivijaya, Majapahit quickly became a great Hindu state. During its golden age (1350-1389) the great Majapahit empire controlled most of modern Indonesia. By the 15th century, the Majapahit princes were frequently at war over the sucession. The war-torn state would limp along until the 16th cenutry, when the invading forces of the sultanate of Demak caused the remaining Majapahit nobles to flee to Bali.

In 746, the city of Mainz was made the seat of the first German archbishop - St. Boniface. Subsequent archbishops acquired considerable territory around Mainz and in Franconia on both sides of the Main which they ruled as princes of the Holy Roman Empire. Very early on they received a vote in the imperial elections and had precedence over the other electors - they crowned the Kings of Germany. From the 16th century the Archbishops-Elector of Mainz was the ex officio archchancellor of the Holy Roman Empire. Under the rule of the Archbishops-Electors Mainz flourished as a commercial and cultural center. Johann Gutenberg (1397–1468) lived in Mainz which he founded the first printing enterprise in Europe.

The African empire of Mali has been founded in the XIth century and unified in 1222 by Sundjata Keita. At its peak, under the rule of Mansa Moussa, it extended from the Atlantic Ocean to the Niger River. Its prosperity lied on the trade of gold, copper, salt and clothes through the Sahara desert. Tombuktu and Djenne became important center of trades but, moreover, intellectual centers with many schools and libraries. The empire of Mali disintegrated and was replaced By the Empire of Songhai in the late XVth century.

A Mamluk dynasty ruled in Egypt since 1250 and the fall of the Caliphate in Bagdad by the Mongols in 1258 and their own victory against them in 1261 helped them to  maintain their power. In the XIVth and XVth century, the Mamluk empire has been stricken by two major plagues, major political unstability periods and the Timurid invasion in Syria. The empire knew a strong economic decline aggravated by the end of their monopoly on spices when Portuguese ships sailed around Africa. At the end of the XVth century, two major opponents appeared, the Ottoman Turks and the Persians. Cairo is captured in 1517 by Sultan Selim who put an end to the Mameluk dynasty in Egypt. The Mameluks stayed as a class, providing many local governors. One of them managed to proclaim himself Sultan in 1769, and if he fell in 1772, the ottomans gave Egypt a great autonomy. The Mamluks were defeated by Bonaparte when he invaded Egypt and lost their power when Mehmet Ali Pacha rules Egypt in 1805.

The city is ancient as it was once an Etruscan settlement. The city passed in 1328 to the Gonzaga family, a Ghibelline supporter, who would hold it until 1708 with the title of Duke of Mantua. The family was a patron of arts in the Renaissance and gave to the city many palaces, frescoes and sculptures. During the Thirty Years War, the duchy was the place of a side war between France, Savoy and the Habsburgs for the succession of the ducal throne. Part of the deal was the Marquisate of Montferrat, a strategic place in the Piedmont, hold by Mantua. France won the peace in spite of a bad military campaign and Charles de Nevers, from a lower branch of the House of Gonzaga, became Duke of Mantua.  Mantua passed to Austria in 1708 after siding with France in the War of Spanish Succession. Mantua was taken by Bonaparte in 1797 and given back to Austria in 1815.

The Manchu people were originally known as Jurchet, a tribe known in Asia since the VIIth century. They were related to the Tungus and were a confederation of nomadic tribes in Manchuria. They swept over North China and Korea in the XIIIth century, overthrowing the local dynasties before being repelled by the Mongols in 1234. The Manchu settled in the Songhua River valley and developed a pastoral and agrarian civilization. In the late XVIth century, they began to unite under the authority of a single chief, Nurhachi. He reformed the social and military organization and invaded China in 1618. The Mandchus progressively took the power in China and created the Chinese Qing dynasty in 1646.

Madagascar, the world's fourth-largest island, is located off the southeastern coast of Africa in the Indian Ocean. It was first settled by Austronesian peoples from Southeast Asia around 700 AD, followed by Bantu migrants from Africa. This unique blend of cultures created the Malagasy people, whose language and traditions reflect both Asian and African influences. The island was a significant center for trade and piracy in the Indian Ocean during the medieval period. In the 19th century, the Merina Kingdom unified much of Madagascar before it was colonized by France in 1896.

Meath - known as the 'Royal County' - is a region in eastern Ireland with a rich historical legacy. It was originally part of the ancient Kingdom of Meath, which was established by the legendary king Túathal Techtmar in the first century. The kingdom was a significant political and cultural center, serving as the seat of the High Kings of Ireland at the Hill of Tara. In the medieval period, Meath was invaded by the Anglo-Normans, leading to the establishment of the Lordship of Meath by Hugh de Lacy in the late 12th century. The county was formally shired in 1297 and later divided into Meath and Westmeath in 1542. Today, Meath is celebrated for its historical sites, including Newgrange, Trim Castle, and the Hill of Tara, which reflect its storied past.

Mecklenburg was inhabited by Western Slavic people from the VIIth to the XIIth century. The land has been taken by Henry the Lion in the late XIIth century and Christianized and settled by German and Flemish people. In 1348 Mecklenburg was raised as a duchy to be split in 1352 in Mecklenburg-Schwerin and Mecklemburg-Stargard. United in 1471, it split again in 1520, creating the duchy of Mecklenburg-Guestrow (and united again in 1610to be split in 1621). Both duchies embraced the Reformation and in spite of these dynastic reorganizations they were stable and flourishing. They maintained their independence, joining the Confederation of the Rhine in 1808 to be established as a Grand-Duchy in 1815.

Mesopotamia is an historical region located between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, and its name is reflected in that fact - meaning, literally 'between two rivers'. It is renowned for being the Cradle of Civilization, including the Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians, and Assyrians. These societies made significant advancements in writing, law, architecture, and agriculture, with notable inventions such as the wheel, cuneiform script, and the concept of time. Mesopotamia's fertile land and strategic location fostered the growth of cities like Ur, Uruk, Babylon, and Nineveh, which became centers of culture and power. The region's history spans from the early settlements around 10,000 BC to the fall of Babylon in 539 BC, and the apogee of the Achaemenid Empire.

After the final conquest of the lands of the Aztecs, the Spanish established a larged colonial empire under the name of New-Spain. The land would extend in what is now Mexico, Central America and most of the Southern United States in California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas. After the initial explorations, came the times of the foundation of cities, the Christianization and the settling. The population would never be very large, benefiting to a few Spanish landholders and some Métis elite. Spain maintained a strong colonial power resented by the local population. Some reforms were brought but the resentment was growing. The first rebellions came in 1810 when Spain was invaded by the French armies but the independence was only recognized in 1821.

The people known as the Zanj (a name given to them by the early Arab traders) have dominated the eastern African coastline for centuries, long before the arrival of Islam. The early tribal peoples and clans that make up this region are better known as the Swahili, which derives its name from the Arabic word 'sawahil' meaning 'the coast people'. From around 1200 to 1500, powerful Swahili city-states, most of them from the native Bantu tribes, began to emerge as thriving centers of commerce in the east African trade. Next to Kilwa, Mogadishu was the next powerful Zanj state. It derived its influence from its location in the north giving it contacts with the Arab world. Mogadishu rose in the 13th and 14th centuries only to gradually decline in the 15th century in comparison to the increasing importance of Kilwa and Mombasa.

The kingdoms of Gowa and Tallo in Sulawesi were founded as a single kingdom in the early XIVth century. It was split in the XVth century. They expanded around 1530 to the surrounding principalities. By the time the Portuguese arrived, in 1540, Gowa and Tallo were controlling the gold and spice trades and Makassar was the main harbour. The kingdoms became sultanates in the early XVIIth century in a way of choosing a Muslim preference for trade rather than trading with the newly arrived Dutch VOC. A struggle began only interrupted by three peace and trade treaties in 1637, 1655 and 1660. In 1666, the Dutch used the call for help of a rebellious kingdom to seize Makassar. The sultanate of Gowa fell in 1669, all fortresses were destroyed and the VOC was now controlling the spices trade.

Malacca was founded around 1400 by a prince of Palembang refusing to be the vassal of the Javanese Majapahit Empire. Malacca claimed its suzerainty over Palembang without being able to enforce it. The city was quickly a major center of trade with China, Indonesia, India and the Middle East. The prince converted to Islam to help Malacca's trade with the Muslims traders and Islam propagated in Malay through Malacca. In 1511, the Portuguese Afonso de Albuquerque came from Goa in India and seized Malacca. The sultan fled to Johor and the friendly sultanates in Java tried unsuccessfully to take it back in the XVIth century. Malacca's wealth was based on the Muslim trade and the Portuguese could not get the full wealth of the trade in the Malacca Straits. In 1641, the Dutch of the V.O.C. allied themselves with Johor and captured Malacca.

The people known as the Zanj (a name given to them by the early Arab traders) have dominated the eastern African coastline for centuries, long before the arrival of Islam. The early tribal peoples and clans that make up this region are better known as the Swahili, which derives its name from the Arabic word 'sawahil' meaning 'the coast people'. From around 1200 to 1500, powerful Swahili city-states, most of them from the native Bantu tribes, began to emerge as thriving centers of commerce in the east African trade. The city of Malindi was founded about the same time as Mombasa and the two were always bitter rivals. However, Malindi never thrived as prosperously as Mombasa. When Portugal invaded in the late 15th century, Malindi gladly aided the Portuguese in destroying Mombasa.

The Kingdom of Mallorca was established in 1276 by James I of Aragon, also known as James the Conqueror, as part of his will to divide his territories. The kingdom included the Balearic Islands (Mallorca, Menorca, Ibiza, and Formentera), as well as territories on the mainland such as Roussillon and Cerdanya. Initially, it was an independent realm under James II of Mallorca, but it faced constant pressure from the Crown of Aragon. In 1344, the kingdom was forcibly reincorporated into the Crown of Aragon by Peter IV. Despite its relatively short existence, the Kingdom of Mallorca played a significant role in the Mediterranean politics of the 13th and 14th centuries.

An ancient and Celtic city originally, Milan became the capital of a duchy, created in 1395 for the Visconti family already holding the city since the XIIIth century.  Galeazzo Visconti, first duke of Milan, extended his duchy to Lombardia, creating one of the most powerful states in Italy. The duchy passed to the Sforzas by marriage with the last Visconti heir and war and conquest during the succession quarrel. The city flourished in the Italian Renaissance, the Sforzas being generous patrons of arts. The duchy was involved in the Italian Wars and was conquered by Spain in 1535. After the War of the Spanish Succession, in 1713, the duchy was given to Austria. Bonaparte conquered Milan and made it the capital of the Cisalpine Republic in 1797. Milan was given back to Austria in 1815.

When Timur attacked Delhi in 1398, the governor of Malwa took the opportunity to proclaim himself Sultan of Malwa. The Sultanate expanded during the XVth century but fell to the Sultan of Gujarat in 1531 originally called for help and, in 1562, Akbar made Malwa a part of the Mughal Empire. When the Mughal Empire weakened in the XVIIIth century, Marathas seized Malwa and subjugated it, forcing the population to pay a tribute. The Marathas ceded this area to the British in 1817.

The Maguindanao Sultanate, established in the early 16th century, was a prominent Muslim state in the southern Philippines, centered on the region of present-day Maguindanao. Founded by Sharif Muhammad Kabungsuwan, a Muslim missionary from Johor, the sultanate played a crucial role in spreading Islam in Mindanao. It reached its zenith under Sultan Kudarat in the 17th century, who successfully resisted Spanish colonization efforts. The sultanate's influence waned in the late 18th century, but it remained a significant cultural and political entity in the region.

Montenegro, located in the western Balkans along the Adriatic Sea, has a rich history dating back to ancient Illyrian tribes. It became part of the Roman and later Byzantine empires. In the medieval period, the region was known as Zeta and later Crna Gora (Black Mountain), from which the name Montenegro is derived. Montenegro maintained a degree of autonomy under Ottoman suzerainty and was ruled by prince-bishops until it became a secular principality in 1852, finally obtaining full independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1878.

The great Mongol heir Bâbur, founder of the Mughal Empire, was indeed very qualified for conquest. Descended from Timur by his father and from Genghis Khan by his mother he ruled the remains of the Timurid Empire from his capital in Kabul, constantly trying, and failing, to recapture the old capital of Samarkand from the Uzbeks. Disappointed, he turned to India, divided between several small kingdoms and sultanates which were constantly at one another's necks. He took advantage of the situation and before his death in 1530 he had established a powerful Empire in northern India on the ruins of the Sultanate of Delhi. The Empire continued to grow until it dominated almost all of India at the beginning of the 17th century, before its long period of decline set in.

In the XIVth century, Moldavia was a federation of fiefdoms, vassalized to Hungary, Galicia or the Tatar Khanate. Expeditions led by Hungary reinforced the Hungarian influence but also opposition and Moldavian rebels managed to create a Voivodship in 1359. Under Stefan cel Mare (or Stephen the Great), the Voivodship of Moldavia extended to its maximum, repelling Hungarian, Poles and Tatars alike but also the newly arrived Ottomans, mainly with gold but also harbours on the Black Sea. In 1512, the principality must pay a tribute to the Ottoman Sultan to prevent being annexed and the Voivod had to be chosen by the Sultan. Moldavia was still under Turkish suzerainty in 1711 when the Ottomans declared war to Russia. The Voivod offered his help to Russia against the independence of Moldavia.  But the Ottomans won the war. In 1774, when Russia won the following war, Moldavia was still vassalized but concessions were offered to the Christian population. Northern Moldavia or Bucovina was seized by Austria in exchange for brokering the peace treaty.  Moldovia was several times more invaded during the Russo-Turkish wars and in 1812, with the Treaty of Bucharest, Eastern Moldavia was given to Russia, renaming it Bessarabia and the rest stayed in the Ottoman Empire.

The people known as the Zanj (a name given to them by the early Arab traders) have dominated the eastern African coastline for centuries, long before the arrival of Islam. The early tribal peoples and clans that make up this region are better known as the Swahili, which derives its name from the Arabic word 'sawahil' meaning 'the coast people'. From around 1200 to 1500, powerful Swahili city-states, most of them from the native Bantu tribes, began to emerge as thriving centers of commerce in the east African trade. Mombasa was found in the 12th century and rose in power because of its exportation of slaves and ivory. Its good harbor and flourishing trade with India helped it to rise to prominence in the 15th century. Although rivaled by Kilwa and Malindi, it would manage to become greater than the latter and survive longer against the Portuguese than the former.

The Hanthawaddy Kingdom, also known as Hanthawaddy Pegu or simply Pegu, was the polity that ruled lower Burma (Myanmar) from 1287 to 1539 and from 1550 to 1552. The Mon-speaking kingdom was founded by King Wareru following the collapse of the Pagan Empire in 1287 as a nominal vassal state of the Sukhothai Kingdom and of the Mongol Yuan dynasty. The kingdom became formally independent of Sukhothai in 1330 but remained a loose federation of three major regional power centres - the Irrawaddy Delta, Bago, and Mottama. Its kings had little or no authority over the vassals. Mottama was in open rebellion from 1363 to 1388. The energetic reign of King Razadarit cemented the kingdom's existence. Razadarit firmly unified the three Mon-speaking regions - Myaungmya, Donwun, and Martaban, and successfully fended off the northern Burmese-speaking Ava Kingdom in the Forty Years' War, making the western kingdom of Rakhine a tributary from 1413 to 1421 in the process. The war ended in a stalemate but was a victory for Hanthawaddy as Ava finally gave up its dream of restoring the Pagan Empire. In the years following the war, Pegu occasionally aided Ava's southern vassal states of Prome and Taungoo in their rebellions but carefully avoided getting plunged into a full-scale war. After the war, Hanthawaddy entered its golden age, whereas its rival Ava gradually declined. From the 1420s to the 1530s, Hanthawaddy was the most powerful and prosperous of all the post-Pagan kingdoms. Under a string of especially gifted monarchs it enjoyed a long golden age, profiting from foreign commerce. Its merchants traded with traders from across the Indian Ocean, filling the king's treasury with gold and silver, silk, and spices. The kingdom also became a famous centre of Theravada Buddhism. It established strong ties with Sri Lanka and encouraged reforms that spread throughout the country.

The city of Marrakech has been founded in 1062 by the first ruler of the Almoravid dynasty. This dynasty built mosques, theologian schools and a center of commerce for the Maghreb and Sub-Saharan Africa. Merinid nomads captured the city in 1269 and created their own kingdom with Fezfor its capital. Both cities would become bitter rivals. In the XVth and XVIth century, Marrakech rose again in power, becoming the Saadian capital. This new dynasty took over the northern part of what is now Morocco and fought against the Portuguese invaders. The decisive victory of Alcazarquivir in 1578 definitively repelled the Portuguese and killed their king leading to the annexation of Portugal by Spain two years later. In 1591, an expedition to the Songhai Empire would rise the Saadian dynasty to its peak.

The city of Moscow was probably founded as a simple outpost of Vladimir-Suzdal. It is mentioned for the first time in the XIIth century, and it was already a fortified city on a strategic position on the Moskva River. The Mongols conquered the area in 1234 and the Tatars burnt the city in 1238. The city is built again in the XIVth century as the capital of a Russian principality vassalized to the Mongol Khans. Dmitri Donskoi was the first to bear the title Grand Duke of Moscow. Ivan III conquered the wealthy Novgorod in 1478, liberated the Grand-Duchy from the Mongol suzerainty in 1480 and proclaimed himself 'Tsar of all Rus'.
