From then on, Muscovy would expand in all directions under the name of Russia.

Minsk, the capital of Belarus, has a rich and tumultuous history dating back to its first mention in 1067. Initially part of the Principality of Polotsk, it later became a major center within the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the 14th century, and subsequently the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The city endured numerous occupations and devastations, including by the Crimean Tatars, French, Germans, and Poles.

The Kingdom of Desmond, meaning 'South Munster' in Irish, was established in 1118 by Tadhg Mac Cárthaigh following the Treaty of Glanmire, which divided the Kingdom of Munster into Desmond and Thomond. Located in what is now County Cork and most of County Kerry, Desmond was ruled by the MacCarthy dynasty. Despite the Norman invasion of the late 12th century, which led to the creation of the Earldom of Desmond in the eastern part, the western half remained a semi-independent Gaelic kingdom (Mumhain - Munster). The kingdom persisted until 1596, when it was fully integrated into the Kingdom of Ireland following the Nine Years' War.

Despite the fact that Mataram was Islamic it still followed most of the Indo-Javanese traditions of the Hindu kingdoms of Java. In the royal palaces (kraton) of the reigning dynasties of Mataram an original model was developed combining animistic and Islamic rites and even European values. Mataram eventually had to face two new powers in order to unify the island: Bantam, the last coastal Sultanate, and the Dutch, who had landed for the first time on Java in 1596.  In For the Glory, Mataram represents not only itself, but the earlier Islamic kingdoms of Demak and Pajang, from which the sultans of Mataram claimed descent.

The Shan are a Tai people who have lived in a patchwork of city states in the mountainous valleys between Kachin, Yunnan and Burma since the early Middle Ages. The most powerful Shan states were Mong Yang, Mong Kawng and Mong Mao, which competed for dominance of the region for centuries, before eventually uniting into a temporary confederation and conquering the Ava Kingdom in 1527. The following decades saw the collapse of the Shan confederation and its destruction by the Toungoo Empire in 1557, after which the Shan lost their independence.

Münster was a bishopric since Charlemagne. Its bishop was an Elector of the Holy Roman Empire. The city was well located, on the roads to Cologne and to Frisia and it became a wealthy member of the Hanseatic League. The city embraced the Reformation in a radical way, claiming all properties, burning books and planning to capture the entire world. The Bishop of Münster and his imperial allies besieged the city and captured it in 1535, processing their own purifications by means of slaughter. The Peace of Westphalia, ending the Thirty Years war in 1648 was signed in Münster. Münster was captured by Prussia in 1802 but recaptured by France and became the capital of the Kingdom of Westphalia. The Bishopric was given to the Prussians In 1816.

Ava was a Burmese Shan kingdom that succeeded an earlier kingdom based on the city of Pagan. The city of Ava was founded in 1364. The location allowed the Shans to control the rice supply from the Kyaukse irrigated area to the south, which became vital after the traditional rice-growing area in southern Myanmar had been lost to a Mon kingdom. The Kingdom of Ava flourished until it was destroyed by a rival group of Shans in 1527. In 1634 the city became the capital of the Taungu dynasty which had united the Ava and Taungu kingdoms in 1531.

The city of Mysore was captured by the Sultanate of Delhi in 1313. The kingdom of Vijayanagar  took it soon when Delhi was destroyed by Timur. Mysore remained a vassal state of Vijayanagar until the dissolution of that state in 1565 after the battle of Talikota. Mysore would then remain largely autonomous if only influenced by its powerful neighbours as the Moghul Empire, the Maratha Empire or later the British Empire.

North Africa, encompassing modern-day Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya, has a rich and diverse history shaped by various cultures and civilizations. Ancient North Africa was home to advanced societies like the Carthaginians and Numidians, and later became a vital part of the Roman Empire - providing at least one emperor in Septimius Severus. The arrival of Islam and the Arab-dominated Caliphate in the 7th century transformed the region culturally and politically, hastening the decline of both paganism and Christianity, as well as curtailing the power of the indigenous Berber peoples. During the later colonial era, North Africa was dominated by European powers - initially Spain and Portugal, and eventually France and Italy.

Charles I of Anjou was king of Sicily but angered the population in setting his capital in Naples and giving lands to his French lords. After the Sicilian Vespers insurrection in 1282, Charles of Anjou had to withdraw in Naples. Sicily proper passed to the house of Aragon and Charles of Anjou and later his son called themselves King of Naples. The kingdom was captured in 1443 by Alfonso V of Aragon, already king of Sicily, who proclaimed himself King of Two Sicilies. It gave a casus belli for the kings of France who used it for their Italian wars in the late XVth century and early XVIth century. Naples remained in the House of Aragon and later of Spain and in 1713 of Austria. The Spanish Bourbon family got the throne of the Two Sicilies in 1738. Naples was conquered by the French during the Napoleonic wars, and freed itself in 1814 but was given back to the Bourbon family.

Between 1512 and 1515 Castile successfully invaded and annexed the southern half of the old kingdom of Navarra. The King moved his administration north but in 1589 France annexed that part as well. Though there were (and are) many rebellions in the Basque territories of Spain, Navarra would never again resurface as a nation.

The Yamato clan unified central and western Japan in the 5th century, around the same time Buddhism was introduced. In 1192, after his final victory over his brother Yoshitsune, Minamoto Yoritomo was awarded the title Shogun, roughly meaning 'barbarian quelling generalissomo'. The title stuck, and the Shogun would be the real ruler of Japan for seven centuries. 1542 marked the opening of Japan to western powers like Portugal, England, Spain and the Dutch. The Jesuits arrived, and gained an ever growing number of converts, but decrees prohibiting Christianity were promulgated in 1612 and 1614, and the persecution of its adherents began immediately thereafter. Persecution became much more severe, until, at length, it became official policy to stamp out Christianity even at the sacrifice of trade. This policy became manifest with the seclusion orders of the 1630s. Thus, in 1635 Japanese were forbidden to make overseas voyages or to return to Japan from overseas, which was a severe blow to Japan's traders. Japan now entered a period of total isolationalism that would last well into the middle of the 19th century.

The Nogai Horde, whose name came from Nogai Khan great great-grandson of Genghis Khan, was born of the disintegration of the Golden Horde, along with the other khanates. They lived east of the Volga River and north of the Caspian Sea, living as pastoral nomads and occasional raiders. They were soon opposed to the Kazakhs on their east to Russian on their west. The Russians successively conquered the Khanate of Kazan and the Khanate of Astrakhan and the Nogais lost the tribute from these countries. The Russian pressure grew in late XVIth century and some Nogais had to migrate to Crimea or in Kazakhs lands. In the XVIIth century, the Kalmycks, warlike Buddhist Mongols, pushed from the east and invaded the Nogais' land, supported by Russia. The Nogais finished by settle with the Crimean Tatars in the XVIIIth century, and when the Khanate of Crimea was conquered by Russia, they were finally pressured into the Caucasus region.

The kingdom of Norway, united in the Viking era, reached its greatest strength in the 13th century, when Iceland and several islands in the North Sea were still under Norwegian rule. However, after the ravages of the Black Plague in 1349 and 1350, the population in Norway was greatly reduced. The Norwegian nobility was greatly weakened by the catastrophe, and became international rather than national in its orientation. In 1397 Norway entered the Union of Kalmar as Queen Margrete became queen of Norway following the death of the last Norwegian king Olav IV. Together with the other two nations, Norway was at war with the Hansa in the 1420s and gradually succumbed to Danish influence and rule as the taxes from Norway were spent abroad. The Norwegian 'Riksraad' continued to elect foreign princes as kings including Christopher of Bavaria and finally Christian II of Denmark. By this time, the Union of Kalmar was just an empty name and Norway had become an integral part of Denmark.

Raids of the Vikings, or Northmen, from the 8th century on, repeatedly devastated the Normandy coast, each time moving farther inland. Finally the French King Charles III the Simple ceded the territory to Rollo, the chief of the largest band of Vikings. The Vikings immigrated in large numbers to settle the country, and they adopted the French language, customs, and religion. These Vikings became known as Normans, and the region they settled became known as Normandy. In 1066, William, duke of Normandy and a distant successor to Rollo, invaded England. He became William I of England (William the Conqueror) and united the rule of England and Normandy in him. During the next four centuries both England and France battled for control over Normandy, until the French achieved permanent control in 1450 after their victory in the Battle of Formigny.

Novgorod (new city) is one of the oldest cities in Russia, founded by the Varangians in the IXth century. Autonomous from Kiev in the XIIth century, it evolved in a merchant republic, extending in all northern Russia to the Urals from the XIIth century to the XVth century. Novgorod maintained its independence from the German knights, Sweden and the Mongols. Furs, salt and iron were traded, principally with the Hanseatic League, even if Novgorod never became a member of the League.  In the XIVth century, Moscow was rebuilt after the destruction by the Tatars and rose as a major local power. Novgorod tried to find an alliance with Lithuania, but political troubles sparked about this alliance and Muscovy took advantage of the opportunity. Ivan III of Muscovy conquered the Republic of Novgorod in 1478.

The Iroquois were undoubtedly the fiercest warriors to roam the St. Lawrence and the northern New York state. They called themselves the Haudenosunee, meaning people of the long house, but their enemies referred to them as the Iroqu, an insult meaning 'rattlesnakes'. The French added 'ois' to make it Iroquois. The Iroquois Confederacy consisted of six nations: Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca, and Tuscarora. They maintained a wide trade network which the Europeans found useful, and subsequently became leading in the fur trade. The Iroquois village of Stadacona became the site of the first French trading post and later became known as Quebec. The Iroquois village of Hochelaga would become the site of Montreal. When the American Revolution came, the Iroquois sided with the British - a gamble that they unfortunately lost. Many were driven into Southern and Eastern Ontario and Quebec, and their power was forever broken. Despite their passion for war the Iroquois were primarily agrarian.

Oldenburg became a county in the XIIth century, vassal to the dukes of Saxony. The counts of Oldenburg became princes of the Empire when the Emperor Frederick I dismembered the duchy of Saxony in 1180. The county expanded slightly on the lands of rebellious Frisian lords in the XIIIth century. In 1448 Christian of Oldenburg became king of Denmark as Christian I. He let his county to his younger brother without trying to annex it to his kingdom. In the XVIth century, the counts of Oldenburg became Protestant but stayed faithful to Charles V in the League of Schmalkalde. Oldenburg gained some more territories. Oldenburg stayed neutral in the Thirty Years war, while selling horse to the imperials: the count managed to save his county from the usual slaughters in this war. When the line of the counts of Oldenburg became extinct in 1676, Oldenburg passed to Christian V of Denmark. In 1773 Christian VII exchanged Oldenburg for ducal Holstein with Grand Duke Paul I of Russia who gave it in turn to Frederick Augustus of Holstein-Gottorp, bishop of Lübeck. Oldenburg became a Duchy in 1777. It was annexed during the Napoleonic wars and liberated in 1813. The duchy became a Grand-Duchy.

Virtually cut off from the rest of the Arabian Peninsula by vast deserts, the Omani became prominent sailors and acquired an early maritime tradition. As they traveled and traded, the Omanis spread the message of Islam as well as Arab culture and language, leaving a deep impact on eastern Africa and reaching as far east as China. In the early 16th century, after the Portuguese under Vasco de Gama had discovered the sea route round the Cape of Good Hope to India they occupied Mascate for a century and a half in order to dominate the trade which had until then been an Omani monopoly. The Portuguese were expelled from Mascate in 1650 by Sultan bin Saif al-Yarubi, reaffirming for a time the the Omani power in the region.

In the XIIIth and XIVth centuries, Orissa resisted both the Muslim threat from Delhi and Bengal and the invasion from their Hindu fellow-believer of Vijayanagar.  The Ganga dynasty, famous for the architecture and arts, was followed by the Surya dynasty in 1435. Orissa expanded on the expense of the Muslims, defeating Bengal and expanding to the Ganga River. Orissa finally lost its independence to the Afghan rulers of Bengal when its king died in 1568. The Mughal emperor, Akbar, annexed orissa in 1592.

The city of Orléans and its surrounding province - the Orléanais - constituted part of the small nucleus of the royal domain, and was often given in appanage as a duchy to the eldest brother of the king of France and to his descendants. In the Wars of Religion during the 16th century, the city was briefly made the headquarters of the Huguenots and was besieged in by Catholic forces in 1563. Orléans remained in Catholic hands until the Edict of Nantes in 1598. During the 17th and 18th centuries the city was a prosperous industrial and commercial center.

The Kingdom of Ormus (also known as Hormuz) was located in the eastern side of the Persian Gulf and extended as far as Bahrain in the west at its zenith. The Kingdom was established in 11th century initially as a dependency of the Kerman Seljuk Sultanate, and later as an autonomous tributary of the Salghurids and the Ilkhanate of Iran. In its last phase Ormus became a client state of the Portuguese Empire in the East. Most of its territory was eventually annexed by the Safavid Empire in the 17th century. The monarchy received its name from the fortified port city which served as its capital. It was one of the most important ports in the Middle East at the time as it controlled seaway trading routes through the Persian Gulf to China, India, and East Africa. This port was originally located on the southern coast of Iran to the east of the Strait of Hormuz, near the modern city of Minab, and was later relocated to the island of Jarun which came to be known as Hormuz Island, which is located near the modern city of Bandar-e Abbas.

Palembang succeeded the glorious Kingdom of Srivijaya, once the greatest power in Indonesia. At one time the unquestioned center for trade, culture and commerce, it declined rapidly during the 14th century, and by the 15th century it was a shadow of its former glory, barely capable of breaking away from the disintegrating Majapahit Empire. Palembang only began recovering after the introduction of Islam in the early 16th century, though it wasn't enough to save them from the invasion of treasure-hunting Europeans. The city and Kingdom of Jambi in central Sumatra is positioned on the busy sea route between China and India, and it played a major part in early maritime trade. Records show Jambi to have been the original capital of the Malaya Kingdom. The ancient Hindu - Buddhist Kingdom of Sriwijaya also had its capital in Jambi at one time. The relationship between Melayu and Sriwijaya was a very close one, although there were some clearly period of Malay independence when Sriwijaya was based in nearby Palembang. As well as functioning as an entreport, Jambi also produced its own exports including a variety of tree resins for use as incense, as well as cloves, tortoise-shell, gardenia flowers and cardamom. From Arab traders it imported cotton, fabrics and sword blades, from China silk gauzes and thread, the latter possibly used in the manufacturer of silk brocades decorated in gold supplementary weft, the songket for which the Malay world later became famous.

An ancient city, Parma has been founded by the Etruscans. A bishopric was created in the vIIth century and Charlemagne gave the authority on the city and the surrounding area to the bishop.  The city became a free city in the XIIth century and was ruled by the Visconti family since 1346 and by marriage and conquest by the Sforza family since 1447. Ludovico il Moro fought against the French invasion in the Italian Wars  but couldn't prevent the occupation of the city in 1500. Parma belonged to the Papal States after the French were expelled and in 1545, Pope Paul III created a Duchy for his son Pier Luigi Farnese. The Farnese family would rule Parma until 1731 when it was given to the house of Bourbon. During the Napoleonic wars was a French department   at first and later a duchy. In 1814, the duchy was given to Maria Luigia of Austria, Napoleon's wife.

'Lo Stato della Chiesa', the Papal States or the Pontifical States, was allegedly formed by a gift of Roman Emperor Constantine in 335, actually a forged document from the VIIIth century. With the disintegration of the Roman Empire, the Popes gained more and more temporal powers in and around Rome. In 754, the French King Pepin gave to the Pope lands taken from the Lombards against the legitimacy of his line as King of the Franks. The lands grew steadily especially in the XVIth century when the Popes opposed France in the Italian Wars, gaining Parma, and when later Cesare Borgia, son of Pope Alexander VI, conquered Romagna and Marche. The Papal States were invaded during the French Revolution and Napoleonic wars and the Pope was ordered to stop his temporal power to only keep the spiritual power. The Congress of Vienna in 1815 would reestablish the Papal States.

The city became a free city in the XIIth century and was ruled by the Visconti family since 1346 and by marriage and conquest by the Sforza family since 1447. Ludovico il Moro fought against the French invasion in the Italian Wars  but couldn't prevent the occupation of the city in 1500. Parma belonged to the Papal States after the French were expelled and in 1545, Pope Paul III created a Duchy for his son Pier Luigi Farnese. The Farnese family would rule Parma until 1731 when it was given to the house of Bourbon. During the Napoleonic wars was a French department   at first and later a duchy. In 1814, the duchy was given to Maria Luigia of Austria, Napoleon's wife.

Pegu was the center of one of the three chief states of Myanmar (Ava, Taungu and Pegu) from the 14th to the late 15th century. In the 16th century it became the capital of a united Burmese kingdom, but when it was destroyed in 1564 and again in 1599, the Burmese moved their capital to Ava. In the 18th century the Talaings rebelled against the Burmese and set up their capital at Pegu. The city was destroyed by the Burmese in 1757 but was later rebuilt as the center of a Burmese province. The city and province came under British rule in 1852.

Persia, or Iran ('land of the Aryans'), is a nation with a history long enough to rival the Greek, and like the Greeks, the Persian people were oppressed by foreign powers for centuries. The old Persian Empire quickly fell to the fanatic Muslims hordes that rode out of the Arabian peninsula in the 7th century, and Persia remained a part of the Caliphate until its fall to the Mongols in the mid 13th century. The Mongols ruled Persia as part of the Ilkhanate until Tamerlane conquered that in the late 14th century. The Timurid realm proved unstable, and the Persians soon found themselves governed by the Ak Koyunlu, whose realm in turn crumbled when the great Ismail Safavid, himself of Turkish origin, rebelled and took control of the whole region. Despite his suppression of sunni muslims and despite his Turkish background, Ismail was hailed as a saviour by the Persians. Safavid Persia endured until 1736, despite the incessant internal and external pressure.

Petra, an ancient city in present-day Jordan, was established around the 4th century BC by the Nabataeans, an Arab Bedouin tribe. Renowned for its stunning rock-cut architecture and advanced water management system, Petra thrived as a major trading hub connecting the East and West. The city reached its zenith under Nabataean rule before falling to the Romans in 106 AD. Over time, Petra's significance waned, and it was largely abandoned by the 8th century. Rediscovered in 1812 by Swiss explorer Johann Ludwig Burckhardt, Petra is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and considered a wonder of the world.

Peru, located in western South America, boasts a rich history that spans over 15 millennia. It was home to the Norte Chico civilization, one of the world's oldest, and later the Chavín, Moche, and Nazca cultures. The Inca Empire, with its capital at Cuzco, emerged in the 15th century as the largest and most sophisticated pre-Columbian civilization in the Americas. Spanish conquistadors, led by Francisco Pizarro, conquered the Inca Empire in 1533, establishing the Viceroyalty of Peru, which became a major center of Spanish colonial power. Peru declared independence from Spain in 1821, achieving it fully after the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824.

The Rhenish Palatine was established in the 12th Century. The power of its rulers rarely extended far beyond the valley of the middle Rhine, but they nevertheless enjoyed great prestige as Imperial Electors. The capital at Heidelberg became one of the centers of Reformation and Renaissance in Germany. The Counts of the Palatinate were among the leading Protestant Princes of Germany. This led to the selection of Elector Frederick V as King of Bohemia in 1619, but he was quickly driven out by Catholic forces. The country suffered heavily in the Thirty Years War, and although the Counts Palatinate were reestablished in their country in 1648 they never again played an important role in German politics.

Picardy, an historical region in northern France, has a long and interesting history. It was part of the Frankish Empire from the 5th century and later became a significant region within the Kingdom of France following the Treaty of Verdun in 843. The name 'Picardy' first appeared in the early 13th century, referring to lands where the Picard language was spoken. Throughout the Middle Ages, Picardy was a battleground for numerous conflicts, including the Hundred Years' War and the Jacquerie peasant revolt.

An ancient Roman colony, Siena became a bishopric in the Vth century. The city became free and independent in the XIIth century. It was the rival city of Florence and chose to be Ghibeline, pro-imperial, when the other was Guelph, anti-imperial or pro-papal. Stricken by a banqueroute in 1298 and the Black Plague in 1348, the city knew an economic and social decline and instability dominated by the Visconti's influence. In 1487, Pandolfo Petrucci tried to revive the city through a tyrannical power. Seized by the French in 1493 and later faithful to them, the city was besieged by Charles V and captured by the Spaniards in 1555. Philip II of Spain offered the city to Cosme I of Florence two years later.

Podlasia is an historical region in northeastern Poland, characterized by its diverse cultural heritage and strategic location. The region's name is believed to derive from the Slavic word for 'forest' - reflecting its lush landscapes. Historically, Podlasia was a melting pot of various ethnic groups, including Poles, Belarusians, Lithuanians, and Tatars. It became a significant part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the 14th century and later the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The region experienced numerous conflicts and changes in sovereignty, particularly during the partitions of Poland and the Napoleonic Wars.

Poitou, an historical region in west-central France, derives its name from the ancient Gallic tribe of Pictones. It was an important part of Roman Aquitania and later became a significant region within the Frankish Empire. Throughout the Middle Ages, Poitou was a contested territory, witnessing key battles such as the Battle of Vouillé in 507 and the Battle of Poitiers in 1356. The region was ruled by the counts of Poitiers, who also held the title of Duke of Aquitaine. Poitou experienced religious turmoil during the French Wars of Religion and played a notable role in the Huguenot movement. In the modern era, it was a center of resistance during the Vendée Revolt in the French Revolution.

Polotsk, one of the oldest cities in Belarus, was first mentioned in historical records in 862. Situated on the Dvina River, it became a significant center of power in the early medieval period, and the capital of the Principality of Polotsk. The city was known for its strategic importance and cultural influence, playing a crucial role in the development of Eastern Slavic culture and Christianity. Polotsk's most notable ruler, Prince Vseslav, reigned from 1044 to 1101 and significantly expanded its influence. The city later became a vassal of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in 1307, enjoying local autonomy until the 1390s. It was fully incorporated into Lithuania in 1504 as the Polotsk Voivodeship, at which point it ceased to exist as a distinct entity.

The first king of Poland was Boleslas I in 1025. The kingdom was Christian and recognized by the Holy Roman Empire and the Pope. On the margin of the Christian world it was facing the Pagan world but also the 'Drang nach Osten' (march to the East) of the Germanic settlers led by the Empire or by the Teutonic Knights. These latter created a vast state in the north. Their power was broken by their defeat in the battle of Tannenberg, in 1410, uniting Pole and Lithuanian knights and also Bohemian and Tatar mercenaries.  The Teutonic Order passed under Pole suzerainty in 1466. The kings of Poland became shortly kings of Bohemia and of Hungary and in 1569, Poland reached its peak with the personal union with Lithuania, creating the largest country in Europe. In 1683, John III Sobieski repelled the ottoman offensive. But the country was already declining, lacking a politic stability. The elective monarchy, the right of veto (liberum veto) given to every member of the Sejm (Diet or parliament), the support given by foreign nations to different factions prevented to act decisively when facing national crises or invasions. It led to the final destruction of Poland through three partitions in the XVIIIth century.

Pomerania became a polish province during the Xth century, when the Piast dynasty accomplished its political unification when it was formerly divided among local nobles. At the beginning of XIth century, Poland was no longer able to maintain her rule there and Pomerania remained mainly autonomous for nearly a century when the Polish rulers came back, dividing Pomerania between an eastern Polish province and a western Duchy. The latter was ruled by the Slavic Griffin dynasty until the XVIIth century, maintaining its autonomy while submitting from time to time to Poland, Denmark, Brandenburg, Saxony or the Holy Roman Empire. The Duchy was converted to the Christianity in the XIIIth century and the population became more and more Germanic while the rulers were still Polish. The Elector of Brandenburg acquired the Duchy in 1637 when the last Polish duke died without issue, but the area had been conquered by the Swedish who seized Stettin in 1631 and Sweden received Western Pomerania by the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

Portugal emerged as a nation state in the early 12th century and ranks as one of the world's longest established countries. In 1143 Portugal was raised to the status of a kingdom. Dom Afonso Henriques became King of an independent Portugal. He had taken three quarters of the present day Portugal from the Muslims, including Lisbon. After his death in 1185 the conquest was completed by his successors. Afonso III expanded this Kingdom southward to the Algarve in 1249 and under João I Portuguese sailors began to explore the African coast and the Atlantic. Its boundaries have been unchanged since the 13th century. The Fifteenth Century was Portugal's Age of Discovery. First it was Madeira Island then the Azores Cape Bojador and Cape Verde. Then the Portuguese explorers reached Africa, rounded the Cape of Good Hope, and gave Portugal its own route to India. Vasco de Gama reached India establishing Portuguese colonies and Pedro Cabral discovered Brazil. Other Portuguese explorers reached the Far East China and Japan. For that brief moment in time Portugal was the richest country in Europe.

Paraguay, a landlocked country in south-central South America, has a complex and turbulent history. It was part of the Spanish Empire until it gained independence in 1811. The country endured significant hardships during the 19th century, particularly the devastating War of the Triple Alliance (1864-1870) against Brazil, Argentina, and Uruguay, which resulted in massive population and territorial losses.

Permia, also known as the Principality of Great Perm, was a medieval Komi-Permyak state located in the Upper Kama region of what is now the Perm Krai in Russia. Established in the 14th century, it emerged as a distinct entity from the Novgorod Republic. The principality was known for its strategic position and rich natural resources, which facilitated trade and cultural exchanges with nearby Komi and Tatar rulers. Great Perm maintained a degree of autonomy under Muscovite rule until it was fully annexed by the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1505. The region's capital was Cherdyn, and it played a significant role in the spread of Christianity in the area - largely due to the missionary efforts of St. Stephen of Perm.

The major part of Provence, held by the house of Aragón, in 1246 passed to the Angevin dynasty of Naples through marriage and under their rule the towns became virtually independent republics. In 1481 Provence was willed to the king of France, and its union to the crown was effected on the condition that Provence keep its administrative autonomy - a condition that was poorly honored.

Porto, the second-largest city in Portugal, boasts a vibrant history that dates back to its origins as a Roman outpost known as Portus Cale. Situated along the Douro River, Porto flourished as a major trading port and shipbuilding center during the 14th and 15th centuries. It was from Porto that Prince Henry the Navigator set sail in 1415, marking the beginning of the Portuguese Age of Discovery. The city is renowned for its production of port wine, which has been a significant export since the 17th century and was a popular alternative to French wine in Britain during the Napoleonic Wars.

The area called Prussia was at first a geographic region inhabited by Balt people called Borus. These pagans were fought by the duchy of Mazovia whose Duke Conrad I invited the Teutonic Knights in the XIIIth century. The Teutonic Order led a crusade and established a Christian state. Germanic settlers replaced the original population. In 1525, the last Grand Master of the Teutonic Order, Albrecht of Hohenzollern, embraced the Protestant faith and created Ducal Prussia as a hereditary duchy, vassal to the still Catholic Poland. In 1618, the Duchy of Prussia passed to Albert-Frederick, the Elector of Brandenburg, creating a personal union. After the invasion of Poland by Sweden in 1657, Poland surrendered its suzerainty on Prussia. In the XVIIth century the immigration grew from the Thirty Years War and from the French repression on Protestant people. In 1701, the Emperor allowed Frederick of Brandenburg to crown himself King 'in' Prussia that the new Frederick I of Prussia quickly translated in King 'of' Prussia. This king made Prussia a military country, with one of the most powerful army of the time. Prussia grew to become the second Germanic power next to the Austrian Emperor.

The city of Pskov was founded as an outpost of Novgorod in 903. However, Pskov won its independence from Novgorod in 1348. The city followed Novgorod's example by severely restricting the power of its prince. The principality produced a code of law in 1397 that was used throughout Russia. Although it was closer to Novgorod it often looked to Muscovy for protection from the expansionist powers of the Baltic rim, especially as the Teutonic Knights. It was finally absorbed into Muscovy in 1511.

Puritanism was a particularly strict branch of protestantism inclined more towards Calvinism than Lutheranism and was mostly concerned with the belief in hard work and pure natural life. It emerged in England in the early 1600s and quickly found support in the South-East. However, due to a number of reasons many Puritans emigrated to the New World. The Puritan Faction was also a significant branch of the Parliamentary forces during the English Civil War, and it was Oliver Cromwell, a Puritan, who came to be Lord Protector of England.

The Qara Qoyunlu ('Black Sheep') were a Turkmen tribal federation that ruled Azerbaijan and Iraq, originally vassals of the Jalayirids of Baghdad and Tabriz. Routed by Tamerlane the Qara Qoyunlu re-established themselves in Tabriz from 1406. Baghdad was captured in 1410 and there was expansion into Persia. In 1468, however, the Qara Qoyunlu had been defeated and overrun by their mortal enemies from the north - the Aq Qoyunlu ('White Sheep').

The Qing dynasty, the last imperial dynasty of China, ruled from 1644 to 1912. Established by the Manchus, it succeeded the Ming dynasty and expanded China's territory to its greatest extent, incorporating regions like Taiwan, Tibet, Xinjiang, and Mongolia. The Qing era was marked by initial prosperity and cultural achievements, particularly under emperors Kangxi and Qianlong. However, the dynasty faced significant challenges in its later years, including internal rebellions, foreign invasions, and the Opium Wars, which weakened its control. The Qing dynasty ultimately fell in 1912, leading to the establishment of the Republic of China.

The French explorer Jacques Cartier first sailed up the St. Lawrence River in 1534 and arrived in the land that would later bear the name New France. Settlement of the region did not begin until the early 17th century, when Samuel Champlain founded Quebec ('where the river narrows') - the first permanent French settlement in the New World. Over the next century the French gradually settled along the banks of the St. Lawrence, where their long-lot settlement pattern exists to this day. In 1759 Quebec was lost to the British on the Plains of Abraham - an event that would ensure British hegemony in North America and indirectly lead to the American revolution.

The City of Ragusa was probably founded after southern Slavs and Avars raided and destroyed the Roman city of Epidaur in the year 614. It is mentioned for the first time in the year 1189 in the trade agreement between the Bosnian ruler Kulin Ban and the Ragusan republic. In 1205 it was vassalized by the Venetians and remained a Venetian subject nation until 1358. In 1419 it was vassalized again, this time by Hungary. Trade increased with the Ottoman Empire and relationships with the Venetians remained strained.

Rajputana was a region in north-western India made up of multiple principalities warring with both themselves and their neigbors. The Rajputanian religion, although Hindu in orgin, is considered by the Rajputs to be above the other Hindu religons which caused constant rebellion, espicially amongst the nobility. During the 15th century they acheived their greatest height of military power, greater than any other in the region until the arrival of the Mughal Empire under Babur.

Ramazan Beg, from the Oghuz Turks, founded the Turkish emirate of Ramazan in 1352,  in southern Turkey, around Adana. He had been supported by the Mameluk Sultan and led his clan from Syria to the Cilician lands of the Armenians. The new dynasty soon tried to break free from the Mameluk domination. They failed and Ramazan became a principality directly ruled by the Mameluks. The area became of strategical importance when the ottomans began to make war against the Mameluks. The Ottomans used the local opposition to the Mameluk rule. The Ottoman victory in Syria in 1515 influenced Ramazan towards the Ottomans and from then on, the Ramazan ruler was appointed by the Ottoman Sultan. Ramazan was annexed to the Ottoman Empire in 1608 and the Ramazan dynasty produced many governors for the Empire from the Balkans to Asia.

Romania, located in Southeastern Europe, has a rich history shaped by various cultures and empires. The region was originally inhabited by the Dacians, who were conquered by the Romans in 106 AD, leading to the formation of the Roman province of Dacia. Over the centuries, Romania experienced invasions and influences from the Goths, Huns, Slavs, and Magyars. In the Middle Ages, the principalities of Wallachia, Moldavia, and Transylvania emerged, each playing crucial roles in resisting Ottoman expansion. These principalities united in 1859, forming the basis of modern Romania, which gained full independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1877.

Romagna, an historical region in northern Italy, corresponds to the southeastern part of present-day Emilia-Romagna. Its name originates from the Latin 'Romania' - referring to lands inhabited by Romans. Romagna has been inhabited since the Paleolithic age, with significant influences from the Umbri, Etruscans, and Gauls. During the Roman era, it became a crucial part of the Exarchate of Ravenna, serving as a center of Byzantine administration. The region experienced various rulers, including the Lombards and Franks, before becoming part of the Papal States. In the 19th century, Romagna was integrated into the new Kingdom of Italy, contributing to its rich cultural and historical tapestry.

When Parliament had been dissolved by Charles I in 1642 in reaction to the rise of the gentry and the burghers and their higher demands for power, most of the lords rallied to the Royal Standard of the King to protect their own interests and privileges. From these days, even after the execution of Charles I in 1649, the English Monarchs had a large group of supporters for a more powerful monarchy, which transformed with the coming of the even more extremist James II and took the name of Jacobites.

In 862 the political entity known as Kievan Rus was established by Vikings from Sweden along their trade route in what is now Ukraine. In the 10th century Christianity became the state religion under Vladimir, who studied both Churches, but chose to adopt the Greek Orthodox rites. The Mongol invasion in the 13th century shattered Kievan Rus and its people were made thralls to the invaders and cruelly oppressed. As Mongol unity dissolved over the next two centuries, Muscowy gradually became the dominant principality and was able through diplomacy and conquest to establish suzerainty over European Russia. Ivan III (1462-1505) married the Byzantine princess Zoe Paleologus in a diplomatic move aimed at gaining prestige for his country. He could now refer to Russia as the Third Rome, and heir to the Byzantine tradition (even if the kings and princes of Europe were not impressed). As century later the famous Romanov dynasty was established at the end of the Time of Troubles by Tsar Mikhail in 1613. During Peter the Great's reign (1689-1725) Russia began a process of modernization and European influences spread in Russia. Peter created Western-style military forces, subordinated the Russian Orthodox Church hierarchy to the Tsar, reformed the entire governmental structure and established the beginnings of a Western-style education system.

Ryazan was one of the many principalities that emerged from the ruins of Kievian Rus in the aftermath of the Mongol invasions of the 13th century. For most of its history it remained a vassal state to the Kahn of the Golden Horde. It was unfortunate in that it laid near the invasion routes to Moscow and the other northern principalities, thus making it more willing to negotiate than fight, even after the Grand Duchy of Muscovy declared independence from the Khan. Ivan III, Grand Prince of Muscowy, inherited half of the principality in 1500. The other half was absorbed by the tsar in 1511 and Ryazan became part of the new Russian nation.

The Ryukyu Kingdom, located in the Ryukyu Islands between Japan and Taiwan, was established in the 15th century and played a pivotal role in regional maritime trade. Unified by King Sho Hashi in 1429, the kingdom thrived as a tributary state of Ming China, facilitating trade between China, Japan, Korea, and Southeast Asia. Despite its small size, the Ryukyu Kingdom developed a unique culture, blending influences from its trading partners. The kingdom's independence ended in 1879 when it was annexed by Japan and transformed into Okinawa Prefecture.

In 1356 the duke of Saxe-Wittenberg was granted the permanent rank of Elector. Electoral Saxony, as his territory was called, was a relatively small area along the middle Elbe. To the south of Electoral Saxony extended the margraviate of Meissen, ruled by the increasingly powerful house of Wettin. The margraves of Meissen acquired, in the 13th and 14th centuries, the larger parts of Lower Lusatia, Thuringia and the intervening territories and in 1423 Margrave Frederick the Warlike also added Electoral Saxony, becoming Elector Frederick I. In 1485 the lands of House Wettin were partitioned between two sons of Elector Frederick II and the division came to be permanent. Ernest, founder of the Ernestine branch of Wettin, received Electoral Saxony with Wittenberg and most of the Thuringian lands. Albert, founder of the Albertine branch, received ducal rank and the Meissen territories including Dresden and Leipzig. Duke Maurice of Saxony, a grandson of Albert and a Protestant, received the Electoral title in the 16th century and it was held by the Albertine branch until the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806.

In 1353, Pere IV of Aragon granted legislative autonomy to the kingdom of Sardinia but from 1365 to 1409 the kings or giudici of Arborea - Mariano IV, Ugone III, Mariano V, and Guglielmo III succeeded in occupying very nearly all of Sardinia except the Castel of Cagliari and Alghero. In 1409 Marti the Younger, king of Sicily and heir to Aragon, defeated the giudicale Sardinians at Sanluri and once and for all conquered the entire land. Shortly afterwards he died of malaria in Cagliari without issue.

The surprisingly resilient state of Savoy was forged by Humbert the Whitehanded, a lord of Arles, out of the various feudal territories in the region. Under Amadeus VIII in the early 15th century, Savoy became a powerful duchy extending far into France, Italy, and Switzerland. By the beginning of the 16th century the rule of the dukes had weakened, and Savoy fell under Swiss and French dominance. The great duke Emmanuel Philibert (Ironhead) greatly restored the territory and fortunes of the border duchy and moved the ducal residence to Turin in 1559, making Savoy more of an Italian than a French state. When Victor Amadeus II acquired the title king of Sardinia in 1713, Savoy became a part of a united kingdom. Annexed by France in 1792, Savoy was returned to Sardinia in 1815.

Scotland as a national entity arose through the union of the kingdoms of Alba and Strathclyde in the mid-11th century. Ever since that time, Scotland's history has been one of action and reaction against her more powerful neighbor England. In 1174 Scotland became a vassal of England but broke loose a few years later. Unfortunately the terms of the release were vague and the kings of England retained a tenuous - and sometimes not so tenuous - hold on their northern neighbour, which had to struggle in the face of near impossible odds to retain its independence. Scottish independence, or at least semi-autonomy, came to a final end in 1707, when its lords accepted the Act of Union and formed Great Britain together with England.

Steiermark (Also known as Styria), a picturesque region in southeastern Austria, has a rich history dating back to ancient times. Originally inhabited by Celtic tribes, it became part of the Roman provinces of Noricum and Pannonia. During the early Middle Ages, the area saw the settlement of Slavs and later came under the control of the Bavarians and Franks. The March of Styria was established in the 10th century as a defensive frontier against the Magyars. It evolved into a duchy in 1180 and played a significant role within the Holy Roman Empire. Styria's strategic location and abundant natural resources, including iron and timber, contributed to its economic and cultural development under the Habsburg Monarchy.

The Seljuk Empire was established in 1037 by the Oghuz Turks under the leadership of Tughril Beg, and became a significant medieval Sunni Muslim empire that spanned from Anatolia to the Hindu Kush. Known for its cultural and political influence, the Seljuk Empire played a crucial role in the spread of both Islam and Persian culture (which, though originally Turks, they heavily adopted) across the Middle East. The empire reached its zenith under the rule of Alp Arslan and Malik Shah, who expanded its territories and solidified its power. The Seljuks are also remembered for their victory at the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, which dealt a mortal blow to the Byzantine Empire and marked the beginning of Turkish dominance in Anatolia. Despite their collapse in the late 12th century, the Seljuks' legacy continued to influence the region for centuries thereafter.

The Serbs, a Slavic people, settled in what is now Serbia between the Ist and Vth centuries. In the XIIIth and XIVth centuries, the Serbs used the weakening of the Byzantine Empire to get lands as far south as Greece. Under Emperor or Czar Stephen Dušan,in mid XIVth century, Serbia was the most powerful empire in the Balkans. Unfortunately, his successors were not as brilliant and the Ottoman Turks began to be a serious threat. A succession of defeats led to the vassalisation of Serbia by the Ottomans. After the fall of Constantinople in 1453, the Ottomans were free to move to the north and Serbia was annexed in 1459. Belgrade, held by Hungary, fell to the Ottomans in 1521. During three centuries, Ottomans would rule Serbia in spite of several Austrian unsuccessful offensives. Two insurrections occurred in the early XIXth century, supported by Austria who had promised a large autonomy in the Austrian Empire, if they were successful. In 1804 it failed, but in 1815, the second insurrection allowed the creation of a Principality of Serbia.

The Kingdom of Seville, established in 1248 following the Christian reconquest led by Ferdinand III of Castile, was a territorial jurisdiction of the Crown of Castile. It encompassed much of present-day Andalusia, including the provinces of Seville, Huelva, and Cádiz. The kingdom flourished as a significant cultural and economic center, benefiting from its strategic location and fertile lands. Seville itself became a hub of commerce and exploration during the Age of Discovery, particularly after the establishment of the Casa de Contratación in 1503, which regulated trade with the New World. The Kingdom of Seville remained an important administrative region until the territorial division of Spain in 1833.

The name Shawnee is derived from the Algonquin word shawun, meaning 'Southerner'. They usually preferred to call themselves the Shawano. The Shawnee considered the Lenape of Delaware as their grandfathers and the source of all Algonquin tribes. They originally inhabited the Ohio Valley, Pennsylvania and West Virginia, but were forced from these lands by the Iroquois in the 1660s. Eventually they settled in South Carolina, Tennessee's Cumberland Basin, eastern Pennsylvania and southern Illinois. In Carolina they established trade with the British, dealing in deerskins and captured native women for firearms and whiskey. The Shawnee fought with the British against the French and against the Americans in the American Revolution. Their greatest leader was Tecumseh.

The Duchy of Holstein was originally created in 1111 as a county of the Holy Roman Empire and given to Adolf of Schauenburg. Since Lübeck and Hamburg were controlled by the Hanseatic League, Kiel and Rendsburg were the chief cities. In 1459 Holstein's Christian I, a Danish heir to the throne, established a personal union with Denmark to the great displeasure of the German majority in the region. In 1474, Emperor Frederick III raised Holstein to the status of duchy under the immediate suzerainty of the Holy Roman Empire (as distinct from Schleswig, which was outside the imperial jurisdiction). Holstein remained independent, if often involved in wars between Sweden and Denmark, until 1866, when it was annexed by Prussia in the Peace of Prague.

An integral part of the ancient Malacca-Johor Empire, Siak became a separate state of its own in 1723. The founder of the sultanate, Sultan 'Abdu'l-Jalil Rahmat Shah alias Raja Kechil, was the putative posthumous child of Sultan Mahmud II of Johor. Although he had managed to seize the throne of Johor in 1718, his hold over the throne remained tenuous. Constant disputes forced him to remove his capital to Riau in 1719. Three years later, the Bugis princes defeated and expelled him from that place. He then moved his court to Siak. Stalemate over the contest for the throne eventually resulted in Siak developing into a separate sultanate. His infirmity in old age prompted a succession dispute between his sons. Raja Alam, the elder son by a commoner, allied himself with the Dutch and seized the throne in 1740. A dual system of government failed to resolve disputes over the succession. The contest for the throne was only resolved with the deposition of the Johor Dynasty. Al-Sayyid Sharif 'Ali, a nobleman of Arab descent and son of a princess, had been increasing his power and influence by allying himself to the Dutch. He assisted them in conquering Selangor, then returned with men and weapons and seized power in 1784. Initially satisfied with the regency, he tired of this subordinate role, deposed Sultan Yahya and established a new dynasty in 1797.

The Khanate of Sibir was a state of Mongol origin, created after the disintegration of the Golden Horde in the mid XVth century. Its capital was located in the city of Sibir, near what is now Tobolsk, and the Khanate extended around the Ob and the Irtysch Rivers. The new Khanate managed to maintain its independence from the other Mongol Khanates, especially the Uzbeks. The Russian expansion to Siberia, began after the fall of the Kazan Khanate, in 1552. Cossacks began to settle in fortified camps and Yermak captured Sibir in 1581. The conquest of the Khanate was completed in 1598 when the last Khan fled. It opened the way to the Russian colonisation of Siberia

The county and then kingdom of Sicily has been conquered from the Muslims in the XIth century by Normans lords. The kingdom passed to the Holy Roman Emperor, what the Popes couldn't accept. Charles of Anjou conquered the land with the Pope's blessing. The kingdom extended on the southern Italian peninsula and on the island of Sicily. Charles chose to set his capital in Naples and to give lands to his French friends over the local Sicilian lords. In 1282, the Sicilian Vespers insurrection obliged the French lords to flee Sicilia. The island became a kingdom of its own given to the house of Aragon. From the late XIIIth century to the early XVth century many conflicts and insurrections occurred until Alfonso V of Aragon conquered the kingdom of Naples, in 1442, creating the kingdom of Two-Sicilies. It would be the sources of the XVth and XVIth centuries Italian Wars.

The region of Transylvania was one of the earliest targets of German colonization. The Germans, who were mainly merchants, lived side by side with Hungarians and Romanians, although the three groups never blended well. Up until the mid-16th century the fortunes of Transylvania (called Siebenbürgen in German) was closely tied to those of Hungary, and the two states alternated in control of each other. Following conquest by the Ottoman Turks however, Transylvania was greatly reduced, and made into a puppet kingdom. Over time this state became more and more independent, to the point that it virtually managed its own destiny by the mid-17th century. Following the reconquest of the area by the Austrian Empire, the region was revitalized by new German emigrants arriving from the early 18th century on.

Silesia is an historical region in Central Europe spanning parts of modern-day Poland, Germany, and the Czech Republic. Originally inhabited by Slavic tribes, it became part of the Polish state in the 10th century under Mieszko I. Over the centuries, Silesia experienced numerous shifts in sovereignty, including rule by the Bohemian crown in 1335, the Austrian Habsburgs in 1526, and Prussia in 1742. The region was heavily industrialized in the 19th century, contributing significantly to the economy of the new German Empire after 1871, with the Silesian capital Breslau being a major center of science and learning.

The history of Sindh has been intertwined since 711 when it was conquered by the Umayyads.  In 1339 the Samma dynasty was found which oversaw the flowering of Sindhi culture and arts.  The dynasty would last until 1519 when it was conquered by invaders, and the kingdom lost its independence with the coming of Akbar in 1591.

Scania, historically known as Skåne, is a province in southern Sweden that was once a core part of the kingdom of Denmark. It became Swedish territory following the Treaty of Roskilde in 1658. The region has a rich history, marked by its strategic location and fertile lands, which have made it a significant agricultural and trading hub.

Slovakia, a landlocked country in Central Europe, has a rich and diverse history. Inhabited by Illyrian, Celtic, and Germanic tribes in the early centuries AD, the region saw the arrival of the Slavs around the 6th century. It became part of the Kingdom of Hungary in the 11th century and remained so for nearly a millennium.

Salzburg can be regarded as the oldest and most important cultural and spiritual center in present-day Austria. Although it had already been elevated to the rank of archdiocese in 798 and from the late Middle Ages onwards had formed a spiritual principality in the Holy Roman Empire, Salzburg is one of Austria's youngest Länder. The development of the region and its ultimate separation from Bavaria, its mother country, was brought about in the 14th century, but it was not until 1816 that Salzburg was formally incorporated into Austria. Of Austria's present-day Länder, or provinces, Salzburg is the only one to have been ruled as an independent state by a prince-archbishop, and it is the only one of the many spiritual principalities of the Holy Roman Empire that still exists as an independent province.

Smolensk, one of the oldest cities in Russia, has a history dating back to the 9th century. It was a significant stronghold and trading center in the Kievan Rus' and later became the capital of the Smolensk Principality. Over the centuries, Smolensk was a focal point of numerous conflicts due to its strategic location, including invasions by the Mongols, Lithuanians, and Poles. It was heavily fortified and played a crucial role during the Napoleonic Wars.

At first a vassal state of the Empire of Mali, located near Tombouctou, the major trade center, the Empire of Songhai rose in the XVth century. Sonni Ali gained fame fighting the Peuls and the Touaregs. He took Timbuktu in 1468, taking advantage of the quarrels of succession in the empire of Mali.  The Songhai definitively took the place of the defunct Empire of Mali during the XVIth century but they were also striken by succession quarrels and the empire declined. It definitively collapsed with the Moroccan invasion in 1591. Small principalities would replace the mighty empire.

Spain was born of the union of the crown of Castile and the crown of Aragon under a single monarch, Carlos I of Habsburg, who was also the Holy Roman Emperor and the mightiest monarch of the western world. With its annexation of Portugal, Spain became the dominant colonial power from the XVth, XVIth and XVIIth centuries, the first 'empire on which the sun never sets'. Such rare goods such as gold, silver, spices and other luxury items (including some chocolate) came to Europe through Spanish ports. Spanish arts, culture and intellectual life set European standards during the XVIth century, 'the Golden Century'. But while the empire was growing in the colonies and for a time in Europe, particularly during the Italian Wars (1494-1559), England was slowly growing into a maritime power and became Spain's direct competitor. The rivalry was culminated in the aborted invasion of England by the Spanish Armada in 1588, a costly political fiasco that marked the beginning of a slow decline for this mighty empire.

The Golden Horde was one of the successor states to Gengis Khan's enormous empire. It occupied most of the Mongols' European territory and held all of the Russian principalities save Novgorod in vassalage. The state went through a slow but steady decline and its mainly Russian population became vassals in little more than name. The great Timur's attack on the Horde in the 1390's weakened the state sufficiently that Moscow's rise to greatness could commence. The Khan attempted to crush the rebellions of his Russian subjects but with the establishment of the splinter Khanates of Crimea in 1430, Kazan in 1436, and Astrakhan in 1466, the Horde was but a shadow of its former greatness. The last surviving remnant of the Golden Horde was destroyed by the Crimean Khan in 1502.

Strassburg was under the temporal rule of its bishop when the city gained the status of free city of the Holy Roman Empire. The surrounding area was still under the rule of the Bishop of Strassburg. The wealth of the trading city will cause many conflicts between the burghers and the local nobles. In the XVth century, Gutenberg began his work on printing in Strassburg before moving to Mainz. The intellectual life flourished and the city welcomed the ideas of the Reformation. The city chose to elect a Protestant bishop alongside the Catholic one, beginning the 'war of the bishops', war won by the Catholic one, Charles of Lothringen, a Habsburg, just before the Thirty Years War, preventing major damages for the city. The peace of Westphalia in 1648 gave the lands of the Habsburgs in Alsace to France, but the city remained a free city of the Empire. The city was besieged in 1681 and annexed. The city would remain a border city for France keeping its privileges until the Revolution.

Stettin, now known as Szczecin and located in modern-day Poland, is an historic port city situated on the Oder River near the Baltic Sea. Its history dates back to the early medieval period when it was a Slavic settlement, before becoming part of the Duchy of Pomerania in the 12th century. Stettin flourished as a key Hanseatic League member during the Middle Ages, which enhanced its prominence in trade and commerce across the Baltic. In the 17th century, it came under Brandenburg-Prussian control and developed further as an important naval and industrial center.

Funj (or Sennar) was a medieval Islamic state in Sudan that existed from the late 15th century to the early 19th century. Centered around the city of Sennar, it was founded by the Funj people, who established a sultanate in the region after the decline of the Makurian and Alodian kingdoms. The Sultanate of Funj played a significant role in the region's history, fostering a blend of indigenous African and Islamic cultures. It became a key player in the trans-Saharan trade networks, engaging in commerce with North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, and sub-Saharan regions. The sultanate was known for its promotion of Islam, which influenced its legal and cultural practices. However, by the early 19th century, the Sultanate of Funj faced incursions from Ottoman-Egyptian forces, leading to its eventual decline and incorporation into the expanding Egyptian realm of Muhammad Ali.

Sulu is an archipelago and historical region in the southern Philippines, situated in the Sulu Sea between the islands of Borneo and Mindanao. Known for its rich maritime history, Sulu was the heartland of the Sultanate of Sulu, which was established in the 15th century by the Muslim Sultan Sharif ul-Hashim. The Sultanate was a significant Islamic state in the region, engaging in trade and diplomacy with neighboring states and European powers. Originally a vassal of Brunei, the Sultanate of Sulu played a crucial role in regional politics and was known for its distinct culture, which blends Malay, Arab, and indigenous Filipino influences. During the Spanish colonial period, the Sultanate resisted Spanish control and maintained a degree of autonomy.

Although its early history is surrounded in legend, the kingdom of Sunda is thought to have first been founded in the 7th century. The kingdom was also sometimes referred to as Pajajaran (located between two parallel rivers), after its capital city. Eventually the 800 year-old kingdom was extinguished in 1579 by the expansive Sultanate of Banten.

Founded around 1024 as a fortress town, Suzdal developed during the 11th and 12th centuries into one of the principal cities of the grand duchy of Vladimir-Suzdal and a political and religious center of North-Eastern Russia. In the early 13th century it became the capital of the Suzdal principality, but it was razed by the Mongols under Batu Khan in 1238, and never recovered its importance. In 1451 Suzdal passed to the grand duchy of Moscow.

Swabia, in southwestern Germany, derives its name from the Suebi, a Germanic tribe that settled in the area during the 3rd century AD. Known as one of the five great stem duchies of medieval Germany, Swabia encompassed parts of modern-day Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, and even extended into eastern Switzerland and Alsace. The region played a significant role in the Holy Roman Empire, particularly under the rule of the Hohenstaufen dynasty, which produced such emperors as Frederick I 'Barbarossa' (1155-1190), Henry VI (1191-1197) and Frederick II (1220-1250).

Sweden is a very old nation with its roots in the misty times preceding the Viking era. In 1419 the country had recently been joined to Norway and Denmark in the Union of Kalmar, but the Swedes soon proved uncomfortable with having a Danish king. Most of the 15th century was spent vacilitating between staying in the union and leaving it. The final bloody farewells were said in 1521, when the Swedish nobleman Gustav Vasa forced the Danes to accept a totally independent Sweden. Both Danes and Swedes kept eyeing each other with deep mistrust however, and each nation dreamed of conquering the other. Gustav Vasa's reign was long and prosperous. Sweden went from being desperately poor and undeveloped to having good finances and a decent army. His death saw renewed strife as Sweden became embroiled in a long war against Russia for supremacy over Estonia, followed by a civil war between Duke Charles and King Sigismund that evolved into war with Poland. In 1617 the wars had been won and Sweden had gained more lands from Russia during the Time of Troubles. Gustav II Adolf was the greatest king Sweden has ever known, and with the help of his chancellor Axel Oxenstierna he totally reformed the country and beat the imperials in the 30 Years War. Sweden was now the Great Power of Northern Europe - a position she would hold until 1718, when the hero king Charles XII died in battle, having failed in his defense of Sweden from her ravenous neighbors. The country faded once more into the periphery of European politics...

Syria, located in the Middle East along the Mediterranean Sea, is one of the world's oldest continuously inhabited regions. Its history dates back to ancient civilizations such as the Sumerians, Akkadians, and Amorites. Throughout the centuries, Syria has been a crossroads of various empires, including the Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians, Greeks, and Romans. The region became a significant center of early Christianity and later, under the Umayyad Caliphate, Damascus served as the capital of the Islamic world.

Tangiers, located in northern Morocco, has a rich and varied history dating back to ancient times. Initially a Phoenician trading post, it later became a Carthaginian and then a Roman settlement. Over the centuries, Tangiers was captured by the Vandals, Byzantines, and Arabs, reflecting its strategic importance. In 1471, it fell to the Portuguese, and later to the English, who eventually ceded it to Morocco in 1684.

Taungu was a Burmese town located on the Sittoung River. It rose to great prominence in 1486 when King Minkyino ascended the throne. His reign signaled a resurgence of the Burmese realm after two centuries of bitter internecine warfare between various petty kingdoms. By 1535, Minkyino's son Tabengshweti continued his father's conquests, until the Taungu Dynasty controlled most of present-day Myanmar. In 1550 Tabengshweti's son-in-law Bayinnaung became ruler. In 1569 he invaded Siam and captured the city of Ayutthaya, but by 1584 Siam had once more become independent. In the following decades the Taungu Dynasty lost most of its influence once again.

Located at the western Mediterranean coast of Asia Minor, Teke was founded by Yunus Beg in 1321 as a vassal lordship of the Hamidites to the north, in ancient Pisidia. Teke survived the annexation of its parent state by the Ottomans in 1389. Its capital was the strategic port of Antalya, which witnessed several invasions by the Latin kings of Cyprus. Although conquered by the Ottomans in 1390, the Beylik of Teke was re-established soon after Timur's victory at the Battle of Ankara. This revival, however, was to be short-lived as Teke's last ruler Osman Beg was assassinated in 1423. Osman's lands, along with the city of Antalya, were once more added to the Ottoman Empire.

The volcanic island of Ternate was the seat of a local dynasty beginning in the XIIIth century and converted to Islam in 1495, the first of the Moluccan kingdoms to do so. The Moluccas were one of the most important the source of the spices trade. Through its XIVth century victories on its neighbours, Ternate was the most important of the four sultanates (Ternate, Tidore, Bacan and Jailolo).  The first contact with Portuguese sailors was in 1512 after Franscisco Serrão's disastrous expedition and shipwreck. The sultan of Ternate allowed the Portuguese to build a fortress in 1522 as he thought to use them in his conflicts with the other islands. It went the other way as in 1535, the Portuguese deposed the sultan. They were expelled in 1575 and Ternate became a fiercely islamic and anti-Portuguese state. In 1606, the Spanish, allied to Tidore, captured Ternate and deported the sultan. The Dutch, who have come in the area in 1599, were called to help in 1607 and allowed to build a fort. The Spanish abandoned Tidore and Ternate in 1663 but the Dutch influence was now so important that Ternate became the seat of the V.O.C. capital, attempting to control all the spice trade.

The Republic of Texas was established on March 2nd, 1836, following its declaration of independence from Mexico. It existed as a sovereign nation until its annexation by the United States on December 29th, 1845. During its brief existence, the Republic faced numerous challenges, including conflict with Mexico, political pressure from the United States, internal struggles, and economic difficulties. Key figures such as Sam Houston, who served as its first and third president, played crucial roles in navigating these challenges. The Republic's legacy is marked by its efforts to establish a stable government and its eventual integration into the United States, significantly shaping the history of the region.

The Kingdom of Thessalonica was a short-lived Crusader state established in 1204 following the Fourth Crusade's capture of Constantinople. Founded by Boniface of Montferrat, it served as a vassal of the Latin Empire and encompassed parts of Macedonia and Thessaly. Despite its initial expansion, the kingdom faced constant threats from neighboring states and internal strife. Boniface's death in 1207 led to a period of instability, and by 1224, the kingdom fell to the Despotate of Epirus. The Kingdom of Thessalonica's brief existence highlights the turbulent nature of the post-Crusade period in former Byzantine territories.

Thuringia is an historical region located in central Germany, with a rich history dating back to ancient times. During the early medieval period, it was inhabited by the Thuringii, a Germanic tribe. By the 8th century, it was incorporated into the Carolingian Empire, and over the centuries, it became part of various territories and states, including the Holy Roman Empire. In the Middle Ages, Thuringia was a large and wealthy duchy, notably ruled by the Ludowinger dynasty. The region played a prominent role in the Reformation, with many Thuringians supporting Martin Luther.

Tibet emerged from an obscure and mostly unknown history to flourish in the 7th century as an independent kingdom with its capital at Lhasa. In the 13th century Tibet fell under Mongol influence, but reverted to independence in 1368 when the Mongols were also evicted from China. In 1270 Kublai Khan, emperor of China, was converted to Buddhism by the abbot of the Sakya lamasery. The abbot returned to Tibet to found the Sakya dynasty (1270-1340) and to become the first priest-king of Tibet. In 1578 the Dge-lugs-pa, or Yellow Hat Sect, asked the Tümed Mongol leader Altan Khan to renew the relationship that had existed in the days of Kublai. In 1642, with exemplary devotion, Güüshi Khan enthroned the Dalai Lama as ruler of Tibet, marking the end of the reign of the old kings. The Chinese invaded in 1720, fearing a Tibet controlled by hostile Mongols. After an initial reverse, their armies drove out the Mongols and were welcomed at Lhasa as deliverers, all the more because they brought with them the new Dalai Lama, Bskal-bzang-rgya-mtsho. For the next 200 years there was no more fighting between Tibetans and Chinese.

Originally the western half of the Chagatai Khanate, the Timurids derived their name from the Great Khan known to history as Tamerlane (Timur Lenkh in Persian) who died in 1405. Tamerlane was one of those few military leaders who seemed to be blessed by the gods. He never lost a battle, and expanded his realm to reach from the frontiers of Byzantium to the gates of Delhi. However, by 1419 the Timurids had already begun their swift decline and their remaining power was concentrated in Afghanistan and Amu Darya. Though their realm was greatly reduced, the fame of the empire was still great and the magnificent cities of Samarkhand and Bukhara were long a by-word for wealth and learning. Their story ended with Bâbur, who transformed the ailing Timurids remnants into the great and vibrant Mughal Empire in the early 16th century.

The Zayyanid Dynasty founded its capital at Tlemcen(in modern-state of Algeria). For over 300 years, the Zayyanids had a tenuous hold on central Maghrib. The regime was plagued by frequent rebellions but learned to survive as the vassal of the Merinids and later the Hafsids. At one time Tlemcen acted as an ally of Spain. Many coastal cities defied the ruling dynasties and asserted their autonomy as municipal republics. They were governed by their merchant oligarchies, by tribal chieftains from the surrounding countryside, or by the privateers who operated out of their ports. Nonetheless, Tlemcen prospered as a commercial center and was called the 'pearl of the Maghrib'. Tlemcen would eventually be devastated by the Spanish and later, conquered by the Ottomans.

Under the fabulously wealthy Medici family, Florence went from being a small but rich city state to becoming the Grand Duchy of Tuscany (1569). Only the Republic of Lucca and the duchy of Massa and Carrara remained independent. After the extinction of the Medici line, Tuscany passed (1737) to ex-duke Francis of Lorraine (later Holy Roman Emperor Francis I), who was succeeded by Grand Duke Leopold I (1765-90, later Emperor Leopold II) and then by Ferdinand III (1790-1801, 1814-24). The French Revolutionary armies invaded Tuscany in 1799 and it was briefly included in the kingdom of Etruria (1801-7) and was ruled under the duchy of Parma before it was annexed to France by Napoleon I, who set up his sister to rule it from Lucca.

Toulouse, located in southern France, was originally a stronghold of the Volcae Tectosages, an ancient Celtic people. Known as Tolosa during the Roman period, it became an important trading hub. In the early medieval era, it served as the capital of the Visigothic Kingdom of Toulouse until it was taken by Clovis I in 508 AD. Throughout the rest of the Middle Ages, Toulouse was the center of the wealthy County of Toulouse and played a crucial role during the Cathar Crusades in the 13th century. The city also witnessed significant events during the French Wars of Religion in the 16th century.

Transoxania, historically significant in Central Asia, refers to the region located between the Oxus (Amu Darya) and Jaxartes (Syr Darya) rivers, encompassing parts of modern-day Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, and Kazakhstan. It was a vital crossroads of trade and culture from antiquity through the medieval period, integrating diverse influences from Persian, Greek, Indian, and Turkic civilizations. The region flourished under various empires, including the Greco-Bactrian, Kushan, and Samanid dynasties, and became a key part of the Silk Road trade network. The great cities of Samarkand and Bukhara were renowned centers of learning and culture, and formed the nucleus of the Timurid Empire in the 14th and 15th centuries. Transoxania's rich history reflects its role as a melting pot of cultures and a significant player in the political and economic dynamics of Central Asia.

When the treacherous army of the Fourth Crusade overthrew the Byzantine Empire and established the Latin Empire of Constantinople in 1204, several Greek successor states sprang up around it. The Empire of Trebizond was one of them. After the Mongol invasion the empire experienced tremendous economic prosperity, as it became the crossroad of trade routes leading to Russia, the Mediterranean and the Middle East. With the decline of Mongol power after 1320, Trebizond suffered increasingly from attacks by various Turkish clans and states, civil wars, and domestic intrigues, until it eventually fell in 1461 after leading a coalition of Greek powers against the Sultan, in a last-ditch attempt to restore the Byzantine Empire. At the height of its wealth and power the court of the Grand Comneni was a great artistic and cultural center and made Trebizond the last refuge of Hellenistic civilization.

After its conquest by the Muslim armies in the 7th century, Tripolitania became subject to various Arab and Berber dynasties, among them the Aghlabids, the Fatimids, and the Hafsids. In 1510 Tripoli was captured by the forces of Ferdinand the Catholic of Spain, who turned it over to the Knights of St. John in 1530. The latter lost the region only 21 years later to the Ottoman Turks, who ruled it either directly or through suzerains for the next 360 years. In 1711 the local governor, Ahmad Karamanli, won recognition from the Ottomans as hereditary pasha (governor), and his dynasty ruled Tripolitania for all but a few years until 1835.

The County of Tripoli was one of the Crusader States that was formed at the conclusion of the First Crusade. It held a strategic location on the Mediterreanean coast but could not survive the onslaught of the Muslims. The province of Lebanon holds a catholic majority so as Tripoli you will have a slight advantage over the other Crusader states in the area in this regard.

A small principality hugging the southern tip of India in 1419, Travancore would grow to be the most imposing native regional opponent of the onrushing European conquest of India during the eighteenth century by annexing several of its smaller neighbors in an expansionist campaign which included victories over the Dutch.

The Berber Hafsid dynasty began in 1228 when Abû Zakariyâ Yahyâ proclaim his independence from the Berber Almohad dynasty. The capital was set in Tunis and flourished through its trade with Genoans, Venetians, Aragoneses and Sicilians. The Hafsids expanded in the XIVth century on the west to Central Algeria and to the east to Tripolitania but soon they declined limited on the west by the Moroccan Merinids, a plague in 1384, succession quarrels, retaliations from the Christian kingdoms to piracy and, after the Reconquista, the difficult integration of the Spanish Moors. The Hafsid became caught in the struggle between Spain and the Ottoman Empire and the latter seized Tunisia in 1574. The Beys of Tunisia were appointed by the sultan but actually only ruled the cities. The local beys became more and more independent and created a local dynasty. Losing the ottoman financial support, Tunisia became the haven for pirates that would cease their art only after the French invasion in 1836.

The first phase of expansion of the heirs of the great Osman was checked and partially reversed by their huge defeat in 1402 at the hands of Tamerlane. The remaining Ottoman possessions were beset by civil war, which gradually cooled down under Mehmet I. Then the Ottomans had a stroke of great fortune: five successive Sultans of exceptional ability, who expanded the empire, enriched its merchants and patronized the arts and sciences. In 1453, Constantinople was conquered, and the Ottomans assumed increasingly imperial trappings. The Mamelukes were overrun in 1517. By the end of the reign of Süleyman I ('the Magificent') in 1566, the Ottomans, the acknowledged leaders of the Islamic world, were, together with the populous Chinese and the globe-spanning Spanish empires, one of the greatest powers of that age. Subsequent internal politics and increasing conservatism led to the loss of their pre-eminence, though the Ottomans remained a great power until the late 18th century.
