Their union with the Choctaw was not happy, and in 1854 the Chickasaw separated and relocated to their own territory in south-central Oklahoma. The Chickasaw Nation remained in existence until dissolved in 1906 to allow for Oklahoma statehood. Although many Chickasaw left or merged with the general population after allotment took their lands, 12,000 still live in the vicinity of their tribal headquarters at Ada.

The Chumash Indians, a Native American tribe, mainly inhabited the southern coastal regions of California, in the vicinity of what is now Santa Barbara and Ventura, extending as far south as Malibu. They also occupied the three northern islands of the Santa Barbara group, a part of the Channel Islands. Modern place names with Chumash origins include, Malibu, Ojai, Point Mugu, Piru, Lake Castaic, and Simi Valley. Estimates of their population range from 10,000 to 20,000 before contact with Spanish settlers in Mexico, though the population had apparently been devastated by disease prior to that. By 1900, this population had declined to just 200, though there are now some 5,000 people who identify themselves as Chumash. The Chumash spoke seven closely related Chumashan languages which can not be connected to any other language family. For a while, it was assumed the Chumash family was part of the Hokan language phylum, but this was based solely on a few easily borrowed words, such as that for shell-bead money. The name Chumash is from the Syuxtun Aqliw (Santa Barbara language) and refers to the people from an island they named Micchumash (Santa Cruz Island). Chumash literally means makers of shell bead money. When outsiders came, they called all people within the Chumash language family, which embraces seven distinct languages, Cchumash. The different spelling here shows that there is aspiration after the [ch] sound. Cchumash people working on resuscitating the languages, are working to create a fixed orthography as of November 15, 2005. The Chumash were hunter-gatherers, who were adept at fishing. They are one of only two New World people who regularly navigated the ocean (the other was the Tongva, a neighboring tribe located to the South). Some settlements built plank canoes called tomols, which facilitated the distribution of goods, and could even be used for whaling. Remains of a developed Chumash culture, including rock paintings (petroglyphs) apparently depicting the Chumash cosmology, can still be seen.

An interesting tribe of Pueblo Indians of Shoshonean stock occupying seven communal pueblo towns situated upon a high mesa within a reservation in north-east Arizona. One of these pueblos, Hano, is occupied by immigrants from the Tewa tribe of New Mexico, speaking a distinct language. Like all Pueblos they are sedentary and agricultural in habit, and although the entire surrounding country is a desert of shifting sand, they carry on successful farming with the aid of water supplied by numerous small streams which issue from the base of the mesa. Besides their abundant crops of corn, bean, squashes, tobacco and peaches (the last an inheritance from the former missionaries), they manufacture a fine variety of pottery and basket-work, and excel in wood-carving and the weaving of native cotton. Many of them are also skillful metal-workers. Their houses are square-built and flat-roofed structures of stone or adobe, sometimes several stories in height, with a sufficient number of rooms to accommodate hundreds of persons, and with store-rooms filled with provisions sufficient to last for a year. For better protection from hostile attack, most of the outer walls are without doors, entrance and egress being made through a hole in the roof by means of a ladder, other ladders being let down at the outside. In former times also the steep trails which constitute the only means of approach to the summit were effectively closed at night or when danger threatened, by removing the ladders which are necessary in the most difficult places. The first white men to make acquaintance with the Hopi were a detachment from Coronado's expedition in 1540, accompanied by the Franciscan Father Juan de Padilla, afterward murdered while preaching to the wild tribes of the plains. They were visited by Espejo in 1583, at which time they occupied five pueblos. In 1598, they were brought regularly under Spanish authority by Governor Oñate of New Mexico, who appointed a priest to take charge of their spiritual welfare, but no regular mission was attempted in the tribe until 1629, when the mission of San Bernardino was established at Awátobi by a party of four Franciscans headed by Father Francisco de Porras. Other missions were founded later at Shongópovi (San Bartolomé) and Oraibi (San Francisco) with visitas at Walpi and Mishóngnovi. The Mission sustained an uncertain existence until the great revolt of the Pueblos, when four resident missionaries were killed and the churches destroyed. The rising was put down twelve years later, but no attempt was made to re-establish the Hopi missions, excepting at Awátobi, with 800 souls, which was visited in the spring of 1700 by Father Juan Garaycoecha, at the request of the inhabitants, but without permanent result. Later in the same year, on account of the evident friendship of the Awátobi for the missionaries, the warriors of the other pueblos attacked it by night, setting fire to the pueblo, slaughtering all the men, many of whom were smothered in underground chambers, and carrying off all the women and children to be distributed among the other pueblos. Awátobi can still be traced in its ruins, including the walls of the old church. In 1726, permission was given to the Jesuits to undertake work in the tribe, but with no result, and in 1745 the field was again given over to the Franciscans, with little success, the Hopi stubbornly refusing to allow the establishment of a mission. In 1778-80 a three year drought with consequent famine and pestilence, almost extinguished the tribe for a time, the survivors scattering among the neighbouring tribes, but still steadfastly refusing any help from the Spaniards.

The original Mahican homeland was the Hudson River Valley from the Catskill Mountains north to the southern end of Lake Champlain. Bounded by the Schoharie River in the west, it extended east to the crest of the Berkshire Mountains in western Massachusetts from northwest Connecticut north to the Green Mountains in southern Vermont. Because they include all Algonquin tribes between the Hudson and Connecticut Rivers, some estimates of the Mahican population in 1600 range as high as 35,000. However, when limited to the core tribes of the Mahican confederacy near Albany, New York, it was somewhere around 8,000. By 1672 this had fallen to around 1,000. At the lowpoint in 1796, 300 Stockbridge, the Last of the Mohicans, were living with the Oneida and Brotherton in upstate New York. However, if the Mahican with the Wyandot and Delaware in Ohio were also included, the actual total time was probably closer to 600. The census of 1910 listed 600 Stockbridge and Brotherton in northern Wisconsin. Three years after the passage of the Indian Reorganization Act in 1934, the Stockbridge became a federally recognized tribe. They currently have almost 1,500 members living on, or near, their reservation west of Green Bay. There are also 1,700 Brotherton Indians (without federal status) on the east side of Lake Winnebago. When James Fenimore Cooper wrote Last of the Mohicans in 1826, he made the Mahican famous. Unfortunately, he also made them extinct in the minds of many people and also confused their name and history with the Mohegan from eastern Connecticut. Unfortunately, this misconception has persisted, and most Americans today would be surprised to learn the Mahican are very much alive and living in Wisconsin under an assumed name ...Stockbridge Indians. With a similar language and name, the Mahican (Mohican) and the Mohegan may have been members of the same tribe before contact. The Mohegan, however, migrated east as part of the Pequot and settled in eastern Connecticut sometime around 1500, while the Mahican stayed in the Hudson Valley. Afterwards, these two tribes followed separate paths. Although culturally similar to other woodland Algonquin, the Mahican were shaped by their constant warfare with the neighboring Iroquois. Politically, the Mahican were a confederacy of five tribes with as many 40 villages. In keeping with other eastern Algonkin, civil authority was not strong. Mahican villages were governed by hereditary sachems (matrilineal descent) advised by a council of the clan leaders. The Mahican had three clans, bear, wolf, and turtle. However, warfare required a higher degree of organization. A general council of sachems met regularly at their capital of Shodac (east of present-day Albany) to decide important matters affecting the entire confederacy. In times of war, the Mahican council passed its authority to a war chief chosen for his proven ability. For the duration of the conflict, the war leader exercised almost dictatorial power. Mahican villages were fairly large. Usually consisting of 20 to 30 mid-sized longhouses, they were located on hills and heavily fortified. Large cornfields were located nearby. Agriculture provided most of their diet but was supplemented by game, fish, and wild foods. For reasons of safety, the Mahican did move to scattered hunting camps during the winter like other Algonquin and usually spent the colder months inside their castles (fortified villages). Copper, gotten from the Great Lakes through trade, was used extensively for ornaments and some of their arrowheads. Once they began trade with the Dutch, the Mahican abandoned many of their traditional weapons and quickly became very expert with their new firearms. Contrary to the usual stereotype, most Mahican warriors were deadly marksmen. The mother of the famous Miami chief Little Turtle was a Mahican.

The Neutrals lived around Southern Ontario north of Lake Erie. Their territory also included a some of western New York (east and south of Niagara Falls) and a portion of southeastern Michigan near Detroit. Because they were neutral in the wars between the Huron and Iroquois, the French called this large Iroquian Confederacy the Neutre (Nation du Neutre, Neuter Nation or Neutrals). Whatever name the Neutrals used for their confederacy has been lost, but most Iroquoian tribes in southern Ontario referred to themselves collectively as the Wendat dwellers on a peninsula. The Huron called them the Attiwandaron (Attionondaron or Attiwandaronk) meaning those who speak a little differently. The Iroquois name, Hatiwantarunh, had a similar meaning. Apparently some of the Neutrals were more closely attached to the Erie than the others, because both the Seneca and Huron often referred to both the Erie and Neutrals as the Cat Nation. The Seneca name in this case was Kahkwa (Kahqua), while its equivalent in Huron was Yenresh.

Before the French became acquainted with this tribe (in 1673) the Quapaw had lived on Ohio River above its junction with the Wabash, and that portion of the Ohio was known as Arkansas River by the Illinois from this circumstance. It was formerly thought that the Pacaha or Capaha met by De Soto in this part of Arkansas were the tribe in question, but it is not probable that they had left the Ohio then, and the name Capaha, the form on which the relationship is supposed to be established, is probably incorrect. In 1673 Marquette visited them and turned back at their towns without descending the Mississippi any farther. La Salle in 1682, Tonti in 1686, and all subsequent voyagers down and up the Mississippi mention them, and they soon became firm allies of French. Shortly after Marquette's visit they were ravaged by pestilence and the Ukakhpakht and the village was moved farther downstream. A few years before 1700 the people of Tongigua moved across and settled with those of Tourima, and still later all of the towns moved from the Mississippi to the Arkansas. Le Page du Pratz (1758) encountered them about 12 miles above the entrance of White River. Sibley (1832) found them in 1805 on the south side of Arkansas River about 12 miles above Arkansas Post. By a treaty signed at St. Louis, August 24, 1818, the Quapaw ceded all their claims south of Arkansas River except a small territory between Arkansas Post and Little Rock, extending inland to Saline River. The latter was also given up in a treaty signed November 15, 1824, at Harrington's, Arkansas Territory and the tribe agreed to live in the country of the Caddo. They were assigned by the Caddo a tract on Bayou Treache on the south side of Red River, but it was frequently overflowed, their crops were often destroyed, and there was much sickness, and in consequence they soon returned to their old country. There they annoyed the the white settlers so much that by a treaty signed May 13, 1833, the United States Government conveyed to them 150 sections of land in the extreme southeastern part of Kansas and the northeastern part of Indian Territory, to which they in turn agreed to move. February 23, 1867, they ceded their lands in Kansas and the northern part their lands in Indian Territory. In 1877 the Ponca were brought to the Quapaw Reservation for a short time, and when they removed went to their own reservation later west of the Osage most of the Quapaw went lands with them. Still later the lands of the Quapaw were allotted in severalty and are now citizens of Oklahoma.

Subsequently under Mamluk and then Ottoman rule, Jerusalem was rebuilt and restored but by the late 16th century it was declining as a commercial and religious center.

The Orthodox Church has had an influence throughout the Holy Land region since Christ walked there. The Patriarchy of Jersualem is one of the major holy sites to the Eastern Christian tradition and historically has been granted rites under Islamic masters. The Thema of Palastine is one regional division of the Byzantine Empire and this country takes on an autonomous mantle from Constantinople under the head of the Greek Patriarch of Jerusalem in vassalage to the Byzantine Basileos.

The Tarascan state was a state in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, roughly covering the geographic area of the present-day Mexican state of Michoacán. At the time of the Spanish conquest of Mexico it was the second-largest state in Mexico. The state was founded in the early 14th century and lost its independence to the Spanish in 1530. In 1543 it officially became the governorship of Michoacán, from the Nahuatl name for the Tarascan state, Michoacán ('place of those who have fish'). In P'urhépecha, language of the Tarascans, the name of the state was Iréchecua Tzintzuntzáni, the 'lands of Tzintzuntzan'. Under the rule of cazonci Tzitzipandáquare a number of regions were conquered, only to be lost again by rebellions or strategic retreats when confronted with Aztec expansion. In 1460 the Tarascan state reached the Pacific coast at Zacatula, advanced into the valley of Toluca, and also, on the northern rim, reached into the present day state of Guanajuato. In the 1470s Aztecs under Axayacatl captured a series of Tarascan frontier towns and closed in on the Tarascan heartland, but were eventually defeated. This experience prompted the Tarascan ruler to further fortify the Aztec frontier with military centers along the border, such as at Cutzamala. He also allowed Otomies and Matlatzincas who had been driven out of their homelands by the Aztecs to settle in the border area under the condition that they took part in the defense of the Tarascan lands. From 1480 the Aztec ruler Ahuitzotl intensified the conflict with the Tarascans. He supported attacks on Tarascan lands by other ethnic groups allied with or subjugated to the Aztecs such as Matlatzincas, Chontales, and Cuitlatecs. The Tarascans, led by the Caconzi Zuangua, repelled the attacks but further Tarascan expansion was halted until the arrival of the Spaniards two years into the rule of the last Caconzi of an independent Tarascan state, Tangáxuan II.

Evidence of human occupation in what is now the state of Tlaxcala extends back to 12,000 B.C.E., with the earliest identified cultures being Tzompantepec (170-1200 B.C.E), Tlatempa (1200-800 B.C.E), and Texoloc (800-400 B.C.E.). The Toltecs also had a presence, but the first major native culture here was the Olmec Xicalanca. This civilization fell into decline after 900 C.E and was replaced by a sub-group of the Chichimecas. In the 14th century, the Chichimecas were driven out by the Tlaxcalans, a Nahua people and the indigenous ethnicity that still dominates the state. The Tlaxcalans founded the city of Tlaxcala and then began to subdue the surrounding peoples. Eventually, the Tlaxcalan nation would evolve into a confederation of four sub-states called Tepectipac, Ocotelulco, Tizatlán and Quiahuixtlán. The Tlaxcalan state developed roughly at the same time as another Nahua people, the Mexica, were building the vast Aztec empire with its capital at Tenochtitlan. From the 14th century, these two nations were in near constant state of war. However, even though the Aztecs managed to build the largest empire in Mesoamerica, they never did conquer Tlaxcala. By the time, the Spanish arrived in the 16th century, Tlaxcala was an independent enclave nearly completely surrounded by the Aztec Empire. This left Tlaxcala economically isolated, leaving it without goods such as cotton and salt. This and the constant warfare with the Mexica would give the Tlaxcalans reason to ally with the Spanish. When Hernán Cortés and the Spanish landed on the Veracruz coast, they were greeted by the Totonacas, who were a subject people of the Aztecs and saw the Spanish as a way to free themselves of rule from Tenochtitlan. They allied with the Spanish, and when Cortés decided to go inland to Tenochtitlan, the Totonacas guided them to other subject peoples who would be willing to ally with them, including and especially the Tlaxcalans. However, after entering Tlaxcalan territory, the Spanish were met by a hostile force of 30,000. The Tlaxcalans and the Spanish (with their Indian allies) fought a number of battles, with the Spanish inflicting heavy casualties on the Tlaxcalans despite their superior numbers. The Spaniards’ prowess in battle impressed the Tlaxcalan king Xicotenga, who then not only allowed the Spanish to pass through his territory, he also invited them to the capital city. Cortés stayed in the city of Tlaxcala for 20 days and forged an alliance with the Tlaxcalans to bring down Tenochtitlan. Cortes added 6,000 Tlaxcala warriors to this ranks and arrived to Tenochtitlan in November 1519. They were received by Emperor Moctezuma II, who understood the potential danger of a Spanish-Tlaxcalan alliance. Despite initial friendliness, intrigue and siege of the capital followed, with the Aztec backlash sending Cortes’ very wounded army limping back to Tlaxcalan territory. The Tlaxcalan king gave the Spanish refuge but promised further assistance in the conquest of Tenochtitlan only under certain conditions including perpetual exemption from tribute of any sort, part of the spoils of war and control of two provinces that bordered Tlaxcala. Cortés agreed. Cortes and the Tlaxcalans returned to Tenochtitlan in December of 1520. After many battles, including street-by-street fighting in Tenochtitlan itself, the Aztec Empire fell in August 1521. For the most part, the Spanish kept their promise to the Tlaxcalans. Unlike Tenochtitlan and other cities, Tlaxcala was not destroyed after the Conquest. They also allowed many Tlaxcalans to retain their indigenous names. The Tlaxcalans were mostly able to keep their traditional form of government. For 300 years of colonial rule, the Spanish mostly kept their promises to the Tlaxcalans.

The Despotate of Morea came into being in 1348, with the first Despot, Manuel Kantakouzenos, son of the Emperor John VI. Later, in 1384, the Palaiologoi came and succeeded in expanding the Despotate virtually throughout the Peloponnese. However, the disaster which dogged the sovereign was not slow in reaching here as well and so when Konstantinos Palaiologos, Despot of Mystras, left for the capital wearing the martyred crown of the last emperor, his brother Demetrios, who succeeded him after the legendary Fall of Constantinople in 1453, surrendered to the Turks in 1460.

The Despotate of Morea was a semi-autonomous province of the Byzantine Empire, established in 1349 by Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos. Located in the Peloponnese region of southern Greece, its capital was the fortified city of Mystras. The Despotate flourished as a cultural and intellectual center during the Palaiologan Renaissance, attracting scholars and artists. It played a crucial role in the Byzantine resistance against the Ottoman Turks until its conquest by Sultan Mehmed II in 1460.

The Principality of Achaea was a feudal state established in the Peloponnese region of Greece following the Fourth Crusade in 1204. Founded by William of Champlitte and Geoffrey I of Villehardouin, it became one of the most powerful and influential Crusader states in Greece. The principality thrived under the Villehardouin dynasty, known for its chivalric culture and strong fortifications, including the famous castles of Chlemoutsi and Mystras. Despite its initial success, the principality faced numerous challenges, including conflicts with the Byzantine Empire and internal strife, eventually falling to the Byzantine reconquest in 1432. The legacy of the Principality of Achaea is marked by its blend of Western European and Byzantine influences, leaving a lasting impact on the region's history and architecture.

The Sultanate of Angoche, established around 1485, was a significant Islamic trading state located along the northern coast of Mozambique. Initially a vassal of the Kilwa Sultanate, Angoche gained independence in 1513 and became a prominent center for trade, particularly in gold and ivory. The sultanate's strategic location allowed it to thrive as a hub for Muslim traders bypassing Portuguese-controlled routes. Despite its prosperity, Angoche faced economic decline and political challenges, including conflicts with the Portuguese, who eventually conquered it in 1910.

Ansbach grew around a Benedictine monastery founded in 748 AD. It became the seat of the Hohenzollern family in 1331 and later the residence of the Margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach. The city flourished during the Baroque period, with notable architectural landmarks such as the Ansbach Residence and the Church of St. Gumbertus. In 1791, Ansbach was annexed by Prussia and later became part of Bavaria in 1806.

The Judicate of Arborea was one of the four independent judicates of medieval Sardinia. Established in the 11th century, it was centered around the city of Oristano and played a crucial role in resisting external domination, particularly from the Aragonese. Under the leadership of notable figures like Eleanor of Arborea, it maintained a degree of autonomy and implemented progressive legal reforms, such as the Carta de Logu. The kingdom persisted until the early 15th century when it was eventually absorbed into the Crown of Aragon.

Avignon, located in southeastern France on the banks of the Rhône River, is a city steeped in history. Originally founded by the Gallic tribe of Cavares, it later became a significant Roman settlement. Avignon's prominence surged in the 14th century when it was chosen as the papal residence by Pope Clement V in 1309, making it the center of the Catholic Church until 1377. The city is renowned for the Palais des Papes (Papal Palace), a testament to its ecclesiastical heritage, and its historic center, which is a UNESCO World Heritage site.

Bahrain, an island nation in the Persian Gulf, boasts a rich history dating back over 5,000 years. It was the center of the ancient Dilmun civilization, a crucial trading hub linking Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley. Over the centuries, Bahrain has seen various rulers, including the Assyrians, Babylonians, Persians, and Portuguese. The Al Khalifa family established their rule in 1783 after asserting independence from Persia, and in turn fighting against Oman. Bahrain later became a British protectorate in the 19th century.

Bologna is a vibrant city in northern Italy boasting a rich history dating back over 2,500 years. Originally an Etruscan settlement known as Felsina, it was later occupied by the Gallic Boii and became a Roman colony called Bononia around 190 BC. Throughout the Middle Ages, Bologna flourished as a free commune and was home to Europe's oldest university, founded in 1088. The city experienced periods of rule by various lords before being incorporated into the Papal States in 1506. Despite suffering significant damage through the centuries, Bologna has preserved its medieval charm, characterized by its iconic towers and extensive porticoes.

Berg, located in the Rhineland of Germany, was established in 1101 as a county and later elevated to a duchy in 1380. Initially part of the Kingdom of Lotharingia, it emerged as a significant political entity under the rule of the Ezzonen dynasty. The duchy experienced substantial growth and influence, particularly after uniting with the County of Jülich in 1348. Throughout its history, Berg was often involved in regional conflicts and alliances, including its union with the Duchy of Cleves and the County of Mark in the 16th century. The duchy was eventually awarded to Prussia in 1815 following the Napoleonic Wars.

The Duchy of Brunswick-Lüneburg, established in 1235, was a significant principality within the Holy Roman Empire, located in what is now northern Germany. It originated when Otto the Child, a member of the House of Welf, was granted the duchy by Emperor Frederick II. The duchy was named after its two main centers, Brunswick and Lüneburg, and experienced numerous partitions and reunifications over the centuries - primarily its elevation to the Electorate of Hanover in 1692. Despite these changes, it remained a cohesive entity until the dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire in 1806. The duchy's legacy continued through its successor states, the Kingdom of Hanover and the Duchy of Brunswick, established by the Congress of Vienna in 1815.

The Canary Islands, an archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean off the northwest coast of Africa, were initially settled by the pagan Guanches, an indigenous Berber people who became cut-off from the mainland millennia ago. The islands were later explored by the Phoenicians and Romans, and by the early 15th century the Spanish had begun their conquest under the French explorer Jean de Béthencourt. In 1496 the islands were declared fully subjugated, and were incorporated into the Kingdom of Castile. For centuries, the Canaries were a crucial stopover for Spanish galleons en route to the Americas, fostering a blend of cultures.

The history of Dalmatia, along the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, dates back to around 1000 BC when it was inhabited by the Illyrian tribes, including the Delmatae, from whom the region gets its name. The Greeks began colonizing the area in the 4th century BC, establishing cities like Issa (Vis) and Pharos (Hvar). Conquered by the Romans in the 2nd century BC, Dalmatia became a Roman province. Over the centuries, it saw numerous rulers, including the Byzantines, Venetians, and the Habsburgs. The region's strategic location made it a contested territory, leading to a diverse cultural heritage.

Fars, a region in south-central Iran, is historically significant as the heartland of the ancient Persian Empire. Known as Pars or Persis in antiquity, it was the birthplace of the Achaemenid Empire founded by Cyrus the Great in the 6th century BC. The region's capital, Pasargadae, and later Persepolis, served as the empire's political and ceremonial centers. Fars continued to be a crucial area under subsequent empires, including the Seleucids, Parthians, and Sassanids. The region's historical importance persisted into the Islamic period and beyond, with its cultural and architectural heritage still evident today.

Florence was founded as a Roman military colony in the 1st century BC, and over the centuries became a major cultural, economic, and political hub. During the 14th to 16th centuries, it became the cradle of the Italian Renaissance, fostering the works of luminaries like Leonardo da Vinci, Michelangelo, and Dante. The city was the seat of a powerful republic famed for its condottieri, later becoming the Grand Duchy of Tuscany. Its wealth, largely driven by banking and trade, supported an unparalleled flourishing of the arts and sciences.

Galicia, located in the northwest of Spain, has a unique cultural history that dates back to ancient times. Initially inhabited by the Celtic Gallaeci tribe, the region was conquered by the Romans around 137 BC and later became part of the Visigothic Kingdom. During the Middle Ages, Galicia was a significant Christian kingdom, known for its pilgrimage route, the Camino de Santiago, and capital, Santiago de Compostela - one of the great holy sites of Europe. The region was later integrated into the Kingdom of Castile in the late 11th century. Despite periods of political turmoil, Galicia has retained a distinct Celto-Iberian cultural identity, including its own language, Galician.

The Ghana Empire flourished in West Africa from the 6th to the 13th century AD. Located in the western Sudan savannah region, it was strategically positioned between the Sahara Desert and the rainforests, facilitating control over the trans-Saharan trade routes. The empire's wealth was largely derived from its abundant resources of gold, iron, and copper, which were traded for salt and other goods. The capital, Koumbi Saleh, became a bustling center of commerce and culture. Ghana's decline began in the 12th century due to internal strife, drought, and the rise of rival powers like the Sosso and Mali Empires.

Halych, an historic city on the Dniester River in western Ukraine, was the center of the medieval Principality of Halych, which later became part of the Kingdom of Galicia-Volhynia. The city flourished in the 12th and 13th centuries, serving as a major political, economic, and cultural hub in the region. Despite suffering from invasions and political turmoil, Halych remained an important site, with notable landmarks such as the Church of the Nativity and the remnants of Halych Castle.

The Kingdom of Hawai'i was established in 1795 by King Kamehameha I, who unified the Hawaiian Islands under a single government after conquering O'ahu, Maui, Moloka'i, and Lana'i. By 1810, the islands of Kaua'i and Ni'ihau had also joined the kingdom. The kingdom thrived as a constitutional monarchy, recognized internationally for its strategic location and prosperous agriculture, particularly sugar exports. However, in 1893, the monarchy was overthrown by American and European settlers, leading to the eventual annexation of Hawai'i by the United States in 1898.

The Kingdom of the Isles was a maritime realm that existed from the early Middle Ages until the late 13th century. It encompassed the Isle of Man and the Hebrides, along with other smaller islands in the Irish Sea and the west coast of Scotland. The kingdom was initially under Norse control, with Viking settlers establishing dominance in the region. It became a significant power in the Irish Sea, engaging in trade and warfare with neighboring kingdoms. The Kingdom of the Isles experienced fluctuating periods of independence and vassalage to larger powers, such as Norway and Scotland, until it was eventually absorbed into the Kingdom of Scotland in 1266 following the Treaty of Perth.

The Johor Sultanate, established in 1528 by Sultan Alauddin Riayat Shah II, a son of the Malacca Sultan Mahmud Shah, emerged as a significant maritime power in Southeast Asia. Located at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, Johor became a crucial center for trade and diplomacy, often engaging with European colonial powers. The sultanate experienced periods of prosperity and conflict, including the assassination of Sultan Mahmud Shah II in 1699, which led to the rise of the Bendahara dynasty. In the 19th century, Johor modernized under the leadership of Temenggong Daeng Ibrahim and his son, Sultan Abu Bakar, who is often credited with founding the modern Johor state.

The Kedah Sultanate, located on the northern end of the Malay Peninsula (bordering Siam), is one of the oldest sultanates in Southeast Asia, with its origins tracing back to the 3rd century AD. Initially a Hindu-Buddhist kingdom, it is traditionally said to have converted to Islam under Sultan Mudzafar Shah I in 1136 AD - the first ruler in Southeast Asia to do so. Kedah's strategic position made it a vital trading hub, attracting merchants from India, Persia, and Arabia. Over the centuries, it faced invasions and influences from neighboring powers, including the Siamese and the rival Malacca Sultanate. In 1909, Kedah became a British protectorate under the Anglo-Siamese Treaty.

Khandesh, an historical region in northwestern Maharashtra, is situated in India's Tapti River valley. It was originally part of the ancient Abhira kingdom and later came under the rule of various dynasties, including the Delhi Sultanate. In 1382, Malik Ahmad established the independent Khandesh Sultanate, ruled by the Faruqi dynasty, with its capital at Burhanpur. The sultanate flourished as a center of trade and culture until it was annexed by the Mughal Empire in 1601. In the 18th century, Khandesh became part of the Maratha Confederacy and was later incorporated into British India following the Third Anglo-Maratha War in 1818.

The Kamata Kingdom emerged in the late 13th century in the region of present-day Assam and parts of West Bengal, India. It was established by Sandhya, a ruler who moved his capital westward to Kamatapur. The kingdom played a crucial role in the transition from ancient to medieval Assam, encompassing areas that were previously part of the Kamarupa kingdom. The Kamata Kingdom saw the rise of the Khen dynasty, which was later overthrown by Alauddin Hussain Shah of the Bengal Sultanate in 1498. Eventually, the Koch dynasty, founded by Biswa Singha in the early 16th century, took over, leading to the division of the kingdom into Koch Bihar and Koch Hajo.

The Prince-Bishopric of Liège was an ecclesiastical principality within the Holy Roman Empire, established in 980 under Bishop Notger. Located in present-day Belgium, it combined both religious and secular authority, with its bishops holding the title of prince-bishop. The principality played a significant role in the region's political and cultural life, often caught between the influences of neighboring powers such as Burgundy and the Habsburgs. It was a center of learning and art, particularly during the medieval period. The Prince-Bishopric of Liège maintained its autonomy until the Liège Revolution in 1789, after which it was annexed by France in 1795.

The Latin Empire of Constantinople was a feudal Crusader state established in 1204 by the leaders of the Fourth Crusade on lands captured from the Byzantine Empire. Intended to replace the Byzantine Empire as the Western-recognized Roman Empire in the east, it was ruled by a Catholic emperor instead of the Eastern Orthodox Byzantine emperors. The empire's creation was heavily influenced by Venice, which sought to benefit from the new political situation. Despite initial successes, the Latin Empire struggled to maintain control over its territories and faced constant challenges from Byzantine successor states and neighboring powers. It ultimately fell in 1261 when the resurgent Byzantine Empire was restored under the Palaiologos dynasty.

Lucca, a city in Tuscany, Italy, was founded by the Etruscans and later became a Roman colony in 180 BC. Known for its well-preserved Renaissance-era city walls, Lucca was an important city and fortress throughout the centuries. During the Middle Ages, it was a significant center of commerce and culture, maintaining its independence as a city-state until the end of the 18th century. The city boasts numerous historical landmarks, including the Piazza dell'Anfiteatro, the Guinigi Tower, and the Cathedral of San Martino.

Meissen, a town in Saxony, was founded by King Henry I of Germany in 929. It became the seat of the Margraviate of Meissen in 968 and later passed to the House of Wettin in 1089. Meissen is renowned for its porcelain, with the first European hard-paste porcelain being produced there in 1710. The Meissen porcelain factory, established in the Albrechtsburg Castle, became a symbol of luxury and innovation, significantly influencing European ceramics.

Modena was one of those roman colonies founded in 183 B.C. It became a bishopric in the VIIth century. From 1288, Modena was ruled by the Este family. It became a duchy in 1452. The Duke of Modena was a vassal to the Holy Roman Emperor while being at the same time Duke of Ferrara and vassal to the Popes. Modena would become the capital when the Pope seized Ferrara. The ducal palace was completed in 1634. The house of Habsburg inherited the Duchy of Modena in late XVIIIth century. During the French Revolution and Napoleonic wars, Modena became annexed to the Cisalpine Republic and later to the kingdom of Italy. The Duchy was given back to the Habsburgs in 1815.

The Multan Sultanate, also known as the Langah Sultanate, was a late-medieval kingdom established by the Langah clan in 1445. Centered on the city of Multan, in present-day Pakistan, it emerged following the decline of the Delhi Sultanate after Timur's invasion. The sultanate experienced its peak under Sultan Husayn I (1469-1498), who repelled invasions and fostered prosperity, attracting Baloch settlers to the region. The Langah rulers maintained control until 1526, when the sultanate was annexed by the nascent Mughal Empire.

The Duchy of Naxos, also known as the Duchy of the Archipelago, was established in 1207 by the Venetian nobleman Marco Sanudo following the Fourth Crusade. Centered on the islands of Naxos and Paros, it included most of the Cyclades archipelago and represented a blend of Greek and Venetian culture. The duchy became a significant maritime state, facilitating Venetian trade routes in the Aegean Sea. It remained under Venetian control until 1537, when it became a tributary of the Ottoman Empire. The duchy was fully annexed by the Ottomans in 1579, although some islands retained Christian rule until the early 18th century.

Nepal was unified into a centralized state by the great warrior-king Prithvi Narayan Shah in the mid-18th century, but before that had been a patchwork of petty kingdoms spread across the Himalayas from Tibet down to Bihar in India. The most important Nepali kingdom had been Khasa, ruled by the Malla dynasty, who were initially Tibetan Buddhists but had converted to Hinduism as their court and nobility had gradually Indianized over time. By the late Middle Ages, Khasa (later known as Gorkha) had become a thriving mountain kingdom and the northernmost bastion of Hindu religion and culture.

The Empire of Nicaea was a Byzantine Greek state established in 1204 following the Fourth Crusade's capture of Constantinople. Founded by Theodore I Laskaris, it became a refuge for Byzantine aristocracy and a center of resistance against the Latin Empire. The Nicaean Empire played a crucial role in preserving Byzantine traditions and governance during its existence. Under the leadership of the Laskaris and later the Palaiologos dynasties, it successfully recaptured Constantinople in 1261, restoring the Byzantine Empire until its eventual fall to the Ottoman Turks in 1453.

The Christian nation of Nubia succeeded in freeing itself from control of Egypt when the latter became an independent Mohammedan kingdom in 969, but in 1173 Saladin's brother Schems Eddawalah Turanschah advanced from Yemen, destroyed the churches, and carried off the bishop and 70 000 Nubians. In 1275 the Mamluk sultan Djahn Beibars sent an army from Egypt into Nubia. Dongola was conquered, the Christian king David was obliged to flee and the churches were plundered. The inhabitants escaped forcible conversion to Mohammedanism only by payment of a head-tax. Nubia began dissolving into petty states, chief of which was Sennar, which was founded in 1484 by the Funj dynasty. From the Middle Ages there is little information as to the position of Christianity, as Islam became supreme partly by force partly by the amalgamation of the native with the Arabian tribes, but in the mid-16th century the Funji rulers converted to Islam, ending the era of Christianity in Nubia for good. For some time Sennar ruled Shendi, Berber and Dongola. In the eighteenth century the King of Sennar also obtained, for a time, the province of Kordofan.

The Oyo Empire, a prominent Yoruba state in West Africa, was established in the 14th century by Oranmiyan, a prince of the Yoruba Kingdom of Ile-Ife. Located in present-day southwestern Nigeria, Oyo became a dominant force in the region through its strategic use of cavalry and effective administrative structure. At its height between the 17th and 18th centuries, the empire controlled vast territories, including parts of modern-day Benin. Oyo's political system featured a powerful king - the Alaafin - and a complex council of chiefs known as the Oyo Mesi. The empire's influence waned in the 19th century due to internal strife and external pressure from European colonial powers, leading to its eventual collapse in 1896.

Pomerelia, also known as Eastern Pomerania, is an historical region located on the southern shore of the Baltic Sea in northern Poland. It has been inhabited since ancient times, with evidence of the Pomeranian culture dating back to around 500 BC. Throughout its history, Pomerelia has seen various rulers and influences, including the Teutonic Knights who annexed it in the early 14th century. The region was later reintegrated into Poland in 1466 and became part of Royal Prussia. Pomerelia's largest and most important city was Danzig (today Gdansk), which has played a key role in the region's economic and cultural development.

Shirvan is an historical region in the eastern Caucasus with a rich and diverse history dating back to pre-Islamic times. It was known for its strategic location between the Caspian Sea and the Kura River, making it a significant cultural and political center. The region was ruled by the Shirvanshahs, a Persianized dynasty of Arabic origin, from 861 to 1538. The Shirvanshahs were known for their patronage of Persian literature and culture, attracting poets like Khaqani and Nizami Ganjavi. Shirvan's history is marked by periods of independence and vassalage to larger empires, including the Timurids and later the Safavids, who eventually incorporated it into their realm in 1607.

Socotra is an island in the Indian Ocean, southeast of Yemen, that is renowned for its unique biodiversity and alien landscapes. Its location has made it a crossroads for various cultures and empires over the centuries, and it has been visited by Greek, Arab, Persian, Indian and African traders and missionaries. The island was once home to an ancient Eastern Christian community, which is believed to have disappeared in the 17th century. With the exception of a brief period of Portuguese occupation in the early 1500s, Socotra was ruled by the Mahra sultans of Yemen - who brought Islam to the island - until coming under British protection in the 19th century.

The Sosso, an ancient West African kingdom, rose to prominence in the 12th century after the decline of the Ghana Empire. Under the leadership of Sumanguru Kante, the Sosso expanded their territory and exerted control over trade routes in the region. However, their dominance was short-lived: in the early 13th century, they were defeated by the rising Mali Empire under the leadership of Sundiata Keita at the Battle of Kirina in 1235. This defeat marked the end of Sosso's influence and the beginning of Mali's ascendancy in West African history.

Sus was an historical region in southwestern Morocco, located along the coastal plains of the Atlantic and bordered by the Atlas Mountains. From the 11th to the 15th centuries, it was a significant Berber kingdom, part of the broader indigenous Berber presence in North Africa. The kingdom was known for its strategic coastal cities and its role in regional trade networks. The most notable Berber dynasty ruling the region was the Almohad Caliphate, which established its power in the 12th century and integrated Sus into its extensive empire that stretched across North Africa and into Spain. The region was crucial for its agricultural production, trade routes, and as a cultural and political center. By the late 15th century, the rise of the Saadian dynasty and the increasing pressure from European powers led to changes in the region's political landscape, but the legacy of Berber Sus remains an integral part of Moroccan history and heritage.

The Principality of Theodoro was a medieval state located in the Crimean Peninsula, existing from the 11th to the 15th centuries. Established in the region around the fortress of Caffa (modern-day Feodosia) by Byzantine and Genoese colonists, Theodoro was a small yet strategically significant principality that controlled the southern part of Crimea. It was ruled by a dynasty of Crimean Gothic origin from their capital at Mangup, and was able to maintain a degree of independence amidst the shifting power dynamics of the region - including threats from the Mongols, Tatars and later the encroaching Turks. The principality was known for its fortifications and its role in trade and regional diplomacy. By the late 15th century, Theodoro fell to the Ottoman Empire, which absorbed it into its growing territories, marking the end of its political and cultural influence in the Crimea.

The Prince-Bishopric of Trent was an ecclesiastical principality within the Holy Roman Empire, established in 1027 by Emperor Conrad II. It encompassed the region of present-day Trentino in Northern Italy. The prince-bishops of Trent held both religious and secular authority, making it a unique political entity. The bishopric played a significant role in the Counter-Reformation, hosting the Council of Trent from 1545 to 1563, which was pivotal in addressing the challenges posed by the Protestant Reformation. The principality was secularized in 1803 and incorporated into the County of Tyrol under the Habsburgs.

The region of Transylvania was one of the earliest targets of German colonization. The Germans, who were mainly merchants, lived side by side with Hungarians and Romanians, although the three groups never blended well. Up until the mid-16th century the fortunes of Transylvania (called Siebenbürgen in German) was closely tied to those of Hungary, and the two states alternated in control of each other. Following conquest by the Ottoman Turks however, Transylvania was greatly reduced, and made into a puppet kingdom. Over time this state became more and more independent, to the point that it virtually managed its own destiny by the mid-17th century. Following the reconquest of the area by the Austrian Empire, the region was revitalized by new German emigrants arriving from the early 18th century on.

The Archbishopric of Trier was a prominent ecclesiastical state within the Holy Roman Empire, located in what is now western Germany. Established in the 4th century, it evolved into a powerful principality by the Middle Ages, with the Archbishop holding both religious and temporal authority. As one of the seven prince-electors of the Holy Roman Empire, the Archbishop of Trier played a crucial role in electing the Emperor. Trier was known for its impressive Roman and Gothic architecture, including the Trier Cathedral and the Porta Nigra, and was a center of trade and political influence. The archbishopric's authority extended over a substantial territory, which included significant urban and rural areas. By the late 18th century, the Archbishopric of Trier was secularized and incorporated into France during the Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars, ending its long history as a political and religious power.

Utrecht, located in the heart of the Netherlands, has a history that stretches back to Roman times when it was known as Trajectum ad Rhenum. Established around 50 AD as a Roman fortification, it later became a significant religious center with the establishment of a bishopric in 696 AD. Throughout the Middle Ages, Utrecht was a powerful and prosperous town, playing a crucial role in the Low Countries' political and economic development. The signing of the Union of Utrecht in 1579 laid the foundation for the Dutch Republic, and despite being surpassed by Amsterdam during the Dutch Golden Age, Utrecht remained a vibrant city known for its historical architecture and cultural heritage.

The Ming dynasty, ruling China from 1368 to 1644, was a period of native Han Chinese governance between the Mongol Yuan and Manchu Qing dynasties. Founded by Zhu Yuanzhang, who became Emperor Hongwu, the Ming era is noted for its significant cultural, economic, and political influence. The dynasty saw the construction of the Great Wall as it stands today, the flourishing of trade and exploration under Admiral Zheng He, and the production of exquisite porcelain. Despite its initial prosperity, the Ming dynasty eventually faced internal strife, fiscal troubles, and external threats, leading to its fall to, and the rise of, the Qing dynasty.

The Northern Yuan dynasty was the continuation of the Mongol Empire's Yuan dynasty after its expulsion from China in 1368 by the Ming dynasty. Retreating to the Mongolian steppes, the Northern Yuan maintained the legacy of Genghis Khan's lineage, with various khans claiming the title of Great Khan and asserting their rule over the fragmented Mongol tribes. Despite efforts to unify and revive their former glory - notably under rulers like Esen Taishi (who held the Emperor Yingzong captive) and later Dayan Khan - the Northern Yuan struggled with both internal division and external pressure from the Ming dynasty. By the late 17th century, the dynasty effectively dissolved as the Mongols were incorporated into the Qing dynasty, marking the end of the Northern Yuan as a political entity.

The Northern Yuan dynasty was the continuation of the Mongol Empire's Yuan dynasty after its expulsion from China in 1368 by the Ming dynasty. Retreating to the Mongolian steppes, the Northern Yuan maintained the legacy of Genghis Khan's lineage, with various khans claiming the title of Great Khan and asserting their rule over the fragmented Mongol tribes. Despite efforts to unify and revive their former glory - notably under rulers like Esen Taishi (who held the Emperor Yingzong captive) and later Dayan Khan - the Northern Yuan struggled with both internal division and external pressure from the Ming dynasty. By the late 17th century, the dynasty effectively dissolved as the Mongols were incorporated into the Qing dynasty, marking the end of the Northern Yuan as a political entity.

Formosa, now known as Taiwan, has a rich and varied history. The name Formosa - meaning 'beautiful island' - was given by Portuguese sailors in 1542. It was a frontier society, often a colony in name and fact, requiring resourcefulness and determination from its settlers. The island experienced periods of both Dutch and Spanish colonial rule in the 17th century, followed by Han rule during the short-lived Kingdom of Tungning (1661-1683), and in turn direct Qing rule (1683-1895). In 1895, following the First Sino-Japanese War, Taiwan was ceded to Japan under the Treaty of Shimonoseki.

Ferrara, located in the Emilia-Romagna region of northern Italy, has a rich history dating back to at least 753 AD when it was captured by the Lombards. It became an independent commune by the 10th century and flourished under the rule of the Este family from 1240 to 1598. During this period, Ferrara became a significant cultural and artistic center, attracting leading Renaissance artists and intellectuals. The city's historic center, dominated by the impressive Castello Estense and the Gothic Cathedral of San Giorgio, reflects its medieval and Renaissance heritage.

Urbino is an historic city in the Marche region of central Italy, best known for its significance during the Italian Renaissance. The city reached its cultural and political zenith in the 15th century under the rule of Federico da Montefeltro, who became Duke of Urbino in 1444. Federico was a renowned military leader and a passionate patron of the arts and education, transforming Urbino into a vibrant center of Renaissance culture. He commissioned the construction of the Palazzo Ducale, an architectural masterpiece that became a symbol of Renaissance ideals. Urbino attracted artists, scholars, and humanists, including the painter Raphael, who was born there in 1483. The duchy of Urbino eventually came under papal control in the early 16th century.

The Despotate of Epirus was a Byzantine Greek successor state established in 1204 by Michael I Komnenos Doukas following the Fourth Crusade's capture of Constantinople. Initially one of the most powerful Byzantine successor states, it briefly expanded to include parts of Macedonia and Thessaly. However, after the Battle of Klokotnitsa in 1230, its influence waned, and it was eventually reduced to its core territories in Epirus and Thessaly. Despite periods of vassalage and internal strife, the Despotate maintained its autonomy until it was absorbed by the restored Byzantine Empire in 1337. The region experienced a brief resurgence under Carlo I Tocco in the 15th century before falling to the Ottoman Empire in 1479.

The Despotate of Dobruja, also known as the Principality of Karvuna, was a quasi-independent Bulgarian polity that emerged in the mid-14th century. It was established by Balik and later ruled by his son Dobrotitsa, who expanded its territory and influence. The Despotate maintained a degree of autonomy from the Second Bulgarian Empire and was heavily influenced by Byzantine and Vlach attempts to resist further Ottoman expansion into Europe. Its capital was initially Karvuna (modern-day Balchik) before moving to Kaliakra. The Despotate had its own navy and engaged in piracy, which led to conflicts with Genoa. It existed until 1411 when it was incorporated into the Ottoman Empire.

Celje (Also known as Cilli), a city in central Slovenia, has a rich history dating back to Roman times when it was known as Claudia Celeia. It became an important medieval center under the Counts of Celje, who ruled from the 14th to the 15th century and maintained close relations with - and at times served as vassals of - the rulers of Austria and Hungary. The city flourished as a cultural and economic hub, with significant landmarks like the Celje Castle, which remains a prominent historical site. Despite suffering damage during various conflicts, Celje has preserved its historical charm and continues to be a vital cultural center in Slovenia.

The Principality of Zeta was a medieval Serbian state that existed from the late 14th century until the early 16th century in modern-day Montenegro and parts of northern Albania. Originally part of the Serbian Empire, Zeta emerged as a semi-independent principality following the decline of centralized imperial authority after the death of Emperor Dušan in 1355. The Balsic family was the most prominent dynasty to rule Zeta, with the principality often serving as a buffer state between the powerful Ottoman Empire to the east and the Venetian Republic to the west. The final truly independent Zetan prince was Balsa III, whose premature death in 1421 left the rump principality to be slowly devoured by its neighbours.

Pisa's history dates back to ancient times, with evidence of Etruscan and Roman settlements. Pisa flourished as a maritime republic in the 11th and 12th centuries, becoming a powerful trading and naval center. The city played a significant role in the Crusades, securing valuable commercial positions in the Mediterranean. Despite its defeat by Genoa in the Battle of Meloria in 1284, Pisa remained an important cultural and economic hub. Today, Pisa is celebrated for its rich architectural heritage, including the Piazza dei Miracoli, which houses the Leaning Tower, the Cathedral, and the Baptistery.

Moravia was initially inhabited by Celtic tribes and later became part of the Roman Empire. In the 9th century, it was the center of Great Moravia, a significant Slavic state that played a crucial role in the spread of Christianity in the region. After the fall of Great Moravia, the area came under the control of the Bohemian Crown and later the Habsburg Monarchy.

Cephalonia (Corfu), the largest of the Ionian Islands in western Greece, was initially inhabited by the Illyrian tribe of the Histri, and was later dominated by four city-states: Pale, Cranii, Same, and Pronnoi. The island played a role in significant historical events, such as the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars. Conquered by the Romans in 187 BC, Cephalonia became a strategic naval base. Throughout the medieval period, it changed hands multiple times, experiencing periods of Byzantine, Norman, and Venetian rule. Following the turmoil of the Napoleonic Wars, Cephalonia became a British protectorate until it was eventually gifted to the modern Greek state in 1864.

The Il-Khanate, established in 1256 by Hülegü Khan, a grandson of Genghis Khan, was a Mongol khanate that ruled over much of present-day Iran, Iraq, and parts of Turkey, Armenia, and Afghanistan. It was part of the larger Mongol Empire but operated semi-independently. The Il-Khanate is notable for its conquest of Baghdad in 1258, which led to the fall of the Abbasid Caliphate. Over time, the Il-Khanate's predominantly Buddhist and Eastern Christian rulers converted to Islam, and the region saw a blend of Mongol and Persian cultures. The Il-Khanate eventually disintegrated in the mid-14th century due to civil war and the impact of the Black Death.

Samogitia is an historical and ethnographic region in northwestern Lithuania, and its name means 'lowlands' - distinguishing it from the 'highlands' of neighboring Aukstaitija. The region has a rich history, marked by its steadfast pagan resistance to the Teutonic Knights during the medieval period, notably winning the Battle of Durbe in 1260. The Duchy of Samogitia maintained a high degree of autonomy within the Grand Duchy of Lithuania until the Union of Lublin in 1569, at which point it became a province of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. The region was known for its distinct culture, language, and traditions, which have been preserved over centuries.

The Principality of Yaroslavl was a medieval Russian state that existed from the early 13th century until its annexation by the Grand Duchy of Moscow in 1463. Centered around the city of Yaroslavl, located along the Volga River, the principality was founded by Prince Vsevolod the Big Nest's son, Konstantin Vsevolodovich, and played a strategic role in the northeastern Rus' lands. Yaroslavl was a significant trade and cultural center, known for its development of architecture and iconography. Throughout its history, the principality maintained relative autonomy, even as it came under the influence of more powerful neighboring states like the Grand Duchy of Vladimir and later Moscow. The integration of Yaroslavl into Moscow marked a step in the consolidation of the Russian territories under Moscow's control, contributing to the eventual formation of the centralized Russian state.

The history of Masovia can be traced back to the first half of the 11th century when one of the Polish nobles, called Maslaw, declared Masovia his own state. It lasted only about two decades. The Duchy of Masovia was created in 1138 when Poland was broken down into 4 princedoms. In theory the Grand Duke was the ruler of all Polish provinces but he met strong opposition led by other remnants of the Piast dynasty. The feudal process of dividing the country into small political entities progressed, granting independence to the strongest of the princedoms. During the renewal of the Kingdom of Poland in the late 13th century and early 14th century, part of Masovia was vassalized by the Bohemian King, Jan Luxembourg, in 1329. The remaining part became a vassal of Poland in 1351. The Masovian princes were in a dire position. All surrounding forces - the Teutonic Order, Poland, and Bohemia - were interested in annexing these terrains. Moreover, Lithuania was not an easy neighbour and some wars were fought. Playing a delicate political game, Masovia maintained its independence into the 15th century, allying with Poland against the Teutons during the Great War of 1409-1411. The last Masovian princes led the happy life of squanderers. The parts of Masovia, like Duchy of Plock (once a vassal of Bohemia), County of Rawa, and others, were annexed by Poland at the deaths of their rulers in the second half of the 15th century. The whole line eventually died out in 1526 and the main Duchy of Czersk-Warsaw was annexed by Poland.

The Mongols under Genghis Khan, swept into Iran, the Caucasus, and southern Russia in 1220-22. His successors attacked Persia in 1231, Eastern Europe in 1236-41, and Iraq and the Caucasus again in 1245-53. They finally sacked Baghdad in 1258, bringing an end to the Abbasid Caliphate. The Mongol territories were divided among the sons and grandsons of Genghis. The eldest son, Jochi, settled in Russia with his followers, the Golden Horde. This group divided into two main sections, the Blue Horde (also called Golden Horde by many historians) and the White Horde, led by Batu and Orda, two of the sons of Jochi. The White Horde covered the Eastern part of the Khanate. Both Hordes were united with in 1378 by Toqtamïsh in the Golden Horde.

Puerto Rico, an island in the northeastern Caribbean, has a rich history shaped by various cultures and influences. Originally inhabited by the Taíno people, it was claimed by Spain in 1493 during Christopher Columbus' second voyage. The island became a crucial military and economic outpost for the Spanish Empire, enduring numerous attacks from rival European powers. In 1898, following the Spanish-American War, Puerto Rico was ceded to the United States.

The Sukhothai Kingdom was a post-classical Siamese kingdom (mandala) in Mainland Southeast Asia surrounding the ancient capital city of Sukhothai in present-day north-central Thailand. The kingdom was founded by Si Inthrathit in 1238 and existed as an independent polity until 1438, when it fell under the influence of the neighboring Ayutthaya after the death of Borommapan (Maha Thammaracha IV). Sukhothai was originally a trade center in Lavo, itself under the suzerainty of the Khmer Empire, when Central Thai people led by Pho Khun Bang Klang Hao, a local leader, revolted and gained their independence. Bang Klang Hao took the regnal name of Si Inthrathit and became the first monarch of the Phra Ruang dynasty. The kingdom was centralized and expanded to its greatest extent during the reign of Ram Khamhaeng the Great (1279–1298), who some historians considered to have introduced Theravada Buddhism and the initial Thai script to the kingdom. Ram Khamhaeng also initiated relations with Yuan China, through which the kingdom developed the techniques to produce and export ceramics like sangkhalok ware. After the reign of Ram Khamhaeng, the kingdom fell into decline. In 1349, during the reign of Li Thai (Maha Thammaracha I), Sukhothai was invaded by the Ayutthaya Kingdom, a neighboring Thai polity. It remained a tributary state of Ayutthaya until it was annexed by the kingdom in 1438 after the death of Borommapan. Despite this, the Sukhothai nobility continued to influence the Ayutthaya monarchy in centuries after through the Sukhothai dynasty.

The Jarwanid dynasty of Al-Haasa was an Arab dynasty that ruled Eastern Arabia in the 14th century. The Jarwanids belonged to the clan of Bani Malik. It is disputed whether they belonged to the Banu Uqayl — the tribe of their predecessors the Usfurids and their successors the Jabrids — or to the Banu Abdul Qays, to whom the Uyunid dynasty (1076-1235) belonged. The Jarwanids came to power some time in the 14th century, after expelling the forces of Sa'eed ibn Mughamis, the chief of the Muntafiq tribe based in the Iraqi city of Basrah. Contemporary sources such Ibn Battuta and Ibn Hajar describe the Jarwanids as being 'extreme Rawafidh,' a term for Shi'ites who rejected the first three Caliphs, while a 15th-century Sunni scholar from Egypt describes them as being 'remnants of the Qarmatians.'  However, the Twelver Shi'ite sect was promoted under their rule, and Twelver scholars held the judgeships and other important positions, including the chief of the hisba. Also, unlike under the Qarmatians, Islamic prayers were held in the mosques under Jarwanid rule, and prayer was called under the Shi'ite formula. A Twelver scholar of the 14th century, Jamaluddeen Al-Mutawwa', belonged to the house of Jarwan. Jarwanid rule came to an end in the 15th century at the hands of the Jabrids, a clan of the Banu Uqayl Bedouins.

The small Hindu kingdom of Bima, on the eastern side of Sumbawa Island in Indonesia, has a shrouded history prior to the 14th century. Though it may well have been a nominal vassal of the Majapahit Empire, it does not seem to have been subject to any interference, and likely survived due to its lucrative trade in slaves and local sappanwood. Islam was spread during the early 17th century by the Gowa (Makassar) sultanate, which soon led to Bima embracing the new religion and becoming a significant regional power. The Dutch East India Company exerted increasing influence over Bima during the 17th century, and following several decisive victories they had integrated the island into their colonial empire by 1670.

Bali was first settled by Austronesian peoples in around 2000 BC, and over the centuries has absorbed influences from Indian, Chinese, and Javanese cultures - particularly during its period as a Majapahit vassal state (1343-1512). Following the fall of the Majapahit Empire to its Muslim vassal the Demak Sultanate in the 16th century, Bali became a sanctuary for Hindu refugees fleeing the spread of Islam in Java. Despite intermittent periods of civil war and foreign rule, the island's unique blend of Hindu, Buddhist and local animistic traditions has endured.

The Kingdom of Bastar, located in present-day Chhattisgarh, India, was founded in 1324 AD by Annama Deva - a brother of the last Kakatiya king, Pratapa Rudra Deva - on the instruction of the local goddess Danteshwari. Bastar was known for its rich tribal culture and dense forests, and its capital Jagdalpur is still famed for its beautiful scenic waterfalls. Fiercely independent, the Rajas of Bastar resisted foreign incursion until eventually falling under Maratha suzerainty in the late 18th century. With the rise of the British Raj, Bastar became a princely state in 1803, and joined the Union of India in 1948.

The Chola Empire, originating in the fertile Kaveri River valley in southern India, was one of the longest-ruling dynasties in history, flourishing from the 9th to the 13th centuries AD. At its zenith, the Chola Empire extended its influence over much of South India, Sri Lanka, and even parts of Southeast Asia, including the Malay Peninsula. Renowned for their naval prowess, the Cholas were instrumental in promoting trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Under the reigns of illustrious rulers like Rajaraja Chola I and his son Rajendra Chola I, the empire saw remarkable achievements in architecture, literature, and administration. The construction of grand monuments like the Brihadisvara Temple at Thanjavur are a testament to their legacy.

The Gupta Empire, which flourished from around 320 to 550 AD, is often heralded as the Golden Age of Indian history due to its remarkable achievements in arts, science, and culture. Founded by Chandragupta I, the empire expanded significantly under his successors, particularly Samudragupta and Chandragupta II, covering much of northern and central India. This period saw significant advancements in mathematics, astronomy, and literature, with the creation of the decimal system and notable works like the Kamasutra and the plays of Kalidasa. The Gupta era is also marked by impressive architectural feats, including the construction of temples and universities, such as Nalanda. Despite its eventual decline due to internal collapse and invasion by the Hunas, the Gupta Empire left a lasting legacy on Indian civilization.

Jaintia (also known as Jaintiapur, after its capital) was an ancient hill kingdom located in present-day Meghalaya, India, and parts of Sylhet, Bangladesh. Established around 500 AD, it was ruled by the Syiem Sutnga clan and known for its unique blend of indigenous tribal (Niamtre) and Hindu cultural influences. Jaintia's territory extended from the Jaintia Hills to the plains of Sylhet north of the Barak river, and its isolation and rugged terrain allowed it to maintain its independence for over a millennium. It was briefly annexed into the Ahom Kingdom (Assam) in the early 18th century, and later drew the interest of the British, who desired its lime quarries. Following a minor diplomatic incident, the British East India Company annexed Jaintia in 1835.

The Khemundi Kingdom, located in present-day Orissa, India, was established in the early 14th century by Narashingha Deba, a son of the Eastern Ganga (Orissa) monarch Bhanudeva II. The kingdom included the regions of Paralakhemundi, Badakhemundi and Sanakhemundi, which were initially unified under a single Raja but after 1608 split into smaller 'estates' ruled by separate cadet branches. The Khemundi rulers maintained their influence and independence through a strategic policy of shifting alliances with neighbouring states, even as the region came under effective British control in 1768. The final Khemundi king, Maharaja Krushna Chandra Gajapati, later became the first prime minister of India's Orissa Province.

The Maurya Empire, established by Chandragupta Maurya in 322 BC, was the first empire to unify most of the Indian subcontinent. With its capital at Pataliputra (modern-day Patna), the empire expanded under Chandragupta and his successors, including Bindusara and the renowned Ashoka. Ashoka's reign marked a significant era of prosperity and cultural development, especially after his conversion to Buddhism following the brutal Kalinga War. He promoted non-violence, religious tolerance, and the spread of Buddhism across Asia. The Mauryan administration was highly organized, featuring a standing army and a sophisticated civil service. Despite its eventual decline around 185 BC, the Maurya Empire left a lasting legacy on Indian history and governance.

The Punjab was the cradle of Sikhism, where the faith was first spread by its founder Guru Nanak in the late 15th century. By the mid-18th century, the loose coalition of autonomous Sikh states (known as misls) had been consolidated into the Sikh Confederacy under the leadership of figures like Jassa Singh Ahluwalia and Nawab Kapur Singh in order to resist Mughal and Afghan invasions. The Confederacy laid the groundwork for the Sikh Empire, established by Maharaja Ranjit Singh in 1799. Ranjit Singh unified the misls and expanded the empire, creating a powerful independent state in the Punjab renowned for its military prowess and religious tolerance. It reached its zenith in the early 19th century but, following the two Anglo-Sikh Wars, eventually fell to the British East India Company in 1849.

Volga Bulgaria was a medieval state that existed from the late 9th century until its conquest by the Mongols in the mid-13th century. It was situated on the confluence of the Volga and Kama Rivers in what is now Tatarstan in European Russia, and began life as a vassal of the Khazar Khaganate. Founded by the Bulgars, a Turkic people, it became a significant trading hub due to its strategic location between the Rus' principalities, Byzantine Empire, and the Cuman and Avar confederations. The state converted to Islam in 922 AD under the rule of Almis Khan, fostering cultural and economic ties with the powerful Abbasid Caliphate. From its great capital at Bolghar (and later Bilär), Volga Bulgaria thrived as an independent and comparatively centralized multi-ethnic state for three centuries, dominating the Eurasian Steppe and its lucrative slave trade. Its legacy lives on in the form of modern Bulgaria, which was formed by the Bulgar Khan Asparuh in 681 AD.

The Kingdom of Wessex was founded around 519 AD by the West Saxon chieftain Cerdic, and over time became the preeminent Anglo-Saxon state within the Heptarchy. It expanded significantly during the reigns of the early kings Ine (688-726) and Ecgberht (802-839), who consolidated West Saxon power and extended the kingdom's territory. Wessex played a crucial role in resisting the Viking invasions of the 9th century, particularly during the reign of Alfred the Great (871-886), who fortified the kingdom and laid the groundwork for a unified English state. This feat was finally achieved by Alfred's grandson Æthelstan in 927, at which point the history of Wessex becomes that of the Kingdom of England.
